column121: On flight to ZZZ; our right engine vibration was trending high in the green for most of climbout until level at cruise (1.2-1.6); at cruise it momentarily went into amber around 1.8. We ran QRH; reduced power; that helped. On descent; vibration went to amber around 2.2 while idle; ran QRH; problem persisted at both higher and low powers; as well as both high and low altitudes. We had one last amber vibration indication while on final at ZZZ; decided to discontinue the approach and take delay vectors to problem solve; ultimately requested priority handling and flew the approach as a single engine like approach; with right engine idle but not shut down; to keep the vibration lower in the green.
column123: High engine vibration gauge and airframe vibrations progressively deteriorated into a critical condition.QRH was accomplished.  No improvement noted.    Max vibration gauge readings were 2.2 and eventually one engine had to remain at idle power.  Single engine approach and landing was reviewed and accomplished.  Dispatch was notified. Communication with flight attendants was clear.   A Calming PA was made to passengers noting an engine vibration; normally landing expected with a possibility of seeing some emergency vehicles as only a precaution.  To add additional safety margine; the crew selected the longest runway with ILS.   A flaps 20 landing was safe and uneventful with smooth touchdown.  Fuel was at 3100lbs at landing due to good time management and fuel management.  The first officer and the flight attendants all did a great job.  Passengers seemed calm and content as they deplaned safely at the gate with no injuries of any type reported to me by anyone.  Maintenance Control reported that the engine did not have visible damage and we discussed the vibrations in detail with the maintenance team.  The duty pilot was called soon after the event and he gave helpful insights and a debrief. Cause: Engine vibration was higher than normal; but within limits during the climbout.  The vibrations started going out of normal limits in cruise; but they were controllable and brought back within limits by a small reduction in aircraft speed. Later  toward the end of the flight; The vibration became more severe. We could not always reduce and manage the vibration level. We had to keep the engine at idle power to keep vibration level within limits. This led to a priority handling request and flaps 20 landing.Suggestions: Please consider installing a second FMS in every Air Carrier X aircraft that now has only one FMS on the left hand side of the flight deck.  Efficiency would be increased in critical events when communicating with dispatch via ACARS.  Both pilots could reach the FMS easier;  Jumping between navigation functions and communication with dispatchers would be more streamlined. Efficiency is especially important in time critical situations or when fuel onboard is getting low. With two FMS units; all required tasks are finished quicker and the plane is ready to land in less time. It can be a safety risk when there is just one FMS during a time-critical event.  I hope that management considers funding the optional second FMS to reduce risk during critical situations.

column121: I; FO (First Officer) was pilot flying. Approaching CMH Captain and I requested ILS 10L and we briefed the potential of getting a short final from approach. Prior to departing PAYJJ we already got cleared down to 3000 and I am at 210 kts. ATC turned us onto base inside of MESRE and Captain advise to active vectors and I agreed. I also began to put out flaps 1 and further slow down. We then got cleared for the visual for 10L. Worried that we are close to the localizer and may overshot it; I went direct to CCREW so that FMS will capture the final approach course; and Captain reminded me that we are above glideslope and needed to come down as we were still at 3000. Initially I selected 2300 for altitude at CCREW and activated FLCH to catch up with the glideslope; then I realized that this was a visual approach and I can go down to field altitude+1000 so both Captain and I agreed to select 1800 ft. The problem was that things were happening very quickly and I didn't realize I was still in FLCH. As I put out more flaps and drop the gear; descent rate began to skyrocket. Realizing that I may about to exceed 2000 FPM below 2000 ft AGL rule I immediately clicked off the Autopilot and manually leveled off at 2000 ft as Captain verbalized 'descent rate'. This is when the controller issued us a low altitude alert and advise us to check our altimeter setting. Right after the alert was issued we intercepted the glideslope. After this the approach proceeded mostly normally; we established on the localizer and glideslope and was configured at 1000 ft and stable at 500; but perhaps I was still a bit shaken by the event I accidentally got high around 200 ft AGL and had to initiate a go-around. The go-around proceeded normally and we landed without further incident.
column123: I was PM; the FO (First Officer) was PF this flight. We were vectored into a right base for night visual approach to Runway 10L. We were slowing and configuring appropriately. We were cleared for the visual; the FO selected 'direct to' the FAF in MCDU instead of intercepting the final in heading; I confirmed. I recommended setting 1800 MSL in the Alt Sel and VNAV to ensure a steady descent as we intercepted the localizer and glideslope. I confirmed 1800 set; called Tower for landing clearance and selected gear down and flaps 3 as the FO called them. Contrary to the plan; the FO left the vertical mode in green FLCH; resulting in descent rate increasing with additional drag. I saw the descent rate increasing towards but not exceeding 2000 FPM; and commanded an immediate level off. The FO immediately disengaged the Autopilot and leveled the aircraft; at 2000 ft MSL from what I remember. As we leveled; the Tower issued a low altitude alert. We responded and corrected on the glide-slope; as we were centered on the localizer as well. We continued the approach stable from that point; until at approximately 200 ft above touchdown then FO became too high on the glide-slope and I commanded a go-around. A normal go around below 1000 ft was flown; and we vectored back around for an ILS to 10L with a normal landing. I mentored the FO on the hazards of using FLCH at altitudes near the ground on approach; and especially that it is not appropriate for a visual with an altitude below the FAF.

column121: Just after level off @ FL330; approximately 40min into flight; the DOOR FWD CARGO EICAS Caution illuminated. At Captain's direction and as PM; I immediately accessed the electronic-checklist; on the lower Control Display Panel (CDU); while pulling up the DOOR SYNOPTIC on my Multi-function Flight Display (MFD). DOOR SYNOPTIC indicated the FWD CARGO DOOR open; with no indication of depressurization or airframe vibration (ever). Captain transferred aircraft control to me; then requested priority handling to ZZZ [ARTCC] and asked for/cleared for a descent to 8000 feet (per checklist) and a turn back toward ZZZ1; initially given direct; w/ subsequent routing provided later. Captain called the Relief Pilot (newly settled in the crew rest bunk) to return forward. Captain contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control to inform them of our situation and pending return. He then briefed crew and passengers to inform all of the plan. We agreed to dump fuel given the gusty crosswinds at ZZZ1. I suspended the DOOR FWD CARGO electronic-checklist since we could not complete until level @ 8;000.'  Per Captain; I began the Fuel Jettison Checklist. We subsequently dumped down to landing weight; completing fuel dump about 75 miles North of ZZZ1; then completed the remaining items in DOOR FWD CARGO checklist & the DESCENT checklist. Step 1 of DESCENT Checklist; Recall & Notes; did not indicate any additional concerns/considerations from the EICAS or the non-normal checklist notes. While cruising at 8000 feet DOOR FWD CARGO EICAS Caution went away; as did the open indication on the DOOR SYNOPTIC. The remainder of arrival/approach was uneventful. When queried by ZZZ1 [Tower] Controller; we told them we'd like to clear the runway and return to the gate XX; w/ no assistance required. NOTE; auto speed brake did not deploy initially upon touchdown/in ground mode. I watched it for ~2 extra seconds. As I was preparing to verbalize 'speed brake;' the handle finally tracked aft to the proper position. Autobrakes appeared to work normally. We did not have any trouble w/ deceleration or stopping the aircraft. Upon clearing the runway XXR and crossing runway XXL; I accomplished After Landing Flow; verified completion w/ electronic-checklist then pulled up the Status Page; curious to see if additional messages appeared on landing in light of the delayed auto speed brake deployment. Status Page indicated the following messages: 1) AUTO SPEEDBRAKE; 2) GEAR INDICATION SYS; & 3) PASSENGER ADDRESS. Upon completion of PARKING Checklist & debrief; we discussed whether to continue or not and agreed fatigue is an issue and would get worse w/ an uncertain timeline. All agreed to not continue. Operations Rep; Chief Pilot (Crew Scheduling through Chief Pilot) and Maintenance personnel were extremely responsive after we opened the aircraft door. Overall; the event was relatively straight-forward and we brought it to a successful conclusion w/ effective communication and CRM; along w/ great support from all parties.

column121: Approaching the ZZZZZ fix in cruise at FL370; we received a PIREP from Airbus at FL350 of Severe Turbulence in the area. We were approximately 10 min from that area. As we approached the area; the airspeed started to increase; indicating a mountain wave. The thrust levers were restarted to idle and the speed brake were deployed to arrest the increasing airspeed. With both action accomplished; the speed continued to increase into the 'barber pole'. The speed was approximately 10 KTS above the barber pole for about 5 to 7 seconds. We had a climb of 500 feet from FL370 to FL375. As the altitude leveled; at FL375; it began to descent at FL367. Shortly afterwards; the aircraft stabilized at FL370. We requested lower altitude to ZZZ ATC and we were given a block altitude of FL370 to FL330. We sent a PIREP and informed Dispatch of the event. We later called Maintenance Control to inform them of the event as well as submitting a maintenance write up. We proceeded to ZZZ without further incident. We called the Chief Pilot on arrival to ZZZ to verbally report the incident.

column121: During the climb out of ZZZ enroute to ZZZ1; the crew noticed the #1 engine vibe was at 4.3. The Captain (PF) passed the controls and radios to the FO (First Officer) and went to the 'Engine High Vibration' checklist in the FM (Flight Manual). The level off at cruise altitude of FL380 coincided with the checklist step of 'retarding thrust' to try and bring the vibe within limits. As the thrust reduced below 95%; the vibe started to decrease. At cruise altitude (.76M) the vibe maintained between 1.7-2.3 (82-88% N1). All other engine indications were normal. After completion of the 'Engine High Vibration' checklist; the Captain (PM) coordinated a call with Dispatch and Maintenance Control. After discussions with this team and with the FO; the Captain made the decision to return to ZZZ and treat the engine as if it could not produce full thrust. The Captain (PM) took the radios back; requested priority handling and coordinated a return to ZZZ. He then spoke with the FAs (flight attendants) and then the passengers to inform them of our return to ZZZ due to a mechanical issue. The crew ran the 'One Engine Inoperative Landing' checklist to set up for an approach/landing with a reduced thrust engine (flaps 15). ATC asked what runway was preferred and we coordinated for Runway XXR due to its location on the west side of the field. At a good breaking point in the 'One Engine Inoperative' checklist the crew briefed the approach/landing plan. When everyone was comfortable and passing 12000' the Captain took the controls back and the FO resumed PM duties. ATC vectored the aircraft to a 15 NM final for the visual approach XXR (with ILS backup). Emergency equipment was not requested; but was standing by on the field. The Captain completed an uneventful flaps 15 landing and then taxied to the gate. After shutdown; Maintenance inspected the #1 Engine and noted several fan blades that had broken off and damaged the abradable shroud. The crew (pilots and FAs) were all moved to another aircraft and successfully completed the flight to ZZZ1.
column123: Normal takeoff and climb out of ZZZ. At approximately FL370; the First Officer noticed an engine vibration out of limits on the number one engine. I noticed an indication of 4.3 units. Upon leveling at FL380; the power levers retarded and the engine returned to within limits; however still indicating higher than engine two. I passed the controls to the First Officer and informed him to handle routine comms. I opened up the engine high vibration checklist. As instructed by the checklist I initiated a call with my Dispatcher and Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control verified that a 4.3 indication is an exceedance. I asked him for a recommendation to continue or turn around from a maintenance standpoint as the aircraft would be down for maintenance wherever we landed. He informed me that Maintenance Control is not allowed to make recommendations. I identified the threat being unable to achieve max continuous thrust on the number one engine; and I recalled that in the FM (Flight Manual); I would need to complete the one engine inoperative landing checklist and land flaps 15. I discussed this with the First Officer and we checked our fuel requirements to return to ZZZ. We agreed that this was the most conservative action and to execute the return. I informed Dispatch via radio that we would be returning to ZZZ. I chose to request priority handling due to not knowing if the number one engine condition would worsen leading to an engine shutdown. We received an immediate 180 degree turn; and proceeded directly to ZZZ. I then took time to inform the flight attendants that we would be landing back in ZZZ due to an engine malfunction; approximately 45 minutes till landing and that there was no intent to evacuate. I also made a PA announcement to the passengers; trying to be honest but not cause anyone to panic about the engine malfunction; and that we would work with the company to get them back to ZZZ1 after landing. The First Officer did a great job keeping me informed of ATC clearances and flying the aircraft with no auto throttles. I ran the one engine inoperative landing checklist as we descended back into ZZZ. XXR was in use per ATIS. We calculated landing distance from the charts and found XXR to be sufficient. We could have requested XXL which would have given us an extra 4000 ft of landing distance. I briefed the visual XXR backed up with the ILS. I completed the deferred items descent checklist; and took the controls. In hindsight I should have taken the controls back then asked for the deferred items. We received vectors to final XXR; configured to flaps 15 and completed an uneventful approach and landing. We checked engine indications after landing and elected to taxi to the gate coordinated by Dispatch. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) met us on the taxiway and followed us to the gate. We debriefed in the aircraft and reviewed required calls and reports per the FOM. Maintenance came to the flight deck and showed us pictures of multiple fan blades missing from the number one engine.

column121: During takeoff from ZZZ; shortly after raising the gear we got a Master Caution light. I punched the Master Caution light to extinguish the light until we were able to look at it once we were safely airborne. The gear and flaps both came up normally; although I did notice it took a little longer for the flaps to go from 1 to up and leading edge lights out. Once we were safely away from the ground and above the terrain I hit the Master Caution recall and say the HYD annunciator illuminated on the FO's (First Officer's) panel. I looked up to the overhead panel and saw that both the left and right engine Hydraulic switches were in the OFF position with the resulting low pressure lights illuminated. I turned them both on and the annunciator extinguished as did both low pressure lights. We continued to ZZZ1 with no further issues. How the switches ended up in the off position I'm at a loss to explain. During the Before Push checklist; I remember looking at the switches and seeing the two low pressure lights illuminated (as usual with both engines off) and normal hydraulic pressure readings. Now I have to wonder if I just saw the two normal low pressure lights and the two electrical pump switches on and just saw what I normally see and missed the two engine pump switches being in the off position. But these switches being in the wrong position should have been caught twice during the two Master Recall checks in the After Start and Before Takeoff checklists yet they weren't and I don't know why. Nothing ever illuminated in front of me on my recall panel or my Master Caution light during both checks. We wondered if maybe we had a Master Caution recall panel issue that might need to be written up; so when we landed in ZZZ1; while parked waiting on marshallers I turned off each engine hydraulic switch one at a time and then back on and the Master Caution and Recall worked properly both times. My FO and I debriefed the issue and how it might have happened. We still don't know how the switches ended up in the off position. He didn't recall turning them off at any time. He did say he turned on the electric pumps during his ground ops set up due to gusty winds. As for the lack of a Master Recall alerts; I mentioned that I have seen numerous times where my FO's have pushed the Recall panel and then immediately subconsciously immediately hit the Master Caution light extinguishing an annunciator that was lit. I happened to catch them because the annunciator was on my recall panel (example FLT CNTRL when the yaw damper kicked off) and I was able to fix the issue. Since the HYD light is on the FO panel; I would not have seen it and been able to intervene if this is indeed what happened. Since the system worked properly on the ground in ZZZ1; this is the only plausible explanation I can come up with.
column123: As the FO (First Officer) I was the PF on this leg. Everything appeared normal until takeoff roll; but after raising the gear a HYD annunciation displayed. I maintained aircraft control and continued the takeoff while the Captain punched off the light. The gear came up normally and we raised the flaps. They came up but at a slower rate than usual. It was then that the Captain performed the recall and noticed the LOW PRESSURE lights on the ENG (Engine) HYD switches and observed the ENG HYD switches were in the off position. He then switched them back on and the Master Caution panel cleared. The rest of the flight to ZZZ1 was uneventful.After replaying the morning events in my mind I believe I know how the switches ended up in that position. I entered the aircraft first; and the winds were gusty and the yoke was moving all around; so one of the first things I did was turn on the electric hydraulic pumps to keep the yoke stable. I believe the aircraft was left with all 4 HYD switches in the OFF position; but in a cursory glance to turn the ELEC HYD switches on; that did not register. I then continued to set up the aircraft and perform my flows. What I believe happed was that during my overhead panel flow; I saw two HYD switches ON and 2 switches OFF and that looked normal to me; except it was the opposite of usual; as the 2 ENG switches were OFF and the ELEC switches were on. Then later when the gate agent came in; I was in the lavatory so the usual trigger for me to double check those switches and turn on the ELEC switches didn't happen. We got to the Before Push Checklist but since the ELEC switches were ON; the system pressure was good and I did not look directly at the switches to check all 4 were ON. At that point we started engines and taxied out and had all normal indications. I performed both RECALL checks for AFTER START and BEFORE TAKEOFF and did not perceive a HYD light on the caution panel. I do not believe HYD ever displayed during the RECALL checks as I have made the mistake of quickly punching off the Caution in the past; and have adopted the technique of verbalizing during single engine taxi After Start Checks 3 lights" prior to punching it off. This was a 2 engine taxi in this case; and I did not expect to see any RECALL lights so I think if they annunciated I would have verbalized them; but it's possible that I inadvertently punched them off; or that the light just did not illuminate. We then performed the takeoff and after raising the gear handle the HYD light annunciated."

column121: After landing at ZZZ; we taxied to the assigned gate and came to a complete stop. The Captain set the parking brake; shut down engine 1 (2 was already shut off) and called for the shutdown checklist. I began the shutdown checklist; which starts with verifying the parking brake is set. Both the Captain and I visually confirmed the parking brake light was illuminated; indicating the brake was set.  The Captain called for the shutdown checklist as normal. While completing the checklist; I looked up and noticed the gate agent standing behind his controls and noticed the jet bridge begin to move. Shortly after; the gate agent exited his position and began waving his arms to get our attention.  The Captain and I looked at him momentarily; and he then made a hand signal indicating the parking brake. At that time; we realized the parking brake release pin was loose and the parking brake had disengaged.  No aircraft movement occurred that resulted in damage; and no injuries to passengers; crew; or ground personnel were reported. The situation was identified promptly and addressed.  Cause: The parking brake release pin being loose.Suggestions: After discussing the event; we confirmed we followed AOM procedures and checklist triggers stating; after the aircraft is parked at the gate with the parking brake set." The brake indication light was illuminated at the time and the aircraft should have been getting chocked while we completed the short checklist.  Moving forward; we will continue to stay heads up (not looking down at the checklist) until we receive the chocks in hand signal before continuing with the shutdown checklist."
column123: After arriving at Gate XX in ZZZ; the parking brake was set; and the I accomplished the Captain's shutdown flow. I then asked the First Officer for the Shutdown checklist. She began reading the checklist shortly after. While reading the checklist; we verified the Parking Brake ON indicator was illuminated and continued the checklist. Meanwhile; after noticing the indicator was dim; I reached up and turned off panel backlighting and verified the indicator became bright. The checklist was completed as usual. The chocks-in hand or wand signal had not been received before or while the checklist was being read. The First Officer and I looked towards the jet bridge and its operator at the controls through my side window and noticed apparent movement. The operator exited his control stand frantically waving his hands to get our attention and then signaled to set brakes. I then looked at the ground and noticed the aircraft was rolling backwards. At that time; I slowly applied toe brakes and brought the aircraft to a gentle stop; noticed the parking brake was disengaged; the release pin was loose; and carefully set the parking brake. After the aircraft was verified to be stationary and verifying the parking brake ON indicator was illuminated; I opened the Direct Vision window; made verbal contact with the jet bridge operator; who then advised me the aircraft rolled backwards too far and needed to be towed back into position. We established communication with the ground Crew Chief via headset and formulated a plan to move the aircraft forward. I switched the Fasten Seatbelts sign on; notified the flight attendants that passengers would need to take their seats; and advised the Crew Chief it was safe to tow the aircraft forward. The Parking Brake was set; toe brakes were held; and chocks-in was verified verbally via headset with the Crew Chief before conducting the shutdown checklist once again. Maintenance Control was contacted via phone advising them of the discrepancy; and the aircraft was placed out of service. A report was filled out and submitted. After speaking with the gate agent and ramp Crew Chief; no damage was sustained to ground equipment or the aircraft; and no personnel injuries were reported. Cause: Possible mechanical failure of the parking brake handle and/or release mechanism. Heads down during and after completing a checklist. Suggestions: The AOM was referenced and reviewed. My First Officer and I verified we were in compliance with AOM procedures. In the future; the ramp agents need to chock the aircraft immediately after the parking brake is set. Toe brakes should be held and the shutdown checklist should be delayed until the chocks-in signal has been received from ground personnel.

column121: Our flight landed and was scheduled to park at N2B. The parking angle has a large angle relative to the building and taxiway. The turn into the bay is maybe 160deg. There is little structural lighting and the lead in line is invisible in the dark. Additionally; the angle is such that the FO (First Officer) couldn't see the lineup. We switched prior to entering the ramp to my taxiing from the left seat. The only guidance was from the follow me truck. That has its own issues because of the vehicle lightning is so bright that the flashing strobes makes it hard to see. Marshallers were of little help and gave conflicting signals.I feel it is an understatement to say that was the most sketchy parking I have ever attempted with an aircraft. Wing clearance on the right side is tight and impossible to judge in a sharp turn in the opposite direction from the wing. Doing this in the dark you are totally dependent on the ramp for clearance of the wingtip with the other aircraft. This is an incident waiting for a time to happen. This should be a tow in only gate. I do not feel comfortable ever taxiing into that gate in the future with anything larger than a Cessna 172! Cause: Design of the ramp is a major issue. The angles are due to aircraft length causing them to stick out. The area also is restricted on lighting as it is under the final visual segment of 26R and no large area lighting exist. Ramp lines have no reflectivity and do not stand out due to buildup of dirt and other materials on the lines. Suggestions: This spot should be a tow in only gate. The entire ramp striping needs to be redone with highly reflective paint. Highly reflective wing clearance lines would also be beneficial for all spots. Consider a solution with embedded LED lighting for the line. New technology could support led lighting for the line using LED strips embedded in the line with minimal challenges. The strip and power could be dropped into the concrete by cutting strips in the concrete and no need to dig it up like you need to with conventional airport lighting cans. This isn't a certified area. An alternative is to use glowing roadway paint that has been developed. This would keep the light pollution issue for runway operations to a minimum but provide a better lineup marking.

column121: FIRE MAIN DECK AFT WARNING EVENTS (Aircraft X) ZZZZ-ZZZZ1. ZZZZ and ZZZZ1This document contains the formal narrative of the events involving multiple FIRE MAIN DECK AFT warnings; two return diversions; a return to stand; maintenance actions; MEL use; fuel spill leak observations; and crew fatigue concerns.1. Aircraft: B7472. Cargo: Approximately 100T strawberries3. Locations: ZZZZ; ZZZZ15. Key Times (UTC):   - Wakeup call received XA:55 UTC    - Report for Duty XC:24 UTC    - First return to ZZZZ shut down: XH:57 UTC    - Second attempt OUT/IN: XM:40 / XN:24 UTC   - Third departure (with updated MEL): XR:34 UTC   - Diversion to ZZZZ1 landing: XU:25 UTC    - Arrival Crew Hotel XX:20 UTC    - Total Duty time 20hrs 56min.A recurring MID CARGO AFT LOOP A status message was present prior to boarding. Maintenance repeatedly cleared it via CB (Circuit Breaker) pull/reset of main deck cargo smoke detection zones. After takeoff from ZZZZ; approximately four minutes after liftoff; a FIRE MAIN DECK AFT master warning occurred. ATC advised; overweight landing completed safely on RWY XXL ZZZZ. No smoke or fumes observed; only strawberry odor.A second attempt to depart resulted in a return to stand C1. After ENG Start status messages Pack 1; Mid Cargo Loop A; EE CLNG (Electronic Engine Control Cooling) Bypass V; EE CLNG Supply V. After previous sector Fire Warning Mechanics elected to do a Fire System Test which subsequently Failed. During pushback ground crew advised of a fuel leak from RH (Right Hand) wing. Leak continued after pushback onto taxiway 1. Aircraft then returned to stand. ATC made several calls requesting reason then advised aircraft would not be permitted to fly in airspace until confirmation is received.On the third departure; operating under addition of MEL M26-14-01-XXXX; FIRE MAIN DECK AFT occurred in Cruise at FL 320. CA and I were taking crew rest in the bunks for around 80 minutes and heard PA from FO that we were diverting. Exited bunk in darkness to find crew dealing with multiple FIRE MAIN DECK AFT warnings that continued during descent and approach into ZZZZ1. NNC (Non-normal checklist) was carried out with communication challenges. All Crew donned oxygen masks. Radio support was given from 3rd seat by Captain that assisted crew. An unstable approach resulted in a go-around; followed by a successful overweight landing on RWY XX ZZZZ1. Post-shutdown; the master warning sounded several more times on the ground after all checklists had been completed.Both CA and I after landing entered the main deck and verified that there was no smoke or fire. Fire chief came on board asked if could assist and was told no requirement; false warning; however he elected to keep his vehicles and crew close to aircraft for another 10 minutes. Ground staff requested to see a copy of Noise Certificate; and this was complied with.CREW FATIGUE:Crew members had been awake up to 17 hours with no horizontal rest; experiencing two airborne emergency events and one return to stand in the same duty period. Duty Manager call-backs were repeatedly promised but did not occur. No crew replacement was offered despite multiple emergency/abnormal events. Opportunity to obtain horizontal rest only for a very short period (less than 80 minutes for myself and CA whilst other crew were not able).Ops Spec is not applicable to our Part 121 operation and only applies to part 117. B747 fleet is not required to have a FRMS (Fatigue Risk Management System).RECOMMENDATIONS:- Review cargo smoke detection system reliability and eliminate reliance on repeated CB resets when carrying strawberries.- Formalize post-fuel-jettison inspection/venting procedures.- Improve paperwork approval workflow.- Implement policy to stand down replace crew after emergency events.- Reinforce communication discipline under oxygen mask operations. Include evidence-based events in recurrent simulator and training. Review Class E compartments (B747-400) andtheir limitations.- Remind crew especially those traveling on the main deck such as Load Masters and Mechanics that in accordance with the aircraft limitations; under no circumstances is anyone allowed to open the door to explore main deck for possible smoke or flames whilst aircraft is in the air. According to FAA Advisory Circular AC 20-42D our aircraft do not have the required equipment to enter the main deck to fight a fire whilst airborne.- Reference FAA AC No:20-42D Date: 01/14/11 Any compartment over 200 Cubic Feet page 20 section 5-part d / (2) Restrict personnel from entering the cargo compartment for the duration of the flight.When to Use Portable Protective Breathing Equipment (PBE) Portable PBE should be worn before entering the cargo compartment and attempting to extinguish a fire; as outlined in 14 CFR 25.1439. Note that AFM and / or Crew Operations Manual are required to have the appropriate procedure including a calling out the use of portable PBE and other emergency equipment necessary to fight a fire.This report is submitted to promote safety; highlight system reliability issues; improve fatigue risk management and assist the reports submitted by Captain X and Captain Y as well as complying with mandatory reporting requirements in SMS Manual.Additional Comments and Observations:Following the ZZZZ event; in which the crew returned the aircraft to the ground within twelve minutes of a Master Fire Warning after requesting priority handling; it was expected that the crew would be stood down and replaced. In most organizations this would be standard practice.Concerns increased as duty continued. The next sector required a return to stand due to technical issues; including a ground reported fuel leak on the starboard side with a large visible wet patch. The crew were already fatigued to a level that would normally require an augmented crew for the originally planned two sector duty. During the subsequent sector; the same Main Deck Aft Fire warning occurred again; forcing another diversion. In total; the same four crew members experienced two diversions; two emergency fire procedures; and one return to stand without any intervention; replacement; or discussion from the company regarding welfare or operational risk. Forgotten altogether in the company's communication was the significant stress and elevated workload placed on the crew while managing multiple non normal events in quick succession. This generates stress.This pattern suggests a wider organizational culture that prioritizes continuation of duty despite cumulative fatigue; time zone changes; and reduced rest opportunities where lie flat deadhead options are avoided; travel policy is economy or over 6 hours premium economy often leaving crew tired before duty even begins as it is impossible to obtain any horizontal rest. Communication from Duty Managers is inconsistent; and the repeated question Did you request priority handling?" along with the lack of dissemination of reportable events to the wider pilot group raise further concerns."
column123: Returned to ZZZZ following a main deck fire warning. We had 100T of strawberries loaded when the aircraft was declared AOG. Cargo was offloaded and we were sent to the hotel. We were given another aircraft to complete the charter. Aircraft X arrived at XD:15 local and we were scheduled for an XF:25 local departure. I thought the inbound LM (Line Manager) would load the strawberries while it was cool but he was told he had to clear customs with the inbound crew. Getting through the airport in ZZZZ takes a minimum of 60 minutes; usually longer. We were picked up on time but didn't get to the aircraft until 15 minutes before scheduled departure. The aircraft was still empty as we had our LM with us. The APU was off and no ground air conditioning was available. First of the load arrived 40 minutes later and loading took 2h 20m. We pushed back at XI:45 local after waiting for a tug driver.When we arrived at the aircraft (which was empty with the main deck cargo door closed) the mechanic had pulled CB's (Circuit Breaker) for cargo smoke detect main deck zones 1-8 and 9-16. This was due to a recurring MID CARGO AFT LOOP A status message. The message had appeared prior to our boarding and this procedure had cleared the message. The message returned during loading and it was cleared again using the same procedure. We started 2 engines on the bay and ran all 3 packs for 5 minutes prior to pushback to maximize airflow. The status message returned and the same procedure was followed with the CB's being pulled and the message reset prior to starting the 2 remaining engines. 7 minutes after liftoff we had the CARGO FIRE MAIN DECK warning. The mechanic later surmised this was due to loop B for the same zone sensing smoke with a faulty loop A.We were maintaining runway heading as per ATC instructions and had just leveled at 6000'. Since we had briefed on a fire warning being a possibility I requested priority handling and left the flap at 1 and maintained 250 kt while we were heading away from the airport. Once we turned downwind we retracted the flaps and accelerated to 280 kt while the checklist was completed. ATC vectored us for an ILS Rwy XXL in VMC. The warning disappeared and I had CA Y set me up for the ILS. ATC tried to vector me to intercept the ILS inside the FAF but I requested 5Nm further downwind. We completed the after TO (Takeoff) and APP/LDG checklist and the warning returned on downwind and again turning base. We configured for a F30 landing with a Vref of 165 and AB4; advising ATC that we would stop on the runway and reassess since once on the ground we could investigate the main deck for smoke or fire. At no time did we have any smoke or fumes; just the smell of strawberries.Landing and touchdown were normal at 327.6T. After landing we stopped on the runway and a crew inspection confirmed no smoke or fumes. We elected to taxi back to the original gate; and the highest brake temp reading recorded during or after the event was 4 units.All of the crew including Capt Y (PM); Capt X and FO in the jump seats contributed in monitoring; ensuring all checklists were completed promptly and that nothing was missed.

column121: During a 121 normal operation flight to San Francisco International AirPort (SFO); I was acting as Captain and pilot monitoring for this flight. It seemed like a very standard flight and while descending for the Tip-Toe Visual 28L; approach control tell our aircraft caution wake turbulence there is a 777 10 miles ahead landing 28R. Thus is a very standard thing to hear while landing in SFO. We talk about it in the cockpit and have visual on the aircraft. At roughly 1;500 feet; fully configured to land on 28L; we feel a slight buffet and immediate uncommanded roll to the left and then the right. The First Officer acts promptly; using ailerons; and pulls on the yoke to gain altitude; and I call for adding more power to gain airspeed. During the roll to the right; I call out my controls;" and execute a go around. Almost immediately during the go-around; the aircraft gives an aural warning; "speed;" for overspeeding the flaps. I immediately pull the throttles out of Max and engage the auto-throttles. During the level off; we did not have an assigned altitude and climb to 3;300 feet. ATC says maintain 3;000; so we descend by 300 feet. At this time we have an EICAS message stating "Bleed 1 and 2 Overpressure." I delegate tasks to the First Officer having him fly and work the radios while I execute the QRH procedure. After completing this; I make an announcement to the passengers and talk to the Flight Attendants about the go-around and that we would be landing in 10 minutes. The First Officer the lands normally on 28L. At the gate; the First Officer and myself brief what had happened and I write a maintenance report about the severe wake turbulence and flap overspeed. I did however forget to mention the Bleed 1 and 2 overpressure message on the EICAS. This was not malicious intent. I simply forgot and was trying to get everything straight about the event. I then called the dispatcher and Maintenance Control. I talked to Maintenance Control about the wake turbulence and the QRH procedure ran for the Bleed 1 and 2 Overpressure.Cause: The cause of this event was wake turbulence from proceeding 777 aircraft on closely spaced parallel runways.Suggestions: Wake turbulence avoidance procedures at low altitudes. Typically this training is done during training and is at high-altitudes. I recommend including wake turbulence avoidance and escape training in the simulators."

column123: During climb out we experienced excessively cold temperatures on the flight deck.  At approximately FL270 we began to run the QRH for Cabin Temperature Cold (Freighter)". I continued to fly as the captain executed "step 24" for the QRH "Cabin Temperature Hot (Freighter)".  This caused a cabin decompression and a CABIN ALT warning.  After recognizing the condition; we executed the QRH procedure.  At that time Center gave priority handling as we requested an altitude of 10;000' and explained the situation. column121: I was the Student Pilot in command of this flight receiving dual instruction from a CFI. I was on the controls for the entirety of the flight. We took off out of ZZZ1 at XA:15 and departed west towards ZZZ. The lesson was a cross country flight with an instrument approach. We got VFR flight following from ZZZ1 Approach then ZZZ Approach. We executed the RNAV XX at ZZZ. On decent into ZZZ; I observed a low thumping feeling at low RPM. I asked my instructor if she felt or heard anything unusual and described what I experienced. After roughly 10 seconds it went away. We continued our descent and executed a touch and go at ZZZ at XB:45. Upon reaching cruise altitude of 3500 at XB:50 we attempted to run the cruise checklist. When leaning the mixture we did not see any rise in RPM. We went back to full rich as we started to slowly and progressively lose 10-30 RPM at a time. We each checked the throttle friction and attempted to lock it at a particular RPM as we observed it fall below each RPM setting we tried; we decided to navigate to a nearby airport; ZZZ2. We notified ATC that we would like to cancel flight following and land early at ZZZ2. We started a descent and flew past the airport to have appropriate time to descend. We noted that the throttle was further in than it normally was for the RPM we needed to maintain and we had to continuously adjust for greater RPM as it lowered. We entered the pattern and reduced throttle to descend for landing. We decided to maintain 1700 RPM rather than 1500 (what we would normally use). I noted on base leg that I was having to add RPM to arrest descent rate. We continued in for Runway; XY; flaps 10 degrees; floated slightly; and made a safe landing. Upon clearing the runway we attempted an after landing checklist and observed no RPM rise when attempting to lean the mixture. We taxied to the ramp and made contact with the maintenance team at the ramp who provided us with chocks for the tires. We immediately called Dispatch upon shutdown and described the incident. column123: We left ZZZ1 for a cross country flight to ZZZ and back to ZZZ1. We told ZZZ1 Approach that we were cutting our flight short and landing at ZZZ2; we did not declare an emergency. We landed XY at ZZZ2; maintained higher RPM than SOP (about 1700-1800 rpm) once we started the descent from pattern altitude since we were not sure we would be able to get more RPM back if we reduced it to 1500. After we cleared the runway; we completed the after landing checklist; noted that there were no RPM rise when we leaned the mixture. We taxied and secured the aircraft and called school Dispatch for notification.

column121: At approximately XA:30 local; I and my Captain departed Kalaupapa headed towards ZZZ. I was the pilot flying at the controls and my Captain was the pilot monitoring. Captain made the appropriate calls on LUP CTAF advising that we would be holding short of RWY 5 and monitoring for inbound traffic. I also checked ADSB on my iPad to confirm that the airspace was clear of any transitioning or landing aircraft. We then held short of RWY 5 in LUP as an aircraft was on short final. Aircraft landed; back taxied and parked. He then made the call on CTAF that we would be taking RWY 5 for a left downwind departure back to ZZZ and would be starting a back taxi. We then reached the approach end of RWY 5 and then began takeoff. As we rotated and climbed through 200ft AGL; a military transport on our iPad ADSB with a traffic warning. They weren't on ADSB when I had checked and cleared the area of traffic nor were they advising on CTAF that they would be overflying the field at any altitude. They were at 500ft AGL. I would estimate that they were 2-3 miles or less from the field at a high rate of speed (250kts+). If we were to remain on our current flightpath; I have no doubt in my mind that a mid-air collision with the military transport was inevitable. Captain quickly took controls from me; pulled the power back; and dove the plane down and back towards the airport; leveling off at 200ft AGL over the water. At the closest I had seen on the iPad; I would estimate that the military transport was 1/4 miles or less horizontal separation and 100ft or less vertical separation from collision. As I leveled off at 200ft AGL and followed the shoreline westbound; the Captain made repeated calls on CTAF in an attempt to hail the military transport if they were on CTAF. I had no communication from the military transport before; during; or after the incident. Captain and I assessed the situation; climbed back to 4500ft; setup the aircraft for cruise and continued the flight home to ZZZ. Captain then contacted HCF center to get flight following and then over to HCF approach for arrival into ZZZ. On approach; we advised them as to what had happened and gave a detailed report to the controller. They then said they handed off the information to the supervisor on duty. We then got cleared into ZZZ via the ZZZZZ arrival and landed on XX without any further incident; taxied the plane into the ramp and shutdown for the day.

column121: Climbing to cruise out of ZZZ; we noticed the amber IMBAL by the tank 1 qty (left side). The imbalance accompanied by a high decreasing rate of the fuel quantity initially suggested a suspected fuel leak. At that point; we concurred on the need to return to our just departed ZZZ. We talked to ATC; requested priority handling and began our return. The FO (First Officer) did a great job flying the airplane; managing the icing conditions while returning back to ZZZ. As he continued flying the airplane and manned normal ATC communications; I pulled the Fuel Leak checklist. As I started reading and going thru the first items; I noticed the fuel qty on tank 1 was not decreasing anymore; but it actually reversed the trend with a slight increase. At that time I paused that checklist; we had good engines; lots of fuel remaining and ZZZ just ahead of us; and with the plane stabilized in a shallow descent; the FO (First Officer) and I started more discussions; and that led us to the IMBAL checklist. We decided to follow that to balance the tanks and while we were still discussing and monitoring the fuel; (once again the #1 fuel qty increased some) we were almost on final for Runway XX. The fuel was balanced. We requested a couple of vectors to complete our checklists; and with the fuel panel properly and normally configured for landing; we continued the approach. Underweight landing with a smooth touchdown; we exited the runway and stopped for fire rescue inspection; and we were told there was no sign of leaks and everything looked normal. Uneventful taxi as we continued to the gate.

column121: The flight was ZZZ1-ZZZ; it was the last leg of a 3 leg day for us on day two of a 4 day trip. The only thing of note up until the event started was maintenance discrepancy 'Company Maintenance stations only' because of multiple write ups for ENG 1 FADEC. So we are at cruise at FL350 and get an ECAM for AIR ENG2 Bleed Abnorm PR. As we are beginning to run the ECAM procedure the warning goes away. I then pull up the BLEED systems page on the lower ECAM and notice that the #2 system still isn't operating quite correctly and told the FO (First Officer) I bet we get the ECAM again. About 10 seconds later we do get the ECAM except now it's AIR ENG2 Bleed Fault. We run through our ECAM procedures and then I notify Dispatch and Maintenance Control via ACARS; they respond and said to put in a logbook deferral sheet for it which I did. At that point I am still not feeling great about the engine and bleed system. I told the FO I was going to get on the Crew Phone and call Dispatch and Maintenance Control to talk to them directly about this just to make sure. Maintenance Control and I talked; and I explained everything and he said what we did was correct procedurally. So I disconnected with them and pressed on. At this point my ears were constantly plugging and popping. I asked the FO if he had the same feelings and he said no. I had a sense or what ever you want to call it that something wasn't right. ATC then asked us to slow from Mach .78 to .75 for sequencing to ZZZ. The FO selected .75 in the FCU (Flight Control Unit) and as soon as the #2 engine got to about 50% N1 we started getting very violent buffering and loud repetitive bangs coming from aircraft right. We immediately got ENG2 STALL ECAM. As we were starting the procedure the FA (Flight Attendant) in the back called to ask about the noise and buffering; I quickly said I'd call her back. As we completed the procedure I asked for; I believe; FL280 and told ATC what was going on. They gave us priority and cleared us to FL280. ECAM actions were complete and QRH follow-ups said we could slowly try and push the thrust back up if engine parameters were normal; which they were. I told ATC what we were doing and that both engines now appeared to be operating normally. They asked what we wanted to do and at this point ZZZ was our closest best option in my determination and with both engines operating normally I said we would like to continue to ZZZ. I asked for slow controlled descents so as to not cause large fluctuations in thrust settings; which ATC accommodated. I informed the FAs of the situation and explained a precautionary landing" in ZZZ is what we were doing; along with a PA to the passengers explaining everything. I told Dispatch of the ENG2 STALL ECAM. We landed in ZZZ with no further events and taxied to park under our own power.Cause: I believe that the shutting off of ENG2 Bleed from the first ECAM; coupled with our relatively high altitude of FL350; and a large power decrease going to idle by the autothrust when slowed to Mach .75 may have caused the compressor stall."

column123: During the descent; at an altitude of approximately 11;000-12;000 feet; a flight control malfunction occurred involving the speed brakes. Upon deployment of the speed brakes to reduce speed; the aircraft experienced an immediate left roll. The Pilot Flying (PF) promptly stowed the speed brakes; and the aircraft appeared to correct itself. The following cautions were then displayed on the flight control page: IB Spoilerons and IB FLT SPLRS.The flight control synoptic page confirmed that one spoiler was deployed; while the other remained inoperative.The flight crew immediately contacted ATC; declared a flight control malfunction; and requested vectors and a level-off to troubleshoot the issue.The crew ran the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) and recalculated the landing distance; factoring in the 30% increase; which resulted in a remaining margin of approximately 50 feet.In light of the low fuel (3;900 lbs) and other factors; the decision was made to divert to ZZZ2; as the landing distance at ZZZ was deemed insufficient.The flight crew also instructed the cabin crew to inspect the spoilers for proper stowage. The First Officer (FO) confirmed that all spoilers were stowed; despite the flight control page indicating one deployed.Contributing Factors:Nighttime operation2-foot snowbanks on either side of the runwayGusty windsReduced fuel reservesLanding distance margin close to limitPotential for uneven spoiler deploymentGiven the above factors; the flight crew made the decision to priority handling and divert to ZZZ2. Emergency vehicles were placed on standby.Landing and Post-Flight:The aircraft landed with no further incidents. Upon landing; the spoilers displayed a delayed green indication; confirming their deployment. The aircraft taxied to the gate without issue.Passenger Communication:Upon arrival at the gate; the captain made a PA announcement to inform passengers of the reason for the diversion.Cause: see aboveSuggestions: Dispatch needs to have the same data that we receive and not quote the temporary repair as the numbers are drastically different. WHILE STUDENT WAS TAXIING BACK FOR ANOTHER TAKE OFF I SENT HIM A TEXT MESSAGE REMINDING HIM THAT HE NEEDS TO DO A GO AROUND IF HE BOUNCES WHILE LANDING. HE RESPONDED; 'YEAH; SORRY ABOUT THAT'. THE SECOND TAKE OFF WAS NORMAL. PATTERN AND LANDING WERE NORMAL; DURING THE 'FLARE' STUDENT OVER ROTATED AND BALLOONED AND PREFORMED A SUCCESSFUL GO AROUND. ON THE THIRD LANDING ATTEMPT THE STUDENT AGAIN HAS A NORMAL APPROACH BUT OVER ROTATED ON THE FLARE AND BALLOONED AGAIN AND EXECUTED A SUCCESSFUL GO AROUND. ON THIS GO AROUND THE TOWER REQUESTED THE STUDENT TO FLY RIGHT TRAFFIC; THE THREE PREVIOUS WERE LEFT TRAFFIC. DUE TO BUILDINGS AND MY POSITION I WAS NOT ABLE TO SEE THE ENTIRE PATTERN HE WAS FLYING. AT THIS POINT I CONTACTED THE TOWER VIA CELL PHONE TO INFORM THEM THAT I WAS HIS INSTRUCTOR AND WAS MONITORING THE RADIO AND TO OFFER ANY HELP THEY FELT WOULD BE APPROPRIATE. I ALSO EXPRESSED MY CONCERN THAT HE HAD TWO PREVIOUS GO AROUND THAT I FELT HE MAY BE BECOMING STRESSED WITH THE SITUATION.I OBSERVED HIM ON THE BASE LEG AND NOTED THAT HE WAS LOW BY ABOUT 100-200 FEET AND APPEARED FAST. THE STUDENT CALLED THE TOWER ON THE BASE LEG AND INFORMED THEM HE WAS GOING AROUND. AT THIS POINT INSTEAD OF TURNING TO ALIGN WITH THE RUNWAY HE CONTINUED FLYING STRAIGHT HEAD ON THE BASE LEG. THIS PUT HIM IN CONFLICT WITH ANOTHER AIRCRAFT ON A EXTENDED LEFT BASE. I WAS STILL ON THE PHONE WITH THE TOWER (GROUND CONTROLLER) AT THIS POINT; THE CONTROLLER BEGAN BERATING ME FOR TEACHING MY STUDENT TO FLY LIKE THIS AND THAT HE WAS NOW GOING HEAD ON WITH ANOTHER AIRCRAFT. I EXPLAINED THAT AT NO POINT HAVE I EVER INSTRUCTED THIS STUDENT OR ANY OTHER STUDENT TO DO WHAT HE WAS DOING AND THAT HE NEEDED SOME ASSISTANCE.TOWER WAS ABLE TO DE-CONFLICT THE TRAFFIC AND TURNED THE STUDENT OUT BOUND FROM THE AIRPORT. THEY TURNED HIM BACK TO THE AIRPORT WITH ABOUT A 3 MILE FINAL. THE APPROACH WAS NORMAL UNTIL SHORT FINAL. AT THAT TIME IT SOUNDED LIKE THE STUDENT WAS CARRYING EXTRA POWER AND WAS NOT AT IDLE JUST PRIOR TO FLARE OR TOUCH DOWN. JUST AFTER THE PLANE TOUCHED DOWN I NOTED THE RIGHT MAIN LANDING GEAR LIFT OFF THE RUNWAY 1 FOOT OR LESS. WHEN CLEARED TO LAND TOWER ADVISED WINDS WERE 120 @ 6 (RUNWAY XX WITH A MAGNETIC HEADING OF 076). I DID NOT OBSERVE THE STUDENT PUT IN ANY CROSSWIND CORRECTION.WHEN THE RIGHT MAIN MADE CONTACT WITH THE RUNWAY THE SECOND TIME THE PLANE BEGAN DEPARTING THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE RUNWAY INTO THE RUNWAY SAFETY AREA. THE STUDENT WAS ABLE TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE AIRCRAFT WITHOUT DAMAGING ANY RUNWAY STRUCTURES OR THE AIRCRAFT. THE STUDENT TAXIED THE PLANE TO THE HANGER AND SHUT THE AIRCRAFT DOWN. WE IMMEDIATELY DEBRIEFED WHAT HAD OCCURRED.DURING THE DEBRIEF WE IDENTIFIED THAT THE FIRST ATTEMPT SHOULD HAVE RESULTED IN AN IMMEDIATE GO AROUND ON THE FIRST BOUNCE. HE STATED THAT HE INTENDED TO DO THAT BUT THE PLANE BEGAN SETTLING DOWN BEFORE HE WAS ABLE TO ADD POWER AND EXECUTE THE GO AROUND. WE DISCUSSED ALWAYS BEING READY FOR THE GO AROUND AND THAT IF AT ANY POINT SOMETHING IS NOT RIGHT TO EXECUTE; AND NOT 'WAIT AND SEE' WHAT HAPPENS. FOR THE SECOND AND THIRD LANDINGS WE IDENTIFIED THAT EVERYTHING WAS NORMAL UNTIL THE TRANSITION FROM THE DESCENT TO LANDING (THE FLARE). BOTH TIMES HE WAS OVERLY AGGRESSIVE WITH THE NOSE UP PITCH CORRECTION AND THE PLANE BALLOONED. SEVERAL FACTORS WOULD CAUSE THIS; EXCESSIVE AIR SPEED ON TOUCH DOWN AND THE PLANE BEING LIGHTER THAN HE WAS USE TO WITH NOT HAVING ME IN THE AIRCRAFT WERE IDENTIFIED AS THE PRIMARY CAUSES IN THIS SITUATION.FOR THE LAST LANDING WE DISCUSSED THAT HE HAD A SLIGHT CROSSWIND AND DID NOT APPEAR TO PUT IN ANY CROSSWIND CORRECTION; HE STATED THAT HE DID NOT REMEMBER ADDING ANY WHEN HE TOUCHED DOWN AND THAT WHEN THE RIGHT MAIN CAME UP HE DID NOT KNOW WHAT TO DO AND 'JUST FROZE'. WE DISCUSSED PROPER CROSSWIND TECHNIQUES AS WELL AS NOT RESIGNING YOURSELF TO THE SITUATION; IT IS IMPERATIVE YOU KEEP FLYING THE AIRPLANE UNTIL THE ENGINE IS SHUT DOWN AND THE PLANE IS SECURED.

column121: On a training flight (pre solo stagecheck); landing Runway 25R at DVT. About a half mile from the runway instructor gave student a go-around scenario to initiate a go-around. Student initiated go-around and pitched for an airspeed of 55; well below Vy (74). Instructor was concerned and focused on this; mostly looking at flight instruments to ensure proper pitch adjustment was made. After airspeed stabilized to Vy; instructor looked up and saw a helicopter crossing midfield at 500' AGL; student was flying directly at the helicopter without any control adjustments. Instructor had to take controls and evasive action was taken - pulling power to idle and pitching nose down to go below the helicopter. Instructor then advised North Tower Controller that we were going around and had to make an evasive maneuver to avoid the helicopter. Tower Controller responded with appreciation for letting him know but also told us that we need to advise about the go-around on the approach end. While instructor agrees; radio frequency was congested and we are always taught to Aviate; Navigate; THEN Communicate.(Instructor does not remember whether or not helicopter was talking on radios; as it would have been transitioning from the south side of DVT talking to the South side Tower Controllers initially then switching to the North).

column121: On a clear night; both 1st and 2nd party were returning north after doing various (presumably) training work to the south. The 1st party; Aircraft X; a high wing trainer; was returning to TIX. The 2nd party; Aircraft Y; a low wing trainer; was returning to COI.The weather was clear and a million; a great night for VFR or IFR training.1st party was cruising at 3000 feet; flying direct to LILAZ for return to TIX. 2nd party had been roughly paralleling 1st party at 4500 feet; a bit to our west; en route to COI.The site of the near-midair was west of COF airport/VOR. The 2nd party initiated a turn and descent towards COI. Being abeam and above our (1st party) wing; we were unable to spot them visually; however our graphical ADSB-IN display had allowed us to keep tabs on them as we cruised. Accordingly; the ADSB data broadcast from 2nd party -- including the descent and velocity data -- enabled us to realize that the 2nd party was forming a high risk conflict to us. Their intended descent cut directly across our course; and the angle of descent had them right at our altitude exactly as they crossed our course.Therefore; we initiated evasive action perhaps a minute before the would-be collision. While  we were turning roughly 270 out of our 360; they crossed our would-have-been course at our altitude a bit over a mile ahead of where we began our turn.We cannot be sure; but if we had been unaware of the traffic; which we were only aware of thanks to ADSB-IN; there was a distressingly high probability of invisible collision (neither party seeing the other). We were doing roughly 100 kts at the time; so we would have been roughly a mile and a half further along our course (compared to 'a bit over a mile' ahead of our turn). Optimistically; it would have been perhaps 3000 feet total separation; pessimistically zero feet. We can't know for sure without a detailed dynamics analysis of the mutual ADSB data.We are deeply thankful we had ADSB-IN to save our bacon.As stated; they were above our high wing so we couldn't see them; and we were probably below their low wing so they probably couldn't see us. We had good position and anti-collision lights; and most probably they did as well; but this was probably irrelevant. We only were able to avoid the situation; take evasive action; because of ADSB-IN. If we did not have ADSB-IN we would have been a critical event; or worse.Based on the fact that the 2nd party chose a descent path that generated such a high risk of conflict; most probably the 2nd party had neither visual contact (on account of us being under their low wing) nor ADSB-IN data. (That; or they were ignoring their ADSB-IN data.) Only the fact that we had ADSB-IN prevented a (very high risk of) midair; in my opinion. See-and-avoid failed; essentially; due to the low-wing-above-high-wing phenomenon. As far as I can figure; see-and-avoid could only have been made to work if clearing turns were required before all changes in course or altitude; which is of course a non-starter in the real world.The only way this would-be midair was prevented was ADSB-IN. We had it; they apparently did not.As far as I can tell; there is no immediate corrective action; other than encouraging further adoption of ADSB-IN by any means practical in all aircraft flying in busy airspace (such as where we were). ADSB-IN clearly proved its merit in my eye; and should be embraced further. (Not 'required'; since edge cases exist everywhere; but in the typical case; ADSB-IN is clearly beneficial.)Night-vs-day was not a factor; I believe. If anything; I find it easier to spot traffic at night; and as stated; all the lights on the planet could not have enabled us to have seen each other thru our wings; only clearing turns could have achieved that.

While crossing from west to east at the noted location; I (instructor) asked my student what he would do if he had a partial engine failure right now; and asked him to simulate that emergency. column121: I took off from my home airport at ZZZ1 to fly to ZZZ with the possibility of continuing on to the ZZZ2 Airport; depending on weather conditions. I did a very long briefing with Leidos before departing primarily discussing the impact of an event on air traffic and the area's airports. The briefer was not sure what restrictions were in place for ZZZ but did advise that some of the local airports were not allowing for landing by any aircraft without a prior reservation and a code. Leidos also told me that despite the forecast for VFR conditions at ZZZ2 by XA:00; he did not think that was likely to happen given what he saw on the radar. So I made plans to meet my husband at ZZZ and decide then whether to fly on to ZZZ1. Before I took off I called ZZZ to determine the situation with landing and parking there during the event. I was advised that transient parking for VFR pilots had been moved from the spot in front of the terminal building to the ramp to the north and that only IFR flights needed a reservation. I took off from ZZZ1 and got flight following from ZZZ Center. I was having problems with com2 which was very static-y so I was just using com1 and switching its frequency when instructed to go to a new frequency. Com1 was coming in loud and clear. I was able to get the ATIS at ZZZ on com2 without static but any transmission to me or between ATC and other pilots could hardly be heard. I was switched to ZZZ [Approach] just about ZZZ3 although on com1 I had a hard time hearing him. I had to ask him to repeat transmissions as they came through very broken. There was considerable traffic. I was coming up to the golf course when ZZZ announced 'traffic; but the transmission was broken. I heard '200 feet' but could not make out direction or altitude. I heard another aircraft announcing  an intended landing at ZZZ but by then I was approaching ZZZ airspace. Then I heard ZZZ say 'Tower' with my call sign and assumed I was clear to go to Tower. By this time I was quite concerned about the situation given the lack of clarity in instructions caused by the radio not working properly; my proximity to the ceiling of the ZZZ airspace and the aircraft I knew was behind me. Tower came in loud and clear fortunately. I was told to make a straight in for Runway XX and I thought was left. I repeated it back but do not remember if I said XXL or XXR. I do know that my brain was visualizing and seeing XXL and that it the runway I was heading to. I was then cleared to land; and again; I repeated the instruction but I don't know about this time if Tower said left or right and I was still visualizing left. I came in a little high and was quite occupied with flying the plane; slowing down; pitching properly and engaging flaps. I knew other aircraft were also in the area coming in to land and one was about to take off on XXL in front of me. My usual practice of repeating the landing clearance twice was not followed either. As I recall I was still shaken by the issue with the radios. I was also thinking about the change in parking spot; not sure exactly where to go and trying to figure out how I would get there from XXL. I was on short final; full flaps and entering the runway environment when I received an instruction to go around. and to make right traffic from XXL for XXR. I powered up; pitched up; released flaps; set trim and climbed. I noticed and aircraft had just taken off on XXL and was on the upwind; but they had lifted off before I got into ground effect and I wondered if that was the reason for the go around. I executed the maneuver and was cleared to land XXR. After landing I asked Tower what had happened. Controller said they were reviewing the tapes but that they thought I had been instructed to land XXR and instead was attempting to land on XXL; which I admitted I was. Ground cleared me to taxi and park at the normal transient spots in front of the terminal. I advised Ground that airport operations had told me VFR pilots were to park elsewhere. He then took a minute to check and came back on to tell me VFR pilots were to park to the north and he cleared me to taxi straight ahead and park. This was a singular event caused I think by a set of unforeseen circumstances; primarily the distraction of the radio not working properly; my concerns about the clarity of the instructions; parking spot changes and the confusion over same. I cannot explain why my brain translated what I heard into 'left' when I must have heard 'right.' Because I was thinking about all the other factors at play; I relied on that image that first went into my head of landing on the left and proceeded to make it so. It was completely inadvertent. No that this had happened to me; I know it will never happen again.

column121: I am submitting this report to formally document an ongoing and significant safety concern regarding frequency 119.3 at HCF.For an extended period of time; this frequency has presented persistent and unresolved operational issues that rise to the level of an extreme safety hazard. Controllers working this position routinely experience severe frequency congestion; blocked transmissions; and unreliable communication that directly degrade our ability to maintain positive control and ensure safe separation.These problems are not isolated or intermittent. They are chronic; well known among controllers; and have repeatedly created situations where aircraft are unable to establish or maintain timely two-way communications. This has resulted in increased workload; delayed clearances; missed instructions; and an elevated risk of operational errors particularly during periods of high traffic volume or complexity.Despite long-standing awareness of the issue; there has been no effective mitigation or permanent corrective action implemented. Controllers are left to manage an unsafe communications environment using workarounds that are neither standardized nor sustainable. This places unnecessary stress on both controllers and flight crews and undermines the safety margins expected in ATC operations.I believe this issue warrants immediate technical evaluation and corrective action; including a review of frequency assignment; coverage; interference sources; and overall system design. Continued operation under current conditions represents an unacceptable risk to safety.This report is submitted in the interest of protecting the National Airspace System; supporting controller performance; and preventing a serious incident before one occurs.Recommendation: Real attention. I understand it has challenges but maybe it's time to consider moving it.

column121: After landing on 28L; our taxi instructions were taxi to the ramp via B K A to eventually get to our gate XX. In front of us was Aircraft X; which we later learned was going to gate XY. On the ground frequency;  it was clear that the crew of Aircraft Y was confused and possibly unfamiliar with SFO. They had turned left onto taxiway K but then inadvertently joined taxiway A overshooting their gate. They then stopped their aircraft. As we were behind them; we stopped as well. The Aircraft Y crew called the ground control and said they needed to go to gate XY. At this point the Aircraft Y caption attempts to make a right 180° turn on taxiway A; right in front of our aircraft. For some reason they were on ramp control frequency 131.0 which told them they need to contact ground and turn around and get permission to go back to their gate . Both of us ; the captain and myself; were convinced that the Aircraft Y captain was intending to try to cut between our aircraft and the terminal in an attempt to get to their gate. Our aircraft was in the intersection taxiway K and A; and there was clearly inadequate room for this maneuver; not to mention; they did not coordinate that with ground control whatsoever. I contacted ground control and asked for clarification for the situation. Ground control; then gave Aircraft Y instructions to taxi to get them back to their gate. During this maneuver; the Aircraft Y captain endangered both of our aircraft by making the decision to make a right hand 180° turn directly into the nose of another aircraft; instead of a left turn; which would have kept them clear. During this maneuver; they came uncomfortably close to our aircraft nose. This demonstrates a shocking lack of judgment and experience and respect for standard operating procedures on the part of the Aircraft Y captain. I understand that all of us can get confused and have a bad day; but this one decision nearly resulted in a very bad day for many of us.

column121: A fuel imbalance was noted during climb out due to IMBALANCE alert. The fuel imbalance seemed to be rapidly increasing and the rapidly decreasing fuel on the #1 side created a feeling of time compression.  As FO and PF; I took the radios and continued as pilot flying so that the captain could focus on looking at the Flight Manual. At about 26;000 feet to captain requested priority handling and requested a return to ZZZ with a suspected fuel leak. We were in engine icing conditions and turbulence from 10k to the time the captain decided to declare and return. I think the weather played into the decision to return earlier than we might have otherwise. Leveling off didn't seem like a great option given the weather and neither did continuing to climb away from ZZZ.At this point; I was busy answering ATC's queries; manning the radios; flying the airplane; and setting up to land back in ZZZ while the captain ran checklists. Initially a fuel leak was suspected prompting the captain to return us to ZZZ. But after having a flight attendant look and observe no leaking fuel; and seeing the fuel flow and quantity looking closer to normal after starting the descent; a fuel leak seemed less likely to me.Upon starting the return to ZZZ the captain began to run the fuel leak engine checklist. When he asked if I was ready to shutdown an engine; I asked him to ensure there weren't more appropriate checklists to run as I remember a recommendation about this similar situation some time ago. At that point; we ran the fuel IMBALANCE checklist as it now seemed more appropriate. With the throttles at idle the condition that confirms a fuel leak ('a change in fuel imbalance of 500lbs/30mins or less') was no longer satisfied. Further leading us to suspect an indication issue or crossfeed problem.We had an uneventful landing. Crash fire rescue confirmed we did not have fuel leaking after we landed.Maintenance Control since replaced 6 fuel probes in the left tank. Of note the next crew had a write up about fuel indication issues in the #1 tank.

column121: Flight was cleared from FL340 to cross ZZZZZ at FL280.  After initializing the descent the following CAUTION and STATUS messages displayed:	-R PACK OFF - CAUTION	-L PACK OFF - CAUTION	-R PACK TEMP - CAUTION	-L BLEED PRESSURE SHUT OFF-VALVE - STATUS	-R PACK - STATUS	-L BLEED HIGH PRESSURE SHUT-OFF VALVE - STATUS	-R CONDITIONING TEMP CONTROL - STATUSI asked Person A to pull up the Flight Manual and find the appropriate checklist and asked ATC for an expedited descent to 9000ft.   Priority handling and traffic was requested as the cabin pressure was slowly rising due to the PACKS being disabled.   The FAs were commanded to be seated immediately due to the rapid nature of the descent.  Upon further observation; it was found that the L DUCT pressure gauge read '0' psi  while the R DUCT pressure read just over '20' psi; with the engines supplying bleed air pressure to both systems.  The L & R PACK OFF NON-NORMALS checklist was accomplished while the I coordinated with ATC and and FO Person B continued to fly the descent as required in that checklist.  After completing APU start; and BLEED TRANSFER; as required in the checklist; it was initially observed that L DUCT pressure as still near 0"psi; and R DUCT pressure was in the "20"psi range.  After the checklist mandated a transfer from AUTO mode to MANUAL mode; it was observed that the L DUCT pressure had returned to a normal '20' psi.  We returned the aircraft to AUTO mode; verified continued L and R DUCT nominal pressure; and successfully reset both PACKS to ON.  Left and Right PACK operation resumed and pressurization was restored to the aircraft.  We concluded that it was not necessary to continue the checklist into a procedure to land unpressurized; unless the PACKS stopped functioning again.  During the descent to 9000ft; cabin pressure altitude climbed from 6000ft to just above 8500 ft.  No CABIN ALT message was observed; nor were oxygen masks deployed.  No adverse conditions were experienced by cabin crew or reported by passengers.  The Purser was briefed on the situation; and what to expect for the remainder of the flight; and in return the Purser briefed the cabin crew.  FO Relief Pilot Person A made a PA to the passengers; at the request of CA Person C; to explain the situation and what to expect for the rest of the flight and upon landing.  It is noted; once pressurization was restored using APU bleed air; the following messages were present:	-L BLEED OFF - STATUS	-L BLEED PRESSURE SHUT-OFF VALVE - STATUS	-L BLEED HIGH PRESSURE SHUT-OFF VALVE - STATUSLanding was successful; smooth; and uneventful.  We were met by Fire/Rescue upon exit off the runway.  It was found that we could not stow the R THRUST REVERSER after slowdown from 80 kts; nor after exit from the runway.  I attempted to actuate and stow the Right Reverser several times; then decided to shut down the R ENGINE after sufficient time for engine cooldown and continue the taxing single-engine to our gate.  Taxi to our gate was uneventful and successful."

I agreed; set my controls for glide speed and landing configuration; then tuned my radio to 121.5 and hailed ATC. The controller confirmed my situation and location; asked me to tune to a new frequency. After changing frequency; I communicated my intentions to make a normal landing with power at idle at ZZZ; requesting priority handling. Once on the ground I received a call from FAA controller confirming I had safely landed with no injuries or damage. I reported a safe; normal landing. I determined that my newly installed fuel filters were possibly defective or contaminated. Drained all fuel; replaced fuel filters; and strained the fuel while refilling the wing tanks. Was able to depart without issue the following morning and began my return trip to my home. Stayed over at ZZZ2 for two days to troubleshoot fuel system. Arrived at my home airport ZZZ3 safely. I have a repairman's certificate for the subject aircraft and will do a thorough evaluation of the fuel delivery system now that I am back at my home airport.
