column121: First leg ZZZ1-ZZZ started with the gate power disconnecting suddenly and we had an APU on MEL for a previous fume event. We waited for about 40 minutes for them to repair the cable to the jetway power unit. Got underway late but that leg went fine.Second leg ZZZ-ZZZ1 we were cruising at FL270 and lost both generators simultaneously. Startle effect for a few seconds as the cockpit went dark and we heard all the systems shutting down and the relays powering off. First Officer (FO) was flying pilot and called 'my aircraft' and just as designed that got things moving. We realized he had no instruments so we switched roles. No Autopilot so I hand flew while he began running ECAM. No seat power so I had to interrupt him to help get my seat into position without losing focus on flying. Airplane was slow to respond but we quickly realized she was flying fine on Alternate Law and manual throttles with two good engines. Aircraft was in the Emergency Electrical Configuration. We requested priority handling and discussed diversion alternates while FO did a such a great job with the ECAM that we soon had both generators up and running. He then was able to restore all the other computers that had failed. RAT was deployed and we could hear and feel it running.With all systems restored we got the Autopilot and auto throttle back on and decided on ZZZ2 for our diversion. Talked to ATC; cabin crew; and passengers and let everyone know our plan. Used flaps 3 for landing to keep speed up in case we lost the gens again - didn't want to lose the RAT also. Uneventful landing. Crash crews were alerted and on standby but I didn't have them come out to runway as we were pretty normalized at that time. In the future I will have them come out.Takeaway was never get too relaxed. Things can change in an instant. FO was awesome and his experience was invaluable. He had two previous priority incidents in his career and it showed. I guess I've been lucky with none until now.Good communication and CRM helped with the whole process. Once we got over the initial shock things settled down and our training kicked in. Being over many airports with pretty good weather also helped. We fly that route over water a lot and I'm sure it would have been a little more nerve racking over the dark ocean. Inop APUs are commonplace but I will now think more about how it can affect the situation if you don't have it. Talking with Maintenance they said it probably would have started and been available for electrical power if we couldn't restore the gens. Definitely good intel as we hadn't really considered that since it had stickers plastered all over the buttons.Cause: Stay ready for the unexpected!
column123: In cruise flight at FL270 in night VMC the aircraft entered the electrical emergency configuration with no warning or prior indications. The APU was deferred. As the flying pilot; I initially maintained control of the aircraft through visual reference alone as I had no flight instruments. Aircraft control was transferred to the Captain who suddenly had the unenviable job of hand flying a badly wounded bird; raw data; in alternate law; in the flight levels; all with his seat in a less than desirable position requiring manual adjustments in the heat of the battle.As pilot monitoring; I informed the Captain of my understanding of the situation; loss of all generators in flight. I also reestablished ATC communication as both audio panels had deselected their previously selected comm radio during the electrical event. After the priority handling request; the flight attendants called and were advised of the situation. I began ECAM actions which eventually restored each generator one at a time. At that point; we elected to divert to ZZZ2 which allowed us to remain VMC with ideal weather conditions for landing. I continued the ECAM actions deselecting the blue hydraulic electrical pump and then successfully resetting both FAC (Flight Augmentation Computer) 1 and 2 which restored Normal Law. This recovered the Autopilot and autothrust as we descended into ZZZ2. I reprogrammed the MCDU (Multi-purpose Control Display Unit) to land on XXC. We discussed the approach and landing with the RAT deployed and agreed upon landing Flaps 3 in order to maintain the 140 kt. minimum RAT speed as long as practicable in case of any further electrical issues.The Captain did a fantastic job flying the airplane while I worked the problem; all while keeping each other in the loop and communicating well. Our combined airline experience of more than 65 years unequivocally made all the difference.The landing was uneventful and we taxiied to the gate under our own power with no further issues. Cause: Although I can't speak to the technical relevance; about five hours prior to our airborne electrical problem the ground power at Gate XX in ZZZ1 unexpectedly failed before our previous departure forcing us to reprogram the jet once it was finally restored. Perhaps fully shutting down the airplane before restoring ground power could have prevented this issue?

column121: This was my first flight after Operating Experience. During the pre-flight phase I was focused on my assigned duties; including cockpit flows; FMS programming; and obtaining the ATIS. I observed the Captain conducting the flight deck oxygen mask test and heard a prolonged; loud hissing sound. I initially suspected a stuck switch or regulator issue. I had the system page displayed and monitored the oxygen pressure; which was approximately 1870 psi and decreasing rapidly (1820; 1780; then about 1720).The Captain stated that we needed to call maintenance. Two mechanics came onboard. The Captain disconnected his mask and the mechanic replaced it. At that time I had not yet performed my oxygen mask test. A mechanic then asked if my side was normal. Then I conducted my test and it was normal. Shortly afterward; while passengers were onboard and we were preparing for route verification; my oxygen mask began leaking with the same loud hissing sound suddenly.The Captain instructed me that the mask be pulled and disconnected. I did not disconnect it myself; someone reached over and disconnected my mask following the mechanic's direction while they were still in the process of servicing/refilling the system. I just confirmed the Relief Pilot disconnected my mask directed by the mechanic. Almost simultaneously; both Relief Pilot's O2  masks were leaking. I then smelled what seemed like burning protein and realized the tip of my hair had burned. I looked back and observed smoke; sparks; and heard a loud explosion.Due to the high concentration of oxygen in a confined area; I was concerned about the potential for a fire and wanted to evacuate the flight deck immediately. However; the Relief Pilot was positioned behind my seat and I did not want to block the escape route by moving my seat aft; nor did I want to move closer to my oxygen mask cavity. I attempted to exit by squeezing between the center console and my seat. My right ankle became caught in the narrow space; causing me to lose balance and sustain a scratch to my right arm. I was able to move clear. The Captain directed the #1 FA to initiate a rapid deplaning of passengers.Cause: Follow SOP. Do not conduct any procedures outside of established protocol unless specifically directed to do so.
column123: After entering the cockpit; I settled in for my pre-flight checks. Ensuring a proper initialization of IRS panel. I then moved to the O2 panel to begin my flow. I could actually hear a hiss coming from my mask. When I did push the test button; the leak in the mask became pronounced; reset/test button; had no effect. I removed the mask to  take a breath; hoping to re-seat the pressure demand function. again; to no effect.With O2 venting from the mask; uncontrolled; and bottle pressure dropping; I disconnected the mask; hose coupling; a simple procedure; which stopped the O2 loss; and obvious threat. I called maintenance right away; and the interest of an on-time departure. I wrote the item/faulty mask up in the maintenance logbook.Any individual having an issue with myself or any other Captain; simply uncoupling an O2 mask as the only way to stop an incredibly dangerous environment on an aircraft with over 300 souls on board; and a full tank of fuel; should consider it done under Captains; emergency authority.When maintenance technicians arrived; all procedures/actions from that point on were conducted by maintenance.As far as causal factors are concerned; the maintenance department at ZZZ should be consulted.  A simple observation from myself might be that anyone concerned should reference the AOM for servicing limits under environmental conditions as to temperature and bottle pressure. The system seemed to have been grossly over serviced at a very high pressure. A quick note. Cockpit crew members observe the tank pressure during pre-flight after testing the mask and THEN conducting the O2 mask microphone check. Not before.

column121: While on the ILS 25L approach into LAX; our flight experienced a Near Midair Collision (NMAC) with a drone aircraft.  The previous aircraft reported a drone sighting to SoCal Approach.  We were advised of the drone sighting by SoCal with about 30 seconds advanced notice.  So; I as the non-flying pilot; was focused on looking for the traffic.  I was able to sight the drone about 5 seconds before the aircraft passed about 50 feet off our left wing at about 10;400msl.  Our position was just west of the KRAIN intersection.  I immediately pointed the aircraft out to the flying pilot.  Because of the size of the drone; and the brevity of the encounter; initially; it was difficult to tell how far away; what altitude; or exactly what the object was.  But at the time of the initial sighting; it was obvious that we would not collide with the drone.  As the drone passed off the left wing and slightly higher than our altitude; the drone maneuvered on its side.  I could clearly see (either the top or bottom) that the aircraft was in the shape of an X and about 1 meter in size.  After the encounter; I reported the NMAC to SoCal Approach.  The aircraft following ours also reported the sighting; so I knew that our aircraft did not collide with the drone.  It was still flying at the same position about 1 minute later.Suggestions: Better adherence to regulations regarding the operation and separation of drone aircraft; by the drone operator.

column121: On approach into ZZZZ airport; we were descending to 7000 and noticed traffic flying towards us from below that was climbing out of ZZZZ. The crew had briefed prior to arrival that there would likely be lots of GA traffic in the area that may or may not be transmitting on radios. We had the TCAS mode set to above and below to allow us to see all traffic around us; so we spotted the aircraft that was headed towards us at least 20 miles out. After observing the clouds with the understanding that we would have to descend into the airport VFR and remain clear of clouds; the crew came up with a game plan to make a slight left turn where there was much more blue sky versus the broken layer to the right; and after the left turn; proceed to fly over the airport above traffic pattern altitude and enter the left down for Runway XX. After we had the airport in view within 50 miles; we requested to cancel IFR with ZZZ Center; and before they approved our cancellation; they notified us of the traffic that we had on TCAS; but were not talking to them and did not have an idea where they would be going. We did not have them insight at this point; but decided to continue with the IFR cancellation and focus our efforts on traffic avoidance with what we could see on TCAS while also looking for the traffic visually. As soon as we canceled IFR; I initiated a descent to 3000 feet and started a left turn to avoid the traffic; as they were climbing out and at this point; were about 5 miles ahead of us and about 1500 feet below our current altitude. We could not initiate a right turn due to the cloud layer that would not allow us to descend to the airport VFR. The left turn would give us plenty of clear sky to descend; while also taking us away from the oncoming traffic. Soon after we initiated the left turn and the decent to 3000; we both noticed that the traffic started a right turn towards us; and we attempted to continue more to the left to avoid the traffic. We then got a TCAS TA; and soon after received an RA to climb; noticing that the aircraft was 400 feet below us at this point and still heading towards our direction; even though we had started the turn away from their anticipated path. I immediately and promptly disconnected the Autopilot and initiated max thrust and a pitch up attitude to comply with the RA that was commanding between a 1500 and 2000 ft./min. climb to avoid the traffic that was climbing below us. As I pitched up (we were at 210 kts. at the time in clean config); we experienced the stick shaker for one second which I respected with a slight relief in pitch up to stay below shaker AOA while keeping climbing. This happened in the few seconds that it took for the engines to spool up to APR thrust; and once thrust was achieved; there was no issue with maintaining the climb to meet RA requirements. The RA only lasted a few seconds as we climbed up to 7600 feet from 6500 feet. After we were clear of conflict; the First Officer (FO) got a short visual on the traffic out his right window below us. We were tuned into the AFIS at this point; but they did not provide any traffic avoidance. The First Officer let them know that we had performed a traffic avoidance maneuver and had been giving position reports to them since we were 60 miles out from the airport periodically. After we were clear of the conflict; we reset our altitude to descend to 3000 as planned to fly over the airport and eventually enter the pattern on the left downwind. All three pilots in the flight deck were fully strapped in via five point seatbelt; and did not feel that the maneuver was overly aggressive; but instead was an appropriate reaction to the RA. About one minute after the maneuver; we received a call from the cabin that the First Officer answered. The Flight Attendant called and asked what had happened; and the FO responded that we had performed a traffic avoidance maneuver. The FO asked if everyone was OK; explained that we would be landing in five minutes; and asked how the flight attendants were doing. The flight attendants mentioned that they had taken a stumble; but that they were OK at that point and they occupied their jump seats for landing. They also mentioned that all of the passengers were seated; and there were no reported injuries. At this point; we were glad that everyone was OK; and continued into the airport and landed uneventfully. We did not declare an emergency; since at this point everyone was doing OK and we were clear of any conflicts. After parking at the gate and starting the deplaning process; the forward Flight Attendant Person A let us know that he was feeling dizzy and was having some pain in his ankle and requested to sit down. We also got a better picture of how Person B was feeling; and she said she fell against a wall and had some scratches and soreness on her body from the maneuver. Person A said he had fallen and hit his head during the maneuver; and twisted his ankle. I asked them if they would like to be evaluated by medical personnel; to which they both responded that they would. I immediately asked Operations if they could arrange for medical personnel to give the flight attendants an evaluation on any injuries they may have sustained; as well as to hold boarding for the next flight. There were no customer reported injuries; but the flight attendants said that they felt unable to continue to work back to ZZZ. The station felt that the quickest and safest way to arrange medical personnel to see them would be to have a taxi service take them to the nearest clinic; which they done promptly. Myself and the line check airman that was with us riding the jump seat down to ZZZZ stayed with the plane; while the First Officer went with the flight attendants to the clinic. Over the next hour or two; I as the Captain talked with the Dispatch Coordinators; Maintenance; Operations personnel; and the FO talked with the chief pilots; providing a rundown and answering any questions that they had. We followed the procedures outlined in the FOM; and the airplane required further inspection due to our abrupt maneuver after FDR download. I made a write up in the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) and logged it with Maintenance Control; making sure to explain that we had achieved APR thrust in the maneuver. We continually received updates on how the flight attendants were doing; despite the poor facilities in the area and lack of good cell service. The flight attendants were given some pain medicine for their muscle soreness; but were not diagnosed with any serious injuries besides what has been described as soreness and bodily scratches. The entire crew was on the same page that the maneuver was necessary to avoid the oncoming traffic; and everyone worked extremely well and professionally together; including Dispatch; Scheduling; Maintenance and management teams. The ZZZZ Operations Station was extremely helpful throughout the whole process in arranging all of the logistics. There were no customer reported injuries during this entire incident.
column123: While we were on approach to ZZZZ airport on Day 0 coming through around 7000 feet we had noticed traffic who had just departed ZZZZ; and was headed roughly in our direction. We had discussed how there would be a lot of GA traffic due to it being non radar; and that they may or may not be communicating on frequency. We knew due to the location of the cloud layer off our right that we would need to maneuver left with the descent to get below any potential occurrence of IMC as we had to maintain VFR. Our game plan was simple. We had the airport in sight; and would begin a left turn descending to 3000 which is above pattern altitude; then over fly midfield for a left downwind entry for runway XX. I had also been making position reports on Comm 2 throughout this hand off to cancel IFR with center. ZZZ Center told us to cancel IFR when the airport was in sight and once we had located it we stated we were ready to cancel. As the controller was handing us off he advised us of traffic which was the same target we had on TCAS; no one was talking to them as they were VFR so we acknowledged the traffic and canceled IFR. Once canceled we began the left turn and the descent to 3000. The left turn was also sufficient to avoid the traffic on its current trajectory. The target was roughly 5-7 miles away and about 1750 feet below us. We had briefed and planned this move both for the protection of traffic avoidance and maintaining VFR.  Once the turn and descent began we almost simultaneously noticed the target had also turned further right now placing them headed towards us. We discussed slowing the descent to provide spacing and increased the left turn to provide even more spacing. Shortly after came the TA followed very quickly by the RA with the target showing about 400 ft below us. The CA responded immediately clicking off the AP and going Max Thrust with a pitch attitude to initiate the escape. I believe due to being at almost idle power setting due to the intent on descending it took a few seconds to get the engines to spool to max power. I think we were around 200-210 knots when this began. The stick shaker occurred very briefly followed by a reduction in pitch and achieving max power which allowed the aircraft to reach what was commanded by TCAS for resolution. As we cleared the conflict I believe I saw that last bit of the tail of the aircraft pass behind us as I had not been able to see him through the entire maneuver. We leveled off and I announced on AFIS (Airborne Flight Information System) of the RA with the intent to recommit to the descent and approach for runway XX. Around this time the Cabin called asking what had happened in which I explained the situation; they stated they had taken a tumble but were ok. I asked multiple times during this conversation to ensure they were ok as well as if the Pax were ok. They assured me they were able to continue. We completed the flight as normal. Upon parking and opening the flight deck door we were made aware that the FWD FA Person A was dizzy and needed to take a seat. The CA upon talking with Person A asked Ops for medics to check him out as it appeared the symptoms were not improving; it was also determined that the AFT FA Person B had gotten some scratches from the fall. A taxi was called to take the FAs to the clinic. The captain and I got together to game plan the situation; and we determined I would go with the FAs as I had a working phone and he would stay and tend to the aircraft and dealing with Maintenance; Ops; Scheduling. I was at the clinic for a couple hours where I was sure to call the on call chief and give a brief statement and update as to the current situation and to answer any questions he had. After a short while I returned to the aircraft to assist as needed. The Ops at ZZZZ were extremely professional and truly helped along the process as best as possible. I also commend my Captain for handling everything extremely professionally.We believed due to the proper entry into the pattern and the position of the outbound traffic from ZZZ1 we had best set ourselves up by making the left turn to descend under the deck for our turn inbound to enter the pattern. The jet that departed never spoke to anyone; turned into our track and continued a climb right into us.

column121: This aircraft had a right Air Conditioning (AC) pack that was inoperative. The release had several steps associated with configuring this panel during several phases of flight. The MEL required takeoff and landing to be bleeds off.The operation was normal until the after takeoff checklist. Following the steps for the right pack inoperative; there was a short period of time that the aircraft was climbing while depressurized.Maybe Boeing did a copy/paste and didn't think about reversing switches? The left pack inoperative would have a slightly different procedure; however; because the isolation valve remains open. So it's not exactly a mirror image procedure.Following the MEL steps for the right pack inoperative; the isolation valve is closed; so when I turn the engine 2 bleed air on; it doesn't do anything. The next step is turning the APU bleed air off; which is what started the depressurization. I paused for a couple seconds to allow some stabilization like would be done in a normal bleeds off takeoff.After realizing the issue; I quickly turned the engine 1 bleed air switch on. The aircraft began pressurizing again; and there was no further issue.For the right pack inoperative after takeoff checklist; the engine bleed air switches should've been reversed. Yes; engine 1 bleed air and APU bleed air would be on at the same time potentially causing the dual bleed air light. However; this is addressed in the notes of the MEL already so Boeing is aware and is OK with this light for a few seconds that it might be illuminated.The risk here is something like this happening at a high elevation airport and triggering the CABIN ALTITUDE warning.There's one other minor issue that could be addressed as well. For the landing checklist; it tells us to turn the APU bleed air on. However; there's no mention of turning the APU on prior to that point. So here's another potential of depressurization.

column121: Before departing; weather reports at the destination were already deteriorating. We knew we would be flying an instrument approach and because of the short flight briefed the ILS on the ground. Once on descent into the destination; the approach controller notified us that the RNAV to the opposite runway was in use. We asked to use the ILS but the controller notified us that ILS approach end tower visibility was reported as being poorer. We accepted the RNAV and briefed and set up for the approach. This was compressed due to our closeness to the field and the fact that the approach was now straight in vs opposite direction. However; we completed required checklists and briefings and upon reaching the FAF altitude everything seemed to be in order and the aircraft was properly configured. I remember seeing the autopilot capture the FAF altitude at 8700MSL; at which point the captain rolled in the missed approach altitude. We verified GPS APPR at 2 miles; computed a groundspeed at 1 mi; and at .2 prior to the FAF the captain rolled in a VSI and began his descent. I noticed that the VNAV snowflake was at full top deflection already; at which point I cross checked our altitude and noticed that we were already quite a bit lower than FAF altitude; in the vicinity of 8200MSL. At first I told the captain to level off; but I quickly realized we had probably been below FAF altitude since before the FAF; almost simultaneously the GPWS issued a 'Terrain; Terrain' alert; so I called for a missed approach. The captain executed the missed and we took vectors out to check our fuel and elect whether or not to try another approach. After discussing the incident and thoroughly preparing for another approach; we attempted the RNAV again. This time it proceeded without incident; though we did not see the runway at minimums due to poorer than reported visibility and performed another missed approach; ultimately diverting to our alternate. Cause: I believe causal factors included being rushed on the arrival/approach; which gave us little time to set up and probably caused us to become task saturated and more likely to miss errors. We did not complete all checklists until on the approach; which tied up our attention on non-flight path items. Also at the time; due to rapidly changing conditions; tower was not recording the full ATIS which required us to receive the complete weather report from the controller once on tower frequency; another source of distraction during a critical phase of flight. We probably became too fixated on the 3-2-1 checks prior to the FAF at the expense of a more complete cross-check. Although I do not know exactly where the descent below FAF altitude was actually initiated; I suspect it was slow and gradual; making it easier to miss.Suggestions: We could have built time for ourselves on the approach by requesting delay vectors or slowing earlier; which would have eased the pace and given us mental headroom. We should have considered discontinuing the approach when we were still running checklists while commencing it. As flight path management is always primary; we should have been incorporating the altitude more regularly into the crosscheck just prior to the FAF to detect a deviation; and were probably too trusting that the autopilot would keep us at the previously captured altitude (assuming we actually captured it and did not misinterpret indications).

column121: After pushback from Gate XX onto Taxiway H and subsequent engine start; we were given and complied with taxi instructions to follow Aircraft Y" who had pushed from Gate XY onto Taxiway H. While monitoring Ground Control on Taxiway H; we heard Aircraft Y in front of us receive instructions to taxi to Runway 8 via Taxiway H-A. I asked why he did not bring this to our attention prior to takeoff; but said he 'trusted us up front.'  I told him to next time please ring the call button or bring it to the attention of a flight attendant prior to takeoff if it happens again. I would like to ensure this is brought to the attention of the appropriate people in a timely manner to prevent a future event.  I contacted an LCP (Line Check Pilot) after we left; as well as another Captain to try and get advice on who to contact; and ultimately decided to call the Chief Pilot but is not in office today. column121: While returning from a solo cross country; my student suffered a lateral runway excursion upon landing on runway XX at ZZZ. Surface winds at ZZZ were below 5 knots so crosswinds were not deemed a factor by me. Prior to commencing his flight; I reviewed his cross country planning and determined that the entire route would be VFR; and the winds would stay well within his demonstrated capability. My student had previously completed two other solo cross countries; and had demonstrated safe practices during dual cross countries with me in the airplane. After the excursion; my student secured and shut down the airplane and called me for assistance. During a post incident discussion; my student admitted that he landed in a side loaded condition which caused a loss of directional control. He also further admitted to me that he knew he should have gone around. This incident further illustrates the importance of not only landing with the longitudinal axis parallel to the centerline of the runway; but also the importance of commencing a go around if the parameters of a stable approach and landing are not met. It is not unusual for incidents such as this to occur in the training environment; especially at a student pilot level. However; I plan on taking corrective action by having him file a report; obtain further training through the WINGS program; and extensive flight training focusing on maintaining directional control on landing; with and without a crosswind component.

Terrifyingly; Aircraft Y then also called a left 360 into me and my Runway 18… this was completely baffling and unsafe; especially at 500'… and there is absolutely no reason for Aircraft Y on Runway 13 to be doing a left 360 into my Runway 18 space… at the very least they could have done a RIGHT 360 AWAY from runway 18 traffic or proceeded on their official missed approach of climbing 2000' straight to COBIM and hold per the HDC RNAV Runway 13 procedure IF they were in fact on a practice approach; which they never claimed to be on until after their go-around.This was a very unsafe scenario; and I hope that such situations can be avoided in the future. column121: While taxiing to the active runway; I was momentarily distracted and looked down and thus removed my focus from the task of steering the airplane on the taxiway. When I looked back up I saw that the airplane was about to taxi off the pavement and into the grass. I tried to correct but the grass was wet and the ground was soft due to a rain storm the past evening and the right main wheel went onto the grass. Because the ground was soft; the wheel immediately sunk into the mud. I stopped the airplane but it was stuck and was not going to move back onto the taxiway. The lesson learned is that when taxiing an airplane the pilot's focus should be 100% on the task of taxiing. The pilot should not try to look at the checklist; tune a radio or do anything other than focus on taxiing. Fortunately the airplane was not damaged nor was any equipment or other aircraft involved or damaged. Distraction can be a very dangerous thing. Pilots must remain focused on the task at hand at all times.

column123: On Day 0; we conducted an oceanic crossing from ZZZZ to ZZZZ1. We were cleared to cross at FL280. I immediately checked the primary flight display and noticed the altimeter tape moving; while the aircraft attitude indication remained normal.It was night conditions dark outside and not visual reference (night conditions); I put my hands on the control to maintain level flight looking at the attitude indicator. I cross-checked the standby attitude indicator as well as the SIC's attitude display; and all three indicated a consistent; level attitude.The entire event lasted only a few seconds. No other aircraft were involved.The altimeter then stabilized; indicating we were approximately 300 feet above FL280. We smoothly corrected back to FL280; after which the remainder of the flight was uneventful.A few seconds later; ZZZZ Radio contacted us and advised that they observed our aircraft climbing toward FL290; which seemed inconsistent with the aircraft's performance; climbing 1000 in a few seconds. We briefly explained the event; and ATC reminded us not to climb without authorization. Shortly thereafter; we were handed off to ZZZZ1.

column121: My student was flying the aircraft in the left seat and I was observing from the right in Aircraft X. We took off from XXL at ZZZ and a Piper Seminole; Aircraft Y; took off after us. They proceeded to climb above us after departure; overtaking us but not passing on the right. After just having departed the class D; ZZZ Tower advised traffic overhead and we confirmed and halted our climb to 7;500' and soon thereafter our intended 8;500' for maneuvers. At this point; after the Seminole had flown over top of us; I told my student to resume their climb to 8;500'. Considering the Seminole was climbing and going southeast away from the multi-engine practices areas to the southwest; I figured they were enroute to another airport or with ZZZ Approach. However; once we got near the practice areas we turned south to follow the road and the Seminole was in the practice box with another 172 maneuvering nearby. I scanned for the Seminole; noting on my ForeFlight EFB that we only had around 300' separation; and once they seemed on a converging path flying west; I called them out by tail number on the practice area frequency by stating our geographic position; altitude; and intentions and asked what they were doing in the area. A pilot responded 'west side of the box and we're doing steep turns' before proceeding to turn right into us; which was when I actually saw the Seminole as it banked. I had my student start a descent from 8;500' out of caution and estimate we were around 8;300-8;200' before I took over. Initially by sight I thought they were turning south - away from us - but then realized the opposite. Our Garmin 430 with ADS-B IN also alerted us; and ForeFlight audibly warned me of aircraft at the same altitude in my headset. I took controls from my student; cut our power to idle; and dove down to 7;800' as the Seminole went overhead before then proceeding southeast. I maintained visual separation until distance dictated otherwise. Due to the sudden and dangerous nature of the situation I did not call on frequency in the moment while I tried to get the aircraft under control and I do not believe the Seminole made any practice area calls thereafter.

column121: Landing ZZZ Runway XX. Approach to the runway was stable; but I carried excess speed over the threshold (approximately 10 kts). Initial touchdown resulted in a bounce due to the extra energy. I applied power in an attempt to minimize bounce but failed to execute an immediate Go-Around which is the proper recovery procedure. This resulted in a Pilot Induced Oscillation. The aircraft contacted the runway multiple times; resulting in a propellor strike.Winds were calm and there were no other extenuating circumstances. The engine remained running and I was able to taxi off the runway and to parking. Upon engine shutdown I observed each of the 3 blades of the propeller were bent. The landing gear also appeared compressed from what I can only assume is the impact from porpoising. I have reviewed the Mooney POH and recovery procedures for bounced landings. Should this happen in the future I will execute an immediate Go-Around if the aircraft bounces or if my airspeed is not on target at the runway threshold.This incident; to the best of my knowledge; does not meet the reporting requirement for an accident per 49 CFAR 830.

Approach was warning the jet about me so I heard the jet state that it had me in sight. Approach also called out to see if I was on frequency which I was; and I responded. I also gained a visual sight of the jet albeit when it was quite close to me. Ultimately I watched it pass in front and below me by about 500 feet below. The Embraer pilot mentioned that an RA was triggered.Our Approach Controllers do excellent work and do the best they can under tough circumstances. In this case I view the controller's decision to turn the jet left as a mistake that contradicts aviation safety principles; which should be discussed at ZZZ TRACON so as to reduce the chances of a mishap. I don't view myself or the Embraer pilot as having committed any errors in this situation.

column121: I filed an IFR flight plan ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was unable to raise ZZZ Departure on the ground despite numerous attempts. No NOTAM was present regarding the frequency XXX.X being unusable; and this was the frequency listed on Foreflight which was current. I troubleshot the radios; connections and headphones; but still unable to contact ZZZ Departure to open my IFR flight plan. There was no phone number in my Foreflight info page to call except for FSS ZZZ. I decided to depart VFR and pick up IFR in the air. I departed Runway XX; conditions were clear VFR weather; with a fair amount of GA traffic. After takeoff; I called ZZZ Departure but no answer. Shortly after departing; I received a RA instructing me to climb; climb; climb. I increased power to full power and climbed and saw a Cessna 172 or 152 close enough that I could see the pilot. I estimated 500 feet away; 200 feet vertical separation. It was the closest I had been to a collision; and it was very unsettling causing an adrenaline response. I climbed to avoid a collision with full power. I overshot into the Bravo airspace and immediately attempted to contact ATC at the Departure frequency in Foreflight XXX.X. I tried both radios; confirmed switch on headphones was on and not to the oxygen mask; but still unable to contact. I went to 121.5 and asked for any pilot to provide ZZZ Departure Control frequency and was able to reach ZZZ Departure.This was a preventable situation; and if I had been more persistent in calling FSS I believe they would have been able to find a phone number for me to call ATC before departure. Given the busy GA traffic on a nice day; it would have been much safer to obtain IFR clearance on the ground prior to departure. The second factor is that after climbing out at full power in response to the RA; I should have focused not on calling ATC but on getting the aircraft out of Bravo airspace. This was a very preventable event which should not happen again if I follow these recommendations.

AGL; when pulling the power back for cruise climb; the right engine manifold dropped more than usual with given throttle input and immediate engine roughness occurred. Power was added back to take off power and the roughness subsided. A second attempt at reducing power gave the same results. It was at this time that I noticed the fuel flow on the right engine was excessive at 45 GPH and CHT's at 150 degrees. I told ATC I wanted to return to ZZZ. ATC asked me if I would like to have priority handling and I said not at this time. I left my take off power in turning back to the airport; but once I got closer to the pattern I started to slowly reduce the power. The engine roughness got worse with the reduction of power; and I needed to decrease and increase power repeatedly to prevent the manifold from dropping significantly. The right engine manifold would fluctuate from matching the left engine to 4-5 inches below the left engine. Fuel flow remained excessive even with slight leaning. I decided not to continue to lean the engine after entering the pattern. When I was handed off to Tower; I decided to request priority handling since I could not reduce my power without the roughness and yawing getting worse. I landed with no incident or injury to myself or my passenger.

column123: Night dual cross country for a student pilot and CFI from ZZZ-RST. Cleared to land RWY 13 at RST; planned full stop; taxi back to RWY 13 for pattern work. Upon exiting the runway; the left main sunk into mud to the left of A8; and soon after; nose gear and right main as well. The plane was unable to be moved without external help; so I called tower to notify them of the event.All lights (landing light; position lights; and red/white anti-collision lights were on during the event. The taxiway diagram was displayed on the MFD. No taxiway centerline was available to follow due to the taxiway exit being a high speed taxiway exit. I believed the mud was the taxiway as they seemed to be a similar color; and difficult to distinguish under the conditions.During post-flight; I saw no damage with the exception of mud on the tires; struts; wing; and propeller/spinner from what looks to be caused by the propwash; and a few small indents on the propeller which looked to be caused by small rocks or pebbles in the mud. No taxiway lights seem to have been struck.In the future; I plan to take extra precautions when exiting runways at night; especially when exiting high speed taxiway exits from the opposite end as primarily intended. I also plan to confirm that I am equidistant from the left and right taxiway edge lights to ensure that I am not falling victim to any illusions or misinterpretations.

column121: I am writing to voluntarily disclose a series of high-altitude excursions involving two separate units of the Holy Stone HS790 drone. On multiple occasions; the aircraft exceeded the 400ft AGL limit; reaching altitudes as high as 1;300 feet. These excursions were uncommanded; uncontrolled; and occurred despite active pilot efforts to maintain the legal ceiling.Evidence from flight logs suggests a systemic firmware calculation error. While the flight controller was set to a maximum altitude of '396' (intended to be 396 feet); the aircraft physically ascended to approximately 1;300 feet. The Conversion Bug: 396 meters is approximately 1;299.2 feet. This indicates the firmware erroneously applied metric units to a numerical limit intended for imperial units.I have been in contact with a Holy Stone representative regarding these safety hazards. In official correspondence; the manufacturer stated: 'Our preliminary assessment is that there may have been an internal component malfunction that caused the altitude limitation to fail.'

I will now use a dual-verification method by checking two independent airspace awareness applications (e.g.; LAANC and Drone Buddy). Furthermore; I have adjusted my drone's flight software settings to permanently limit the maximum altitude to 60m (197 ft) to provide an automatic safety buffer below the legal limit. At this time the vibration got louder. We ran the Checklist for EDP (Engine Driven Pump) 1A fail caution. As we followed the Checklist; when turning off the PTU (Power Thrust Unit) the hydraulic pressure started to drop off. The Checklist drives us shut down the EDP and use the PTU (Power Transfer Unit). With this accomplished we still had a loud vibration going on. We discussed it and with the FA's (which they had already called up for the vibration) and made the decision to divert. We got on with dispatch/ maintenance to discuss the situation. We chose to divert to ZZZ as it was the most reasonable station in front of us. We made the decision to divert due to the continued loud vibration that was still going on. HYD system 1 continued to work normally with the use of only the PTU. The landing gear was put down 4-5 miles early to make sure we had no issues with its operation working solely on the PTU. Flaps were moved separately from gear to not overload the system. Landing was normal and performed by the FO as he was PF. ZZZ Center gave priority handling for us after initial contact about the situation.

column121: We had just operated Flt ABCD into ZZZ and we were in the process of turning the aircraft to operate Flt ABCE back to ZZZ1 when we heard an unfamiliar call sign on the CTAF making traffic pattern announcements (ZZZ tower was closed for the night).  The callsign in question was a little difficult to make out.  Shortly thereafter the flight was closed out and we announced our pushback onto taxiway 1 and our intent to use runway XX for departure.  During the pushback the mysterious aircraft announced that he was back taxiing on runway XX and would clear at taxiway 2.  At that point we were abeam taxiway 2.  I looked out of my left window and was more than a little surprised to see a military MQ-9 Reaper drone sitting on the active runway; waiting to exit onto taxiway 2.  I instructed my pushback crew to push us deep past taxiway 2 so the drone would have enough room to clear the runway.  In addition; I warned my pushback crew to use caution as the drone would be operating in close proximity to us.  We announced our intention to push past taxiway 2 and the drone operator responded that he had us in sight and would clear the runway.  I did then observe that the sensor turret on the chin of the drone was pointed at us which seemed to be how the drone operator was able to see us.  The drone then proceeded down taxiway 1 ahead of us.  We disconnected from the pushback and announced our taxi.  As we started down the taxiway we contacted ZZZ center for IFR release.  ZZZ center advised that he was unable to release us as the drone had not yet cancelled its IFR flight plan.  We contacted the drone operator over the CTAF and requested that he cancel with ZZZ. He complied with our request and ZZZ released us.  We continue to follow the drone down taxiway 1; assuming that he was going to pull into one of the hangars to the right of the taxiway.  This was an incorrect assumption as the drone proceeded all the way down to the approach end of runway XX and came to a stop short of the runway.  We pulled up behind the drone at which point my taxi lights illuminated the drone and gave us our first really good look at it.  I was quite alarmed to discover that the drone had two underwing weapon pylons with each pylon occupied by a brace of anti-tank missiles and here I was pulled up short directly behind this fully armed and un-safed aircraft.  I could; at this point; clearly identify the yellow markings on the missiles indicating that they were live ordinance with a High Explosive fill.  After a brief halt; the drone crossed the active runway and appeared to head for a small; partially lit parking area on the far side of the runway.  We then announced our departure and took off uneventfully from runway XX.

column121: I was the pilot monitoring while the FO performed the take off from ZZZ XXL.  We were aware of the 787 on final to XXR as the controller had made reference to it in the take off clearance.  We were above 80 kts call as the last lights of the Runway Status Lights/Take Off Hold system illuminated just as the last light elements disappeared under the nose.  I recall seeing 96 knots in the HUD (Heads up Display) as we were well into the takeoff roll just past 1 intersection.  I looked and saw the 787 was on very short final; looked ahead and could not see any other threats entering the runway and decided it was best to continue. As we flew through the intersection the tower was already telling the  787 to go around; I again looked right and could see the 787 was in the flare and low enough that it was causing mist and water to displace out from the jet blast and wing downwash. They appeared to be just short of 2 intersection on XXR.  We continued our departure with no other issue or anything being said by ATC.The illumination of the lights so late in the take off caused me some confusion as to perform an RTO (Rejected Takeoff) or continue.  I quickly was thinking it is not a condition we brief to reject for above 80 kts; and if I did reject it might put us stopped right in the intersection of the runways possibly in the path of the 787.  Continuing seemed best but what if the lights were for a threat of another vehicle or aircraft we did not see yet and not the 787.  In the end I believe it was the best decision given the circumstances but it brings up some deficiency in our awareness and reaction to these lights. Had the lights illuminated earlier with more in view; I would have been more inclined to stop. However; only seeing the last lights illuminate in a split second as they disappeared from view created great uncertainty.  I tried searching our company documents for reference to these lights and could only find one article from an report; Day 0that discussed a similar event with a crew out of ZZZ1.  This leaves us with the guidance that is found in the AIM as our only reference.  Inclusion of the THL lights in the take off rejection considerations section of the AOM/FOM and training would be appropriate.

column121: Cessna 150M flying back to ZZZ airport; heard radio call from aircraft on a final approach; aircraft #2 called turning crosswind for Runway XX and aircraft #3 on a left base Runway XX. Cessna 150M called 4 miles southwest of ZZZ inbound for a left downwind Runway XX. VFR day; using visual avoidance; cessna 150M flew at 900 ft. entering in downwind Runway XX; made radio call entering left downwind Runway XX. Roughly 30 seconds later a 172L calls for a position clarification of the downwind aircraft. 150M calls that we are on the downwind for Runway XX with the local high school directly to our right; calls that we see the upwind traffic in sight to our left. Traffic of 172L above and off to our left; called to confirm we had 172 traffic in sight. The 172L next call gets blocked intermittently but states they are extending their upwind. After 150M lands; the 172L landed as 150M was clearing the hold line. After the 172L takes back off the pilot makes a call that their transponder is not working and is remaining in the pattern; will make radio calls. 150M - should have entered the 45 downwind at more of a 45 rather than straight in. Come in at 1000ft instead of being below traffic pattern altitude. 172L- If they were concerned about intermittent transponder;they should have stayed grounded to fix the issue; called their upwind; extended their upwind for entering downwind traffic; slowed down in the pattern to allow for spacing for landing traffic. 150M was visually trying to avoid crosswind traffic; did not immediately see upwind traffic. Pilot in 172L seemed flustered due to transponder issue; there were 4-5 aircraft in the pattern and making radio calls. Contributing factors were stress with the amount of aircraft in the pattern; 150M was on training flight with new student which is also a distraction; both pilots in incident are aware how how close they got to each other. In the future for the 150M we will enter in on downwind using a true 45 degree. Take a wider route coming in from the east to avoid upwind traffic. Continue to monitor frequency and see and avoid other traffic.

column121: During a VFR flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ at 10;500 feet MSL. As described above; the avionics began failing. First the Garmin 430 then the Aperro transponder. I transmitted to ZZZ Approach; as I had been using VFR flight following and informed them of an electrical problem. I received a broken acknowledgement after which all of the avionics failed except for the Garmin G5 AI (Attitude Indicator) and DG which continued to operate on internal battery. The aircraft ammeter indicated in the center position; no charge or discharge and the aircraft had no way to monitor bus voltage. I descended to 8500 to stay out of the ADSB required airspace and proceeded to my destination; avoiding all airspace requiring a transponder. Upon arrival in the destination area I manually extended the landing gear and made an otherwise uneventful landing. The problem was found to be the left generator output wire being secured directly to the intake manifold by a plastic zip tie. The wire chaffed through and shorted to ground. This was in front of the ammeter so gave no discharge indication. The right hand 35 amp generator accepted the load but it was later found that a 50 amp regulator had been installed causing the generator to exceed its output rating; overheat and fail. After this; the battery drained and the system failed altogether. This is a maintenance failure. Improper securing of electrical cabling and installation of the incorrect regulator for the installed generator. The Cessna service manual even makes it clear not to mismatch these components in a precautionary note.

column121: During a routine climb in IMC; the aircraft's ADC1 altitude indication froze at FL230. Prior to the freeze; the altitude had intermittently lagged and the VSI had shown abnormal spikes. Shortly thereafter; the indicated airspeed on (Primary Flight Display) PFD1 froze; began declining; displayed a yellow caution; and was eventually flagged invalid with red X's on both PFD1 and the standby GI275.We were assigned FL270. PFD2; operating on its independent ADC; continued to indicate a normal climb consistent with reaching FL270. Based on the instrument behavior; I suspected a static system blockage or freeze affecting ADC1. I transitioned to hand flying using PFD2 indications and advised ATC that our instruments appeared unreliable. I informed them that PFD1 was frozen at FL230 while we were continuing the climb to FL270 based on the alternate ADC. ATC confirmed they were observing FL230 via Mode C.During this time; the autothrottle was responding to the erroneous low indicated airspeed by attempting to add power. ESP protections in the G1000 NXi attempted to re-engage; increasing workload during a high-task phase of flight. I eventually disconnected the autothrottle and used my free hand to disable ESP in order to reduce automation interference and maintain stable manual control. There was an Airbus aircraft behind us requiring vertical separation. I stated that we were climbing to FL270. Some confusion developed regarding whether we were maintaining FL230 or climbing to FL270 due to the discrepancy between what ATC was observing on their display (derived primarily from Mode C) and what we were indicating on PFD2.I had previously understood that ATC altitude depiction was derived from both radar returns and Mode C; and that discrepancies between the two would be readily apparent. In this case; ATC was primarily referencing Mode C altitude; which remained fixed at FL230. Although separation was ultimately maintained and no loss of separation occurred; the mismatch between actual altitude and transmitted Mode C altitude created the potential for reduced situational awareness and separation risk from both pilot and controller. The issue resolved later in the flight. Post-flight; maintenance evaluation of the static system was requested.

column121: The AWOS-3 at ZZZ is out of service (NOTAM). Winds at nearby airports to the west southwest of ZZZ had winds around 240 -270 degrees. Nearby airports to the north were reporting gusty winds from 300 degrees. To get a better sense of the winds at ZZZ; I stayed in the traffic pattern and made several approaches looking for flags or wind socks as I passed over the Runway XX before executing a missed approach. There was no intention to land on the first three passes down the runway at usually at 25-50 feet AGL; ending in missed approaches to stay in the pattern. On perhaps the third approach on final approach; a business jet was seen moving slowly towards and less than a couple hundred feet from the approach end of Runway XX closer to the south side of the runway. He passed an exit taxiway. I assumed he was back taxiing to the approach and of Runway XX or alternatively he had just landed. Less likely in my mind considering the winds.I added power and went missed approach at a couple hundred feet above the runway and went around the pattern again. Sensing no cross winds on the low passes in the pattern for Runway XX; I proceeded to land uneventfully. When I parked on the ramp; two men approached and falsely claimed I almost hit them on the runway after they landed on Runway XY. I told the jet pilots; I was a little surprised they landed on Runway XY considering the winds clearly favored Runway XX. The jet pilots then stated the winds had just turned around. The reports I later printed out showed the winds had not changed and favored Runway XX for 40 minutes.A representative of the airport later called me to ascertain my perspective of the events. I sent him the wind data on which I had based my decisions. When it was apparent he was not going to clear the runway prior to my landing; I executed a missed approach back up to pattern altitude.I called out my position reports; Crosswind; downwind; base and finals. I never heard the jet pilots announce position reports for an apparent straight in approach.

column121: Climbing through 16;000 feet the First Officer's (FO's) airspeed indicator failed with a red flag. After checking all my instruments I determined my airspeed indications and engine indications were completely normal. I then told the FO that I had the flight controls and the radios and to get out the QRH and go to the back of any tabbed page and look for 'AIRSPEED'. The only checklist for our situation is the known as the 'AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE' checklist. Having done many sim sessions I am very aware of this 8 page checklist that covers a myriad of possible airspeed malfunctions and things can get extremely confusing when trying to navigate this checklist; and how our relatively stable situation could be easily rectified by doing a simple test. I have seen the exact malfunction on the ground perhaps over a hundred times during my career.It is a very common maintenance issue. Maintenance will be called out to the plane and will simply recycle the airspeed circuit breaker. My intention was to return to ZZZ regardless of whether the First Officer's airspeed was working or not and then write it up upon arrival. But if we could get the First Officer's airspeed indicator working again I would most likely not need to request priority handling. So; I instructed the First Officer to find the First Officers airspeed circuit breaker but not to pull it yet. When the circuit beaker was found and we both agreed that that circuit breaker was; absolutely in fact for his airspeed indicator; I instructed him to pull it and reset it. The result was exactly what happens on the ground. The airspeed indicator reset and went to the appropriate airspeed. In our case it went to 296 kts.; the same as my airspeed indicator. I then tested if his airspeed indicator would follow mine by simply accelerating to 320 kts. As we accelerated my airspeed indicator increased normally and his stayed frozen on 296. I knew immediately that we would need to request priority handling. Moments later; due to the discrepancy between our airspeeds; his airspeed indicator again flagged out.We requested to return to ZZZ and requested priority handling. We landed on Runway XXR with no incidents; returned to gate and wrote up the maintenance issue in the logbook. I recognize; as a Captain I am to simply followed the QRH checklist; however; given the circumstances; I was very concerned about making a relatively simple problem far worse by trying to navigate a very complex checklist in our QRH and end up possibly making our situation more dangerous.

column121: It was a 2-man crew ZZZ- ZZZ1. We got to the airplane; and I got my vest to do the walk around; and then of course the security check when I went upstairs. By the time I got to the flight deck; it seemed like almost nothing had been taken care of. The Captain (PF) was sitting in his seat with the paperwork and not doing anything. I sat down; and he handed it all to me; said the route wouldn't uplink and to please type it in manually and then verify the routing. I told him I would; but he also needed to verify it. I had to ask him a few more times before I saw him take the flight plan and verify everything. In doing this; I saw they still had XX closed (there had been discussion about it being reopened prior to departure because we were expecting the ZZZX SID); departures were off XYL; and we needed a new clearance. I asked the Captain to join me for a voice clearance; it was again an argument from him; almost hostile; and he told me not to call and ask. I did as he said; keeping it in the back of my mind for closer to departure.Thankfully; the Captain noticed a few trucks were driving up and down the Runway (XX) and asked me to go ahead and check to see if our departure would be changed. I asked him again to join me on voice; where we were given the ZZZZZX from XYL. I loaded it into the box and had him verify it. After this; he sent for performance; and when it came up; he asked me to load it in the box; but would not let me verify the ZFW from the document- yet again; I had to ask multiple times; and at this point I thought to myself 'how much more of this before I should get off the airplane?'. I did not put in the performance since he would not hand me the document. He ended up doing it himself and then getting up. I then looked over the document and performance numbers to verify it was correct.With no further issues; we got the setup done; and he gave a correct briefing; accurately highlighting the left turn to heading XXX in our departure; contingencies including 2000 or 4.0; whichever comes first. I very clearly remember watching him put everything in the MCP (Mode Control Panel); including arming LNAV and VNAV; because he did not do it before the briefing; and I was trying to think of a way to ask him or do it myself without making him upset again. I also clearly remember verifying on the ND (Navigation Display); the SID looked accurate; because after the XXX heading; it was vectors then ZZZ1; so the magenta lines looked a little odd at 5 scale.We did the appropriate checklists and procedures and eventually ended up at XYL; cleared for takeoff. After reaching 2000; the FD (Flight Director) indicated a left turn; and he stayed on runway heading. He then asked me if it was a right or left turn. I told him left; but could not recall the exact heading; and the legs page had already sequenced; so I grabbed my iPad to see. At this point; he had already started a turn to the right; and ATC asked what we were doing. I told them a turn to the south; and they gave us a low altitude warning as we were rapidly approaching the mountains off XYL.For the remainder of the flight; I felt I could not get up and leave him alone in the flight deck; as even after this event; he operated in a nonstandard manner. He would want to get up to get food; etc.; and I had to strongly tell him multiple times to give me control of the aircraft instead of just saying 'I am going to the back'. After each time; I told him; 'Okay; go ahead and give me the airplane first'. He eventually started doing so without me telling him.The PF should have entered the route; and this likely would have helped him remember which way to turn; and kept the operation standard. The PF also should have followed his command bars or automated when he realized he wasn't sure what to do; after verifying the FMAs (Flight Mode Annunciators).After the nonstandard events leading to the deviation; I should have worked harder to better anticipate the next nonstandard thing;be it from the FOM or an ATC instruction; and been stronger in my stance to stay within the clear lines we are given to operate. Which I did for the remainder of the flight; as given in the last part of my description narrative.
column123: I was the flying pilot. We departed Runway XYL in Day VFR weather; with correct SID which was ZZZZZX. As I approached the heading bug to turn manually; the ATC  informed us we need to turn immediately. The ATC also asked if we are turning north or south. I accidentally grabbed heading bug into wrong direction in a hurry; and soon realized of my mistake. However; it was too late to correct.I usually write down the engine out procedure and keep it on control column clip. The engine out procedure of XYL is RT heading XXY. I think I mixed up with the engine out procedure and late to catch my mistake.Quick glance and double check on the departure chart before making turn; could have been a solution.

At approximately 38;500 feet; I noticed the air speed was increasing at a rapid rate. I mentioned to the Captain watch your air speed. As I began to deploy them; the Captain at the same time grabbed the speed brake handle and he pulled towards full deployment. He grabbed the controls at that point; clicked off the auto pilot as VMO was exceeded and not trending towards a correction. This caused the entire speed tape to show full red. Once we were stabilized at 36;000 feet and the autopilot was reengaged; I made a report to air traffic control that we had just experienced a very strong mountain wave. A maintenance write up was then reported for this exceedance. Maintenance met us upon reaching the gate.

column121: Taking off Rwy XXL ZZZ on the ZZZZZ SID tower instructions were to turn to heading 110 and climb to 10000 ft and cleared for takeoff. At approximately 40 kias I heard another aircraft on tower frequency declare a missed approach so I was mentally prepared to hear tower instructions to the aircraft to deconflict us as I knew the missed approach would place the aircraft in our previously cleared path. Upon rotation and climbing out I noticed the TCAS indicated a target at +300 feet above and in amber. At approximately 700 to 800 feet the TCAS issued an RA to descend which I did immediately as I had already almost leveled off so as not to hit the missed approach aircraft. I also chose to fly the runway heading initially vs tower instructed heading as the latter would have placed us even closer. Tower never once issued any instructions to myself to do anything other than the initial one to fly 110 heading and climb to 10000 ft. The missed approach aircraft came as close as .08 nm and within 100 feet according to info I have been told.Cause: The lack of subsequent missed approach procedures to allow separation from a previously cleared departing aircraft and one executing a map.Suggestions: Improve ATC handling and plan for the possibility of a missed approach for every arriving aircraft and its consequences in re to previously assigned instructions to departing aircraft.
column123: We took off out of ZZZ on runway XXL on the ZZZZZ SID while their was another aircraft landing on runway XXc. Aircraft Y advised Atc that they were going around. The Captain on my flight flew straight out towards the end of the runway while making all the standard call outs; I'm complying while keeping my eye outside the aircraft and especially to my right side window before making the right turn since Atc's instructions after take off were to fly to a heading of 110 and climb and maintain 10;000. While I'm looking to my right; I don't see anybody. I believe Aircraft Y was still behind us at that moment. They then accelerated and caught up to us and saw them appear on my right side window. I didn't take my eye off of them to see what they were going to do and make sure we kept flying straight and not turn into them. In that second; the RA came alive and told us to descend. I started yelling as well to descend in which the CA did.Thankfully; I did not have to take any controls since the CA maintained his straight lateral flight path. Data shows the cork was writhing .08 nm laterally and 100 feet vertically. Cause: Atc never gave any instructions to us or the Aircraft Yto fly a different heading or turn us away from each other until after both airplanes had received and responded to the RA alert.Suggestions: Atc should have assigned different headings/instructions for both aircraft in order for the outcome to be to not run into each other. The TCAS/RA alert should have been the last resort to use.

column121: Landed Runway 14 at MYNN. My PM and I had briefed a long rollout to avoid a lengthy wait for runway crossing into the ramp. We were instructed by ATC to exit the runway at Taxiway B and hold short of Runway 10. We exited the runway and immediately realized that the hold point for 10 was much further back than we anticipated; and that the space between the hold short line for 14 and 10 was only about 20 to 30 feet apart. There was insufficient room for our airplane to fit between the two lines without hanging over them. Additionally there were planes landing on both 14 and 10 so we were unable to cross the runway.We noticed when exiting the runway that the hold short lines were so close together it was hard to decipher which one was for what runway. And very easily could have been crossed if we were not as attentive as we were. A fatigued crew likely would have crossed unknowingly due to the expectation of the hold line for 10 to be closer to the runway.Cause: The runway hold line markings are in an odd spot and are too close together for a jet aircraft to fit between them without hanging over into the runway area.We taxied in as far as we could to maintain a safe distance from both runways. This probably meant that we were hanging over each line by approximately 5 feet. But we were unable to notify ATC due to frequency congestion and the fact that there was an aircraft landing on Runway 10 and Runway 14.Suggestions: A note in company app to alert crews of the odd placement of the hold line and the insufficient space for aircraft to safely clear both runways.

column121: Taxi out terminal; Ramp cleared us to spot 23. Ground Control cleared us 17R EK - L. Approaching spot 23 FO noted 2 aircraft approaching on the right. Ground did not tell us the intentions of the aircraft approaching from south on K. We held at spot 23 watching traffic approaching from south on K as we were unsure of where they were going. First aircraft turned into the ramp next to us at the (non-existent/closed due to construction) spot 24. Captain set the brake.From the time we saw the aircraft was turning into spot 24 until they were already committed and past us was a very short time; approximately 5 seconds. We could not alert the aircraft or controllers as we were on Ground frequency and they were on Ramp Control. The aircraft did not contact (impact) our aircraft. The second aircraft stopped on K.Relief Pilot called Ramp to query whether the first aircraft was cleared into the ramp; they said no" and that spot 24 was not a spot due to closure for construction. It was unclear what their actual clearance was.10-9 Airport Moving Map (AMM) Chart does not depict closures. As it is; the chart leads one to believe spots 22 and 24 are open. This is contradicted by Jepps Chart DFW 60-7A-4T which shows construction closures.Change AMM chart to show closure of spots 22 and 24 in alignment with Jepps Chart DFW 60-7A-4T. Spots 22 and 24 closure signage in the field is inadequate. Add clear; large signage on field indicating spots 22 and 24 are closed.Ground Control did not advise us of the taxi intentions of the two aircraft. Ground Control should advise fellow aircraft of the intentions of those around them."
column123: Flight DFW - ZZZZ. Position - Relief Pilot. Departed out of Gate XX at XA:15. Upon taxi out Ramp cleared us to spot 23. Approaching spot 23 FO switched from Ramp to Ground frequency. FO noted 2 aircraft approaching on the right on Taxiway K.On Ground frequency we were cleared to 17R via Lima - Echo Hotel. Ground did not tell us where approaching traffic was going; they did not tell us to hold for traffic. We were holding at spot 23 watching traffic approaching not sure what they were going to do so the Captain stopped our aircraft and set the parking brake.First aircraft turned into the ramp over the previously named spot 24. This spot was closed due to construction. We were parked in the center of the taxiway. We believe there was not enough space for aircraft to taxi in with safe clearance distance. There was no time to alert the aircraft because we were on Ground frequency and they should have been communicating with Ramp.Other Relief Pilot called Ramp to notify them of our concerns. They were aware and told the other Relief Pilot that they were trying to get in touch with Ground to have them enter spot 25. We did not hear any communication between the aircraft with Ground Control or Ramp Control.Cause: Jepps Chart DFW 60-7A-4T. Chart depicts that spots 22 and 24 are closed due to construction. This is information only found if opening all taxi pages. These closures are not depicted on that 10-9 Airport Moving Map (AMM) Chart.With so much construction going on in DFW it is difficult to be aware of all the changes and those closures are not depicted. There should be clearer signs and taxiway markings denoting closed taxiways and closed area of the ramp.Ground Control did not clearly communicate with us about the aircraft's intentions. We did not know if the aircraft were taxiing to the runway or holding short to wait for us to taxi out. We have no idea what their taxi instructions were. Ramp did not warn us about any inbound traffic.

column121: We were climbing out on the ZZZZZ departure. There was a radar return at our 1-2 o'clock in the vicinity of our turn to the south. As we climbed out; we could see clearly underneath the clouds and there was no precipitation from the return. Aircraft Y had departed just before us and went through the area with no complaints. As we entered the cloud; the Total Air Temperature (TAT) jumped up to +14c. As we secured the Engine Anti-Ice we got a small flash of St. Elmo's Fire followed by an explosion and brilliant flash of blue light. The Head-up Display briefly turned a blue color from the normal green. It sounded like a stick of dynamite going off rather than a crack of nearby lightning. My hands and teeth felt like I had briefly grabbed a bare wire and my ears felt like they did when I was too close to a grenade simulator explosion. The explosion came from somewhere around the TAT/Pitot Probes. I coupled the autopilot so I could gather my composure and it seemed to have a hard time holding airspeed. Given all of this information the FO and I decided that the most prudent course of action was to return to ZZZZ to have the aircraft inspected. The prospect of continuing to ZZZ at FL400 (our Flight Plan Alt) did not seem worth the risk if we had sustained damage to the nose of the airplane. Cause: ATC vectoring us near the radar return caused this to occur. I thought about asking for an early turn; but given all the other information; it seemed like the turn was acceptable. Suggestions: Insisting on turning early would have prevented the incident. Next time I find myself in a scenario like this; I will be more insistent on an early turn. Just because it is cold outside doesn't mean there's not sufficient energy inside a radar return to cause something like this to occur.

column121: Flight diversion recovery flight to ZZZ. On the recovery flight to ZZZ after landing poor taxi conditions lead to very slow taxi to the gate. Approaching gate XX the Captain lined up with what we thought was the lead in line for the gate as the ground crew scrambled to get vehicles out of the gate area. The line was completely obscured by snow and ice. Once we were lined up we started to taxi into position almost immediately the left wing walker threw up an X with his wands because they had missed a baggage cart that was in the safety area. The Captain stopped and we waited as two of the walkers tried to push it out of the way by hand. They moved it and signaled that we were clear to start pulling in again. We were moving super slowly; cautious of the ice and trying to find the line the whole taxi but especially when entering the gate area. As we were pulling in the Captain noticed the wing walker on his side throw up the X again as we had gotten close to the baggage cart they attempted moving. The Captain stepped on the brakes in an attempt to stop the aircraft but we started sliding on the ice and slid to the left bumping the baggage cart.The aircraft only came to rest after the Captain cracked the thrust reversers. After investigation and coordination with the ground crew and airport ops with clearance we decided it was best to have the tug back us out and tow us in rather than doing it under our own power. Which was a good decision because even the ground ops tow vehicle was not able to get traction with us. The ramp was sprayed and sanded twice before they got the grip to get us to the gate. After we arrived to the gate we ran all procedures as necessary. On post-flight walk around it was found to have a cracked nav light cover with no other damage to aircraftI believe the cause for this event was primarily the poor ramp conditions first and foremost. Had the ramp not been icy; or snow covered the aircraft would likely have been much closer to centerline to start and would not have slid further towards the cart during braking. I think that had either the ground or flight crew stopped and said that the ramp needed to be cleared first that would have saved this event from happening. This is very easy in hindsight but is something I will pay more attention to in the future and not be afraid to refuse a parking spot. I think a secondary cause was the ground crew giving little to no directions as we were entering the ramp area while having better reference to where we should and should not have been; the marshaller had sticks up and was waving straight in until the walker signed the X.In the future I will be more forward about refusing a parking spot if ramp conditions are poor or at minimum request extra caution from the ground crew.  Better training for ground and flight crews about what are and are not acceptable ramp conditions would also likely result in better safety and fewer events like this happening in the future
