column121: Aircraft X; a C172; was on an approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. The radar controller assigned a climbout of runway heading for Aircraft X. Aircraft X was cleared for the option and executed a touch-and-go. Once Aircraft X was on the go I initiated a rundown for Aircraft Y; a C68A; on a heading of 170. The rundown was then acknowledged by the radar controller and I switched Aircraft X to their frequency when Aircraft X was about a half a mile off of the departure end of runway XX. I observed on the radar scope that Aircraft X appeared to be drifting a couple of degrees slightly east of the runway heading that he was assigned; possibly due to wind. As a result; I called down to the radar controller on the recorded shout line with an approval request for a 150 heading for Aircraft Y to ensure more separation between Aircraft Y and Aircraft X. The radar controller then said that he was going to 'crank Aircraft X on a 090' heading. This did not make sense to me as a 090 would create even more of a conflict with Aircraft Y who was already on a 170. Thus; I reiterated my approval request of a 150 heading for Aircraft Y and the radar controller replied 'approved.' I then switched Aircraft Y to the radar controller about a half mile off of the departure end of runway XX on a 150 heading. After both aircraft were switched to the radar controller's frequency I observed Aircraft X; who was at this point about 2 miles south of the runway; turn directly towards Aircraft Y with targets appearing likely to merge at co-altitude. Ultimately; a 170 heading was coordinated in the rundown for Aircraft Y and another more eastbound heading of 150 was coordinated and approved by the radar controller. The radar controller decided to turn Aircraft X directly towards Aircraft Y creating a near mid air collision. Lastly; I think that it is worth noting that the radar controller is a supervisor who is certified only in one position in the facility and received that certification with zero recommendations from a CPC in the building. I would like to recommend that all those in training whether they are developmentals or supervisors be required to receive a recommendation from a CPC before they are considered for certification.

column121: This aircraft had a L engine exceedance and engine swap prior to report time. This was the first flight after engine change with a MEL deferral It required an ETOPs verification flight (1 hour cruise; all systems normal per FOM 5.60.2) before legal to enter the ETOPs area of operation.  Showing at aircraft about an hour before departure; three Maintenance personnel were working in the cockpit.  The crew gained cockpit access around the departure time. After a few maintenance issues were resolved on the ground (L thrust REV status message; Auto Spoiler EICAS; and previous exceedance that wasn't cleared); we pushed about an hour late.  All was normal until takeoff roll.  Around 80-100 knts; the left engine N1 vibration indicator was higher than normal and the box inverted to white with black digits in the 4.0 range.  Takeoff was continued (no EICAS indications) and vibrations weren't felt on the throttle and airframe until past the low-speed abort phase and into initial climb. One of the Relief Pilots also thought he smelled something not normal.  The FO noted an additional vibration surge above 5.0 occurred during power reduction at 1500 AGL. The non-normal engine indications made ETOPs entry illegal; so the decision was to hold over water and dump 200;000 lbs. of fuel or land overweight   Dumping fuel would delay landing an additional 45 minutes.  AAs the engine was not working normally on its first flight; I decided landing overweight to be the safer option to get on the ground sooner with long runways available back in ZZZ.  This had been coordinated previously with dispatch regarding the ETOPs verification options.  After initial climb out; we completed the After Takeoff checklist as I wanted to clean up and get some altitude to discuss the issue.  The crew concurred to return to ZZZ per our plan with Dispatch on the ETOPs verification.We requested a level off with ATC and were assigned 14;000MSL on the ZZZZZ SID; then a request to return to ZZZ.  ATC cleared us direct ZZZ and descent to 11;000 MSL and to expect the ILS XXR.  While I (PF) and the FO (PM) prepared for the approach; the Relief Pilots assisted by getting a SATCOM with Dispatch.  I had them inform the FAs and Passengers of our plan to return to ZZZ.  We run the electronic Overweight Landing checklist and determined we had to use Flaps 25 for landing as the target speed was over 161KTS.  I believe the final target speed was 167KTS.  The FO pulled up ACARs landing data for RWY XXR that we knew was slightly longer than the takeoff RWY XXL.   Brakes 4 selected.  Approach was brief and Descent checklist completed.  ATC vectored us similar to a ZZZZZ1 STAR down the bay as we slowed and descended.   The approach was uneventful on the ILS to XXR.  Landing checklist and callouts per SOP.  Touchdown was smooth rolling to the end and exiting RWY XXR.  After crossing XXL on Taxiway 1; the brake temps began to increase; so we coordinated with ground to hold on taxiway 1 and have the ear inspected for hot brakes.  APU was started and engines shutdown to allow the parking brake to be released with no aircraft movement.  Brakes began to cool and we verified no fire or fuse plug issues from fire rescue vehicles. We requested to be towed back to gate to avoid using brakes or need to restart engines. After the brakes had cooled around 30 min and began going from amber back to normal; Maintenance and tug crews connected and towed aircraft back to gate XX.  Normal checklists completed at gate and passengers deplaned.  Maintenance write-ups for the engine vibration experienced on the left engine and the BRAKE TEMP EICAS.

column121: I was jumpseating SFO - ZZZ. During climb below 5;000 ft.; NorCal Departure cleared the pilots speed at your discretion." I observed the Captain tell the FO to delete the 250/10000 line on VNAV climb page. Then he started to accelerate. I was sitting in the second jumpseat so I asked the FO why we were accelerating above 250 KIAS below 10;000 ft. He said that ATC had given them high speed. I told him that we are never authorized to exceed 250 KIAS or clean maneuvering (if higher) in the US airspace. The FO did not correct the Captain; so I spoke up and advised the Captain not to exceed 250 below 10;000 ft. He too told me that ATC had given us high speed. I corrected him as well. We did have a thorough discussion of the applicable FAR 91.117(a).This is a regular occurrence climbing out of SFO as NorCal is in the dangerous habit of giving the nonstandard clearance of "speed at your discretion." This has been occurring for years and I observe it regularly giving line checks and on line flights where the pilots mistakenly interpret that instruction as a clearance for high speed below 10;000 ft. Several of us Line Check Pilots (LCPs) have been reporting this and have called NorCal TRACON to try to get them to stop this practice. We have had no effect on stopping this from happening."

This condition persisted until we reached 1000 feet above airport in which time we decided to execute a missed approach. As earlier briefed; we elected to leave the gear in the down position and only clean up to flaps five. The rationale behind this decision was the fact we had a problem with the nose wheel coming down as well as the delayed retraction of flaps and gear associated with the MEL. The concern was possibly exacerbating the gear situation with the possibility of other gear not extending in the second attempt. It had been 10 minutes since we selected the landing gear lever to down with no nose gear indication thus far and with our fuel level in the back of our mind and the additional drag; we elected to run the QRH procedure for gear disagree. After running the checklist manually deploying the gear we heard and felt the nose gear release and fallen into place. We then received a green nose indication in advised ATC we would like to start the approach for the airport and as a precautionary; we decided to request priority handling to have equipment standing by. Just in case the nose wheel was not locked and collapsed upon landing. One of our jump seaters who was an ZZZ FO moved to the first observer seat and backed us up with the checklist as well as per our request; contacted maintenance and dispatch updating the company of our situation. The approaching landing was uneventful; and we proceeded to parking.

With the Captain as pilot flying he selected flight change for a pitch mode and set the altitude for SANGO (2800) in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude window. He and I have a discrepancy in what we remember being set in the altitude window.  I remember confirming 2800 and he remembers setting the altitude for the FAF (1800). I didn't realize the wrong altitude was in the MCP until approach gave us a low altitude warning.  At this time we climbed and corrected the altitude deviation.  I reset the appropriate altitude in the MCP and the rest of the approach was uneventful. Lessens learned are taking more time in holding to prepare for approach; verifying what you see; and use of VNAV.

column121: While at cruise; FL360; a ECAM chime and message appeared and disappeared quickly. I happened to be looking at the ECAM when it happened and registered the words main cargo loop. It happened again; too quickly to read fully. The third time it happened; it stayed on the ECAM and we were able to confirm the main cargo mid 2 loop fault. I ran the checklist for it out of the QRH; page 22-15; without incident. Less than 10 minutes later; the master caution light and bell came on; with the ECAM displaying the SMOKE WARNING and associated items. It went away without any input from us; but then came right back. The captain and I immediately donned our O2 masks and established comms; then accomplished the ECAM items. The warning began to intermittently come back and go away within seconds of each other; so we made the decision to divert. I had just looked at the nearest airfield page; so I knew ZZZ was the closest major airport with Crash Fire Rescue (CFR) capabilities. As a crew we agreed that ZZZ made the most sense; so I  requested priority handling with ZZZ center and got a descent and direct turn to ZZZ coordinated with them. The CA flew a high speed descent while I messaged dispatch our divert intent and got all required information for landing at ZZZ. We flew a visual approach in a 15/20 flap configuration to XXL without incident; stopping straight ahead abeam taxiway 1. CFR used their thermal imaging instrument to ensure no hot spots were detected; which none were. After they gave us the all clear we taxied to the gateway and shut down.We never smelled any smoke; nor had any other indications of it in the flight deck. The ECAM smoke warning went away after we initiated the descent. Dispatch did a good job of letting ZZZ tower know of our situation before we got there; and all ATC agencies were quick and professional at getting us on the ground quickly.

column121: A series of systems failures led to an engine fire shortly after takeoff.Just after raising the landing gear after lift off we; the crew; heard and felt a vibration that was very much like a nose wheel rubbing on the scrubbers; and we smelled what we thought was burnt rubber.  We all thought that a nose tire had perhaps failed and was disintegrating against the scrubbers.   Each of us had experienced this before.  However; this vibration went on too long.  At this point we were at around 1000 AFE and the #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity.The #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity to the standpipe level; but we still had hydraulic pressure.  I decided to wait until we were in a lower threat phase of flight to deal with this issue.  We were perhaps now at 1500 AFE and I noticed that the #2 engine vibration was very high.  I called this out to the crew.  I don't remember the exact number.  All other engine indications were normal; and the N1 and EGT matched the other engines (as far as I can recall). Then; the #2 engine failed. The Relief Pilot called out #2 engine failure.  I decided to run the engine failure checklist.  The FO advised me to wait until flaps were up.  This is the correct procedure following a V1 cut; but I felt that in this case we were high enough to begin the checklist.  However; I agreed to the FO's suggestion.  At this point we were probably 2000 AFE.  I notified ATC and the engine caught fire. The #2 engine caught fire and I ran the fire checklist while the FO flew.  At this point the vibration was gone and we knew what the problem actually was.  The fire went out after the first fire bottle.I now took over pilot flying duties.  We returned to ZZZZ for a landing and the fire department checked the aircraft while we were on the runway.  The fire was out and we had the necessary hydraulics to taxi back to the ramp so we taxied back and shut down.Maintenance later showed me that we had multiple bird strikes all over the aircraft and much damage as a result; including a hole in the right wing root.Perhaps I could have ran the severe engine damage checklist before the engine failed.  However; all engine indications except the vibration were normal.  I would have expected a high EGT; surging N1 and banging noises if we had severe engine damage; and we had none of these.
column123: Upon gear retraction; we heard what we thought was nose gear scrubbing. The sound persisted; and grew louder; and we even commented how none of us had ever had a nose gear make that sound for that long. We then smelled what we thought was burning rubber. Passing through 1500; we got engine vibrations indications on the EICAS engine display. Shortly after; HYD QTY 2 LO caution alert. As Relief Pilot; I kept an eye on number 2 engine indicator; and shortly after called out that #2 was rolling back. We then got ENGINE 2 FAIL alert. Captain notified ATC; called for checklist; but FO (PF) recommended we wait until cleanup. Capt agreed. Shortly after; we received OVHT ENGINE 2 NAC; then subsequent FIRE ENGINE 2. At this time; we were around 3500; climbing to 4000; and decided to run Engine fire 2 checklist. We reported engine failure with ATC; and began immediate vectors back to ZZZZ for an approach to RWY XXL. Being below max landing weight; we had no concerns with the relatively quick vectors; Captain and FO ran checklists and set up the FMS; I ran landing performance; and we reported to ATC our information and Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) requirements. Still suspecting nose gear and hydraulic issues causing the fire; we discussed stopping on the runway for inspection. Capt flew the approach; and we landed uneventfully. We stopped on the runway; ARFF trucks inspected and saw no further damage or fire; and we opted to taxi to parking under power. Upon parking; maintenance teams discovered significant bird evidence and damage. We had discussed birds during the CRM/threat briefing. However; suggestions the future include caution against confirmation bias. The timing of the vibrations and noise were perfectly coincident with what we thought was a nose gear spinning in the wheel well; and further confirmation bias from what we thought was burning rubber. Aside from that; we all acknowledged external factors; such as the recent similar accident; caused a little extra stress that might not otherwise exist. However; this incident certainly cemented the importance of having a full crew; as we all worked together and each was able to contribute to bringing the event to a safe conclusion.

column121: During transition into DFW from FL310 we executed the appropriate 'Descent Checklist' and set the altimeters to 30.57. Throughout the arrival there was no indication of error from ATC. Upon reaching DELMO at what we believed to be 12;000 MSL we were given a frequency change to 118.42 and instructed to continue our descent to 6000 MSL. During the descent we were instructed to expedite and given additional clearances to 5000msl while turning base; 4000 MSL on base; and 3000 MSL on base to final. While rolling out on a 160 heading to intercept the 18R LOC for the visual approach. ATC asked us to verify our altitude. At this point we were still descending to 3000 MSL indicated. ATC then verified the altimeter setting of 29.57 and instructed us to level at 2300 MSL. Nearly simultaneously ATC issued a 'low altitude alert'. I immediately disengaged the Auto Pilot and pitched slightly nose high to level and reduce speed from 210 kts. While maneuvering the aircraft the  PM was able to get the appropriate altimeter setting and we were able to use his PFD (Primary Flight Display) to verify altitude. Once acceptable altitude and heading for the approach was achieved I was able to set my altimeter to the appropriate setting and proceed with a stable approach to landing. Cause: Multiple factors contributed to causing this incident. Pilot complacency with higher altimeter settings associated with cooler climate therefore not being alerted to the significant change when arriving in a warmer environment. Misinterpretation of the ATIS altimeter setting; failure to verify the altimeter setting; and lastly a lack of warning from ATC that previous altitude restrictions at altitude had been missed by nearly 1;000 MSL. Suggestions: Apply common sense when returning to warmer climates after conducting consecutive operations in cooler weather.
column123: When descending on the boove7 into DFW passing 18k we set the wrong altimeter setting. 30.57 instead of 29.57. We descended down to 12k indicated with approach and when handed off told to descend to 6k and expedite. We continued to descend and were told to continue down to 5k and turn 15 degrees right eventually. We continuously descended from 12k towards our final cleared altitude of 3k as we turned final. Approach asked if we were going down to 2300 because we were cleared to 3000 and I replied were at approx 3300 going to 3k. ATC responded we were already below that and gave us the correct altimeter setting. Fo flying disengaged autopilot to stop descent and begin climbing. We reset the altimeter to the correct setting and were cleared for the approach and handed to tower. FO continued to hand fly the visual to landing. Cause: Usually an altimeter that high would cause a second glance but with this weeks cold front that had been a typical setting. Checking the ATIS against the setting an additional time would have also caught the error. Our printer was having clarity issues and we read our takeoff v speeds off our EFB to verify they were correct due to a misprint. ATC never noticed or alerted us that we had been low on the arrival even when leveling off at the bottom altitude then we were given a continuous descent down until the lower than assigned altitude was noticed. When approach gave us the altimeter on initial contact it wasn't noticed that it was different than what we had set. Suggestions: Double check the ATIS printout more regularly and if ATC notices an aircraft below the level off final altitude it is indicative of an incorrect altimeter setting.

Upon landing some GPS functionality started to return such as terrain displays and the FO's clock.Caused by the military doing broad and unannounced jamming operations. Either the military adequately warns of such activity or cease them all together. Disruption of civilian air traffic into terrain sensitive airports is not acceptable.

While in route the first report was 2/2/2 with 3 inches of wet snow on the runway of intended use. We were informed that they were currently working on the runway to improve conditions. With full thrust reverse almost any application of the brakes cause the airplane to slide on the runway. We managed to eventually slow the aircraft and had to come to a complete stop before attempting to turn off at the very end of the runway but still slid a great deal while attempting the turn. Taxiing very slowing back to the gate the taxiways were no better causing us to slide with any attempt to slow the aircraft. Out of safety concerns we did not operate the flight back to ZZZ that night.The next day we returned to the airport to attempt to return to ZZZ. The trucks worked on the runway conditions for several hours and the reported to us 3/3/3 with 1/8-inch dry compacted snow. After the events of the previous evening we asked if they would take us out to see the runway conditions for ourselves. It was at the time we discovered that it was 1/8-inch or more of 100% ice with 1/8-inch or more snow on top over the entire runway surface. The truck taking us to the runway slide every time doing a brake check going only 20 mph. He allowed us to get out the truck and confirm it was ice which was difficult to even walk on. The ice was obvious yet the station did not want to report it.Cause: The airport not accurately reporting the runway conditions.Suggestions: Audit the airport and their runway condition reporting procedures.

column121: ZZZ - AGS. Upon landing in AGS on Runway 17 at approximately XA:00; we slowed to make our taxi off at the end of the runway onto Taxiway Foxtrot. It was difficult to identify a taxiway lead-off line as it was not painted entirely onto the runway. Additionally; because of airport construction there appeared to be an extra piece of pavement prior to Taxiway Foxtrot that was not accurately depicted on the airport diagram. Due to this misinterpretation and dark conditions; my Captain preemptively made the turn onto the additional concrete before the taxiway. We both realized that we had initiated the turn too early and immediately came to a stop. We explained to Tower that we had made the turn too early but were still on the runway. In communication with Tower; we attempted to make a 180-degree turn to get ourselves back into a position to enter the taxiway. However; the taxiway lights were positioned into the runway and prevented us from making a turn. My Captain then attempted to make a turn in the other direction. However; I had to ask him to stop as one of the runway marking signs was in the way of our expected path. We decided as a crew that it was best to come to a stop and have a tug come out to push us back. Tower helped us to coordinate with Operations to have a tug enter the runway and assist in pushing us back. Communication was made with the passengers and flight attendants before the tug pushed us back about 20 feet. This was enough for us to then disconnect and move under our own power. We then back-taxied down the runway and finally to our gate.Cause: I think both my Captain and I could have done a better job of confidently identifying the taxiway before making the turn using the taxiway lights as cues. Overall; I believe the cause of the mistake was the lack of markings and mapping of this additional pavement caused by the ongoing construction. Once we had initiated this turn; there was no way of straightening back out to correct the mistake as the taxiway lights protruded far into the runway and the runway marking sign impeded our path in the other direction.
column123: Upon landing on Runway 17; we rolled to the end to get off runway. As we made the turn we realized we were not on taxiway; but rather some piece of pavement next to taxiway. Multiple construction vehicles still working.

column121: While operating as PIC from FAR to ZZZ; we prepared for push. We had good communications with ramp crew. During pushback; we were cleared to start engines. My FO started the right engine. The push crew pushed us; stopped; and continued the push several times. I had been told my previous trip to Fargo that they were still creating the proper procedures to push aircraft off of the new gates; so we attributed the several stops to the push crew being unfamiliar with the new area and push procedures.At one point; we stopped for a longer period of time. I asked the push operator if we were complete with the push; but got no response. I then noticed we seemed to be moving forward. I asked why we were moving forward and got no response. I looked further down below the nose while trying to determine why we were getting no response and saw what looked like people working near the nosewheel while my FO announced that we were definitely moving forwards.I chose to slam on the brakes to avoid possibly running over the ground grew who appeared to be near the nosewheel. I then told the tug operator to stop everything and tell me what was going on before we continued. column121: On day 0 I was put on the engine change crew to continue with the remove & replace of #2 engine on aircraft x. My first job was to apply the protective coating on the bottom of the aft engine mount due to corrosion that was found during the after removal of engine lower pylon inspection. Upon first application of the primer i noticed that the bottom outboard mating surface of the aft engine mount had in my opinion a substantial amount of pitting. I ceased operation and notified the inspector of my finding. The inspector did a visual of the area and told me that it was ok to continue the application of the second coat and the area was within limits.the initial found fault of corrosion found during the engine inspection was already documented and signed off as removed corrosion per the applicable aircraft maintenance manual (amm). I initially took his word for it and continued because i was just coming to a somewhat extensive and lengthy job and assumed that everything had been researched and performed per any applicable amm or structural repair manual (srm). While waiting on the paint to cure enough for work to be performed i did start research in the srm to look for limitations on corrosion in certain areas. I found a few items in the srm that went over engine mounts and brought it to the inspectors attention. There were some limits that we went over and came to agreement that .020 was a max allowable limit on certain areas. I do recall looking mainly in the srm i did also eventually look in the amm and found a ref for the inspection of the aft engine mount. At this point i was still taking into consideration that he is a quality control inspector and that he has  more extensive training in limits and expectations of repairs of damaged areas on the aircraft as well as the experience of seeing discrepancies like this on a more regular basis. After we had hung the engine and installed engine mount bolts i looked back at the task card and noticed that the engine install( the task the inspector said was used for the inspection) referenced the removal of corrosion amm for both the inspection of the lower pylon fwd and aft fittings as well as the lower longeron and the remove corrosion if found item. In my opinion i could not see how you can use a reference to remove corrosion as a reference for doing an inspection. I went to the amm for the inspection of the aft engine mount and found that it calls out for the removal of the mount itself to do the inspection. I then brought it up to everybody i believe and pressed the issue until we were instructed to remove the engine by our manager. We subsequently found a substantial amount of corrosion in the pylon bolt holes at the point where i went off shift. I was questioned as to why; if i believed that the pitting corrosion was not in limits then why would i assist in the engine install up to the point of where i called for the removal. The only answer i can give is that i was trusting of the judgement of my fellow mechanic/inspector but for my sake and the safety of the aircraft/lives i was still going to continue research until i was either satisfied with the inspectors signoff or i found documented evidence that disputed him. I was concerned about flight safety and my fellow union members that were working on it and was willing to call for the engine removal no matter what step of the install we were on. For the human factors i believe i can attribute: 1: lack of communication on my part by not communicating my concern to someone outside like technical support/engineering/maintenance control; 2 lack of knowledge: not knowing the corrosion limits and stopping the job until everybody was in agreement that the aircraft was safe in a timely manner; 3 lack of assertiveness: not injecting my concerns severity sooner.;  this report has been submitted in good faith and the events/timeline that happened have been reported to the best of my recollection.

column121: Event: Pilot A (Instructor) and Pilot B (member tasked to look after the plane 'MX OFFICER') took the C172S for a maintenance checkout flight after the 100hr inspection with Maintenance at ZZZ. The fuel tanks had no visible debris. The left tank had 15 gal and the right tank had 16 gal of 100LL. The right tank had tiny water droplets (about 1 mm); which were poured away. No water observed in the left tank. Three laps in the pattern (.6 of hobbs time) were completed without issue. The plane was placed back in service. No fuel was added given that there was a line at the fuel pumps and the fuel truck was not available. The next flight was scheduled right after the end of this flight. The next flight was an aircraft transition training flight with Pilot A (Instructor) and Pilot C (PPL only with about 240hrs). Three laps in the pattern were completed. The first lap was Go Around due to a gust during flare making the aircraft climb. Pilot C initiated a Go Around. The second lap was a normal landing and takeoff (touch and go). During the third lap; Pilot C completed a GUMPSS flow: fuel selector BOTH; mixture FULL RICH; light switches ON and seat and seat belts SECURED. Once abeam the numbers; Pilot C reduced the power and aimed for 1500 RPMs. The RPMs showed 1200 RPMs. Pilot C realized the difference and slightly added power. The MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) displayed 1700 RPMs. Pilot C was distracted by the RPM settings and started to extend the downwind leg while descending. Pilot A noticed a change in propeller sound different from the usual increase in RPMs and similar to an rudder only turn during cruise. Pilot A checked the position of the 'ball' in the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and confirmed it was centered. Pilot A then noticed the altitude of about 600' MSL and prompted a turn to base. Pilot C noticed higher than usual RPM changes and asked Pilot A to take over to rule out Pilot C's improper throttle changes. Pilot A took controls during the base turn and confirmed the propeller sound was still present and decided to do a full stop landing to troubleshoot on the ground. Pilot C agreed. Pilot A turned final and confirmed the fuel selector was BOTH; fuel shut off was IN; mixture was FULL RICH; and magnetos were on BOTH. Oil pressure was in the green arc; oil temperature was in the green arc and fuel flow was still in the green arc. When Pilot A confirmed the aircraft could glide to the runway; he reduced the throttle to IDLE. The propeller slowed down more than usual. Over the numbers; Pilot A set the flaps to 20 degrees (10 degrees already added on downwind). After touchdown the propeller stopped windmilling and came to a complete stop. Pilot A used the energy remaining to let the aircraft roll to the first exit; ([Taxiway] 1) and called [clear of the runway attempting to roll all the way clear]. After crossing the taxi intersection; Pilot A applied brakes and brought the aircraft to a complete stop. Pilot A called Pilot B and reported the issue. Pilot A restarted the plane without prime and the aircraft started without a problem. The aircraft was taxied to its parking spot and shutdown. A magneto ground check did not show any issues. Pilot B met the aircraft with a representative of Maintenance. The aircraft was secured and was not refueled. What I believed caused the problem:I believe the throttle control settings may caused the problem. After repeated use of the throttle controls the settings inside the cowling may have come loose and caused the engine to stop. I believe something was not properly secured during the 100hr inspection. No debris or water was found after inspection of the fuel sumps (left; right and engine). There were no changes in the mixture during flight. The aircraft restarted and taxied without problems on the ground. Not sure what can be done to prevent the recurrence

column121: We were enroute to MWC.  We were eventually cleared direct to MWC.  We were in between layers at 6000 ft with an overcast deck about 2000 ft below.  Handed off to MKE approach. ATC cleared us direct IVALY; cross at or above 2600 ft; cleared the RNAV 4L approach to MWC; circle to runway 33R.  We descended to 4500 ft just above the deck; crossed IVALY and began an expedited descent to the next step down of 2300 ft at OWYAL.  We broke out at about 3000 ft  and advised approach with a report of light rime ice at about 3500 and our break out altitude just above 3000. Approach instructed us to contact tower.  At this point we were still about 3 miles from OWYAL.  We contacted tower with position reported as outside OWYAL.  Tower asked if we wanted to land runway 4L or circle to 33R; winds 300 at 10kts.  We elected to circle and tower said 'circle southwest of the airport and enter left base for 33R.'  We had the airport in sight and began to maneuver to enter an extended left base for 33R descending to  pattern altitude of 1745 ft.  Tower calls out an altitude alert saying 'we don't have a standard approach altitude.'  We believe we were cleared on a visual segment of the approach via circling instructions.  We replied that we were entering an extended left base for 33R and asked tower to confirm that we were cleared to land.  Cleared to land 33R ahead of traffic from the NE.  Landed and cleared at taxiway C; B; B1 with no further comment or issue.  Why the altitude alert?  Tower may have been tracking the profile for a straight in approach to 4L which would have alerted the altitude below the stepdown floor of 2300 prior to reaching OWYAL.  Raises another question:  when should you break off your approach and begin circling?  Wait until the MAP?  Or proceed visual when cleared to circle while maintaining visual contact with the airport?    Wait until within the circling radius for your category?  At the MDA the protected area at the circling altitude for category A aircraft is 1.1 nm radius from the approach end of the runway.  But at pattern altitude the whole class D area should be OK.

column121: On this night we were on approach to the ZZZ airport. My CA was high mins so I was pilot monitoring for the flight. Roughly 20 miles out we were given direct to ZZZZZ and pilots discretion to descend and maintain 2000' which we complied with given we were doing the visual approach to rwy XX backed up by the ILS. As we were switched to tower and I was completing the final configuration and before landing check the Captain had bugged 1000 feet and asked me to confirm which I did; however I also advised we were still below GS intercept and can remain level. We did begin our descent to 1000 feet still which prior to alts cap ATC had advised us of a Low Altitude Alert which we corrected immediately and recaptured to the proper GP on the PAPI. We landed uneventfully and no GPWS event was triggered as well. Looking back at the situation I realize as the PM and FO I should have been more assertive with my CA to level off the aircraft and capture the GS before descending and I should not have confirmed 1000 feet as we were already below MSA and the lowest we could have descended to was 1700 feet for the TPA. In the future I will make sure to be more assertive in ensuring the PF makes the proper corrective action regardless of position and be more aware of TPA and MSA's when setting altitudes to descend to on visual approaches.

column121: While flying day; VMC to DEN RWY34R; we were cleared for the visual approach on a dogleg heading and 9000' with instructions to maintain 170 kts to CORDE (FAF). FO had a 2 mile ring around CORDE for SA; and as a spot where he briefed he would drop the gear and call for flaps 15. FO armed the approach but we did not set a lower altitude. CORDE altitude is 7000' or above. Just outside of the 2 mile ring from the FAF I mentioned that we were high and needed a lower altitude set with the autopilot on; did he want 7000?  We then set 7000' and the plane began a shallow descent; but we were still high. Just inside the 2 mile ring (1.5 miles from CORDE) we were 600-700' high and going higher on the path. We lowered the gear; he called for flaps 15; and began to slow to his target speed of 160. We were now over 800' high; and I mentioned that it would be helpful to keep his speed up to lose the required altitude. He responded by increasing the MCP speed back toward 170 with the autopilot on. When I saw that we were over 1000' high on the path deviation scale I told him we that wasn't going to do it; we needed to get the nose down and increase our rate of descent; whereupon he disengaged the autopilot and pitched down a bit. We also went flaps 25 at this point. I assessed that we were too high to use V/S to capture glideslope from above in time to make the stabilization windows; but we were nearing glideslope as he hand flew the plane; at between 165-170 kts. I told him that the 1000' window was coming up; we should reduce the descent rate from what I recall was reading over 1800 fpm.Big failure on my part was that; as I was distracted with helping correct the descent rate and glideslope; I failed to mention that we still did not have final flaps at the 1000' window.FO was able to arrest the rate of descent; but; as we were nearing 600'; I recall that the PAPI was displaying 4 red (low); and we got a couple of 'glideslope' calls. As we were still slowing to our target speed I felt that by leveling off he would recapture glideslope from below about the same time we would hit our target speed; so I figured we'd be able to achieve the 500' stability window. However; as we neared the 500' window we received a 'too low; terrain' call and went around. The 'too low; terrain' call surprised me; as we were completely VMC and nowhere near dangerous terrain on final; but I then realized that we were not at flaps 30. I know that will sometimes cause a 'too low; terrain' call instead of a 'too low; flaps' call; which would've been more obvious as to what was wrong.In hindsight a 'too low; terrain' callout should be followed by a terrain escape maneuver instead of the go-around that we did.The go-around was uneventful; as was the subsequent landing on RWY35R.
column123: Upon receiving final vectors and being cleared for our approach to runway 34L; we were at 9000 MSL. This was 2000 ft above the FAF altitude leaving us high for the approach. I failed to notice this in a timely manner and did not request a lower altitude. This resulted in us being; high; fast and not fully configured as we approached our stabilization gates. I disconnected the autopilot in an attempt to capture the glide slope. By 1000 ft AGL; we had gear down; flaps 25 and were on speed but had not yet fully configured. By 500 AGL; I inaccurately stated that we were stable. We heard an aural callout as we descended below 500 AGL stating that we were too low. As we continued descending; we were still at Flaps 25 and had not completed a landing checklist. My CA then called for a go-around which I immediately initiated.

column121: On Day 0; I was pilot flying ZZZ1-ZZZ. When descending on the ZZZZZ arrival between 10;000-11;000 MS; we got an EICAS message of HYD 2 LO PRESSURE. I looked on the hydraulics page and there was no hydraulic pressure in system 2. The Captain requested ATC assistance and advised approach that we had XX souls on board and 4900 pounds of fuel. The Captain requested vectors so that we could stay out of the way of other aircraft and could run the checklist per the QRH. Once the Captain located the checklist he started going through it and while doing it; we also got the SPOILER FAULT EICAS message. The Captain completed the HYD 2 LO PRESSURE checklist items and HYD 2 LO PRESSURE remained annunciated; after that he worked on the SPOILER FAULT checklist and once that was completed; SPOILER FAULT extinguished. The Captain then calculated the landing numbers to get the appropriate V-speeds and landing distance. Once he got those numbers we transferred controls and he became the flying pilot and I became pilot monitoring.When the Captain called for gear down I moved the gear selector and the gear did not come down and we got the LG LEVER DISAGREE EICAS message. After completing this checklist; it called to go to the Alternate Landing Gear Extension Checklist which we completed and the gear came down.  After this; we notified ATC that we were ready to come in for landing; they gave us runway XX L which is up sloping. This was the most ideal choice as it would aid in stopping the aircraft. The landing was successful and soft but the plane did not have nose wheel steering; so differential braking was used to keep directional control. The Captain was able to slow the aircraft enough to make the high speed exit and clear the runway and make a slight right turn onto taxiway 1. Once on taxiway 1; the aircraft was stopped and we notified tower that we would need to stay there until we could get tugged in.Once tower was notified; the Captain notified the passengers; operations; and dispatch of the issue. We left the plane in the landing configuration; started the APU and left both engines running until the tug arrived. After waiting 25-30 minutes; tug came and we secured both engines and got towed. Once at the gate; all passengers deplaned and the Captain spoke to the dispatch supervisor and Maintenance Control and made the appropriate logbook entries.Cause: Aircraft loss of Hydraulic System 2.Suggestions: As second in command; I could've done a better job suggesting that we get in contact with dispatch; the passengers; and the flight attendants to keep everyone informed on the situation.

column121: On Day 0; I; Captain A; was operating flight ABCD from ZZZ1 to ZZZ as Pilot Monitoring. While on the ZZZZZ X arrival into ZZZ; at around 10;000 to 11;000 MSL; HYD 2 LO PRESS appeared on the EICAS. I looked at the Hydraulics page on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and noticed that there was no hydraulic pressure within system 2. I requested priority handling with ZZZ Approach; notified the controller of the fuel on board; which I believe was roughly 4900 pounds of fuel at the time; and that there were XX souls on board the aircraft. Because I was not the only operational aircraft arriving at ZZZ at the time; I requested with the approach controller to be vectored off the arrival procedure to stay out of the way while I began working on the QRH checklist items. I located the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist within the QRH and began going through the listed items. While completing this checklist; SPOILER FAULT also appeared on the EICAS. I continued with the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist items and completed the checklist. Once completed; HYD 2 LO PRESS remained annunciated. I began working on the SPOILER FAULT checklist. After completing the checklist items; SPOILER FAULT extinguished from being displayed on the EICAS. Following this; I used the non-normal section of the ERJ landing app to set the appropriate Vspeeds for landing. At that point I took control of the aircraft as Pilot Flying from First Officer Person B and had him run the Loss of Hydraulic System 2 QRH checklist.Once the landing gear was extended and all checklist items were complete; ZZZ ATC was notified that we were ready to come in for a landing. The landing runway that we were using was XXL as it is an upsloping runway. It was decided that this would be the best course of action to aid in stopping the aircraft. Additionally; I had also requested that emergency services follow the aircraft up the runway after we land. The landing was successful and soft. Because I had no rudder control or nosewheel steering upon touchdown; differential braking was used to keep directional control of the aircraft. I was able to slow the aircraft enough to make a slight right turn onto Taxiway 1; clear the runway; and make another slight right turn onto Taxiway 2. At that point; I stopped the aircraft; communicated with the tower controller that I would need to remain in the current position; as I was unable to make larger right or left turns and would have to be towed into the gate.After communicating with the tower controller; I informed the passengers; operations; and dispatch of the issue; and that the airplane would have to be towed to the gate. I left the aircraft in the landing configuration; started the APU; and left both engines running until the tug arrived roughly 25 to 30 minutes later. Once the tug arrived; I secured both engines; the tug was attached to the aircraft; and the aircraft was successfully towed to gate XX. Once at the gate; all passengers were deplaned; dispatch transferred me to a supervisor to notify them of the event; and I conversed with Maintenance Control in the logbook entry for the event.Cause: Aircraft loss of hydraulic system 2.Suggestions: According to the HYD 2 LO PRESS QRH checklist; if the HYD 2 LO PRESS remains annunciated on the EICAS; after turning the associated HYDRAULIC ELEC PUMP to the OFF position; the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist is complete; and I am supposed to complete the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 checklist. Instead of doing this; I went ahead and completed the SPOILER FAULT checklist instead. Had I continued with the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 checklist; as I should have; I would have known that it is stated not to accomplish the SPOILER FAULT checklist.Additionally; because of the feeling stress; I failed to inform the dispatcher; the flight attendants; and the passengers of the situation at hand. Looking back at the situation; I had plenty of time and fuel remaining that I could have accomplished communicating with dispatch; the flight attendants; and the passengers.

column121: In cruise; we noticed lightning on the horizon across a very wide area and activated the on-board radar. The tops were stratiform in all directions. The stratiform layer rose as we progressed; so we requested FL360 to maintain the ability to corroborate what we were seeing outside with the weather radar. The radar began painting a few isolated cells in the vicinity of ZZZZZ when we were 160nm away. The cells appeared well-defined and reasonably dispersed. We discussed a preliminary plan for diverting around the weather and agreed to proceed unchanged until we were approximately 80nm from the cells where we would have a more clearly-defined understanding of the weather as depicted on the radar. We also coordinated with center to verify the information we were seeing. At approx 80nm from ZZZZZ; we began a left deviation with the intention to later turn right direct the ZZZ VOR and then direct ZZZ. According to on board radar and center control; this was a safe path well clear of cells. As a matter of caution; I turned on the seatbelt sign and ordered the flight attendants to take their jump seats. We were still in smooth air; but conditions began to deteriorate to occasional and then to continuous moderate. The FO said to take over the airplane if I felt it necessary. Suddenly; airspeed dropped precipitously by approx 30kias. I said;Power! Power!" to the FO. He rapidly responded by applying TOGA power and asked if APR was necessary. I said no as airspeed was rapidly recovering. It is important to note the weather radar had previously showed no weather at or beneath the location where this happened at any point leading up to or at this location. Moments later; the autopilot disconnected as the airplane lurched suddenly into approximately 20 degrees of left bank and 7 degrees of pitch up accompanied by a rapid loss of airspeed. I took control of the airplane and called;"My aircraft." I leveled the nose immediately and leveled the wings while simultaneously reapplying TOGA thrust. Focused on maintaining attitude; I allowed deviations in altitude but remained very conscious of airspeed as it fell. I ordered the FO to call a descent to FL340 to ATC as a means of maintaining airspeed as the airspeed was initially completely unresponsive to the increased thrust and I felt a descent necessary to stay on the correct side of the power curve. In approximately negative 2 degrees of pitch; the airplane initially began descending to approx FL355 and then rapidly climbed to approx FL365 while still pitched down as the airspeed rapidly recovered before the FO could inform ATC. The airplane came back under positive control and I modified my instructions to the FO; 'Inform ATC of a severe turbulence encounter with deviations +/-500 feet.' The airplane remained under positive control thereafter; although for 5 or 10 minutes a very high thrust setting (CLB) was frequently necessary to maintain .75M; which we had been flying at before; during; and after the encounter. I returned control to the FO and the rest of the flight proceeded as normal except for a later STALL FAIL caution message in the descent to ZZZ. No one was injured and there was no apparent damage to the aircraft."
column123: In cruise at FL340 we notice build up from weather ahead; our radars indicated widespread perception in direction of our flight. After talking to ATC with the information they made available to us we requested to climb to FL360 and received the clearance to do. Looking at the on board radar and talking to center about what they're seeing up ahead; we determined it was best to deviate left of course where there weren't any radar echos on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) or what ATC was seeing on their side. We request a deviation left of course and receive the approval. A few minutes into the new cruise altitude; we start getting moderate chop to moderate turbulence with airspeed fluctuations requiring me to put in TOGA thrust to get back up .75 Mach. When then hit severe turbulence getting major altitude and airspeed fluctuations disabling the autopilot. Captain took over pilot flying duties and I took over pilot monitoring duties during the upset recovery from the severe turbulence. We alerted/requested ATC that we were descending from FL360 to FL340; for a greater buffet boundary as we were having a hard time maintaining airspeed and altitude due to the turbulence. After leveling at FL340 the fluctuations continued with moderate chop to moderate turbulence. The turbulence stopped approximately 3 minutes after leveling at FL340; we determined with the radar and ATC that it was clear ahead. I called in the back to talk to the flight attendants to make sure everyone was okay and no one was hurt. The captain gave me control of the aircraft back and rest of the flight proceeded as normal; except for receiving a STALL FAIL caution message in the descent into ZZZ.

column123: Once jet bridge was pulled Captain called for rampers via operations since no one had answered our calls down below. column121: On Day 0 while operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We experienced a pressurization issue shortly after departure. During the climb; the cabin was not pressurizing as expected and cabin altitude indications were not responding normally.we had a rapid rate of cabin altitude ascent. We proceed to stop the climb out and stop at 7;000 feet to stop the cabin from climbing.Prior to departure we did write up that the N1 gauges were showing a big split between each other on the ground at the gate. Maintaience came and looked at the issue which was written up a similar way for this aircraft earlier. Maintaience put the right pack back on Mel even though it had been cleared in ZZZ2 just prior to this flight. I questioned that choice and spoke with the dispatcher; duty pilot and maintenance control. Maintenance control went through the previous write up and looked to see what was done. I was informed that the problem the aircraft had for the pressurization issue prior was not related with the pack and that they performed tests of pressurization in accordance with Boeing standard procedures. After speaking with maintenance control my FO and I were comfortable taking the aircraft as they said what test and checks were done by maintenance and the plane was safe to continue for service.Once we leveled off and communicated with ATC. I immediately directed my attention to the abnormal indication and the FO and I accomplished the applicable QRH procedure for pressurization malfunction. The aircraft was leveled off as required and we began coordinating a return to ZZZ.Given the proximity to the departure airport; ATC coordination; aircraft configuration considerations; and time compression associated with the abnormal condition; my focus was primarily on safely flying the aircraft; completing the QRH; and setting up for the return and landing. The decision was made to return to ZZZ.During this period of high workload and compressed timeline; I overlooked referring the FOM for additional considerations related to overweight landing and did not formally declare an emergency with ATC. ATC was informed about what the situation was and that we were doing a checklist and our plans to return to ZZZ. The QRH checklist was followed for the overweight landing and what to expect and to do a landing assessment. In that QRH under additional items which was after checklist completion it had a few lengthy paragraphs about overweight landing characteristics and a line about going to the FOM for more guidance which I overlooked about the FOM. In retrospect; referencing the FOM would have prompted a formal emergency declaration due to the overweight landing condition.The approach and landing were uneventful. The aircraft landed safely without injury to passengers or crew and without aircraft damage. After clearing the runway; we coordinated with maintenance and completed the appropriate write-ups in the aircraft logbook regarding the pressurization malfunction and overweight landing.Upon reflection; this event reinforced the importance of deliberate consideration of administrative and procedural follow-through such as emergency declaration requirements even when the operational outcome appears controlled and manageable. In the future; I will ensure that; workload permitting; I take a moment to cross-check FOM guidance when abnormal situations involve potential overweight landings or other criteria requiring formal declaration.Safety was maintained throughout the event; and all required documentation was completed.Cause: Aircraft had recent pressurization-related write-up. The Right pack was re-MEL'd after being cleared.Although maintenance stated issue was unrelated; prior history may have increased system vulnerability. There is also a potential normalization of repeat discrepancy.I think to mitigate this would be to not dispatch an aircraft with a repeat item in the same day with similar write up issues and investigate the problem closer.
column123: While completing fms preflight tasks; I noticed that the takeoff N1 settings were mismatched and fluctuating. This mirrored a similar maintenance issue the previous crew had with this aircraft; that resulted in a loss of pressurization. Maintenance was already at the aircraft due to other write ups; and they were notified right away. Eventually; an MEL was applied to the right pack; but as the captain and I were noticing that this event felt very similar to the events leading up to the previous loss of pressurization; the captain called both the duty pilot and maintenance control to express our concern. Ultimately we felt convinced that the aircraft would be safe after a thorough explanation from maintenance control; explaining that a leak test was conducted; and that the right pack MEL and N1 differential was most likely not associated with the cause of the pressurization issue earlier in the day. After an hour from when maintenance was first called we pushed back. On departure we noted that the actual takeoff N1 settings were not within .5 percent of the performance data setting; but we interpreted that to be in accordance with the pack inoperative MEL. The taxi and take off went normally; but on the initial climb out we noticed cabin altitude climbing at around 2000 feet per minute; and our ears were popping. We leveled off at 7000; and the captain transferred radios to me(I was already pilot flying); and then notified dispatch. The bleeds were set in accordance with the MEL; with the right pack off; the left pack on; and the isolation valve closed. It was then determined that we should return to ZZZ; which was coordinated with dispatch and then ATC. The captain ran the overweight landing checklist; and the non routine landing considerations checklist; while I flew the aircraft and set up the aircraft for a landing in ZZZ. The cabin altitude warning checklist was not completed; as we never received a cabin altitude warning. Unfortunately both the captain and I missed that an emergency needed to be declared when landing overweight. We landed safely; and returned to gate XX; and all passengers were deplaned right away.Cause: I believe that a more thorough investigation by maintenance could have prevented this incident. Both myself and the captain continuously expressed concern about the similarities of our situation and the event described to us by the previous crew. With hindsight I wish we would've held more firm in not accepting the aircraft.

column121: This report is documenting a flight did not operate event for an airplane without an APU that we were scheduled to fly for two legs (ZZZ-ZZZZ-ZZZ1). The day before this; I operated Flight ABCD from ZZZZ1 to ZZZ without an APU. Although the APU was listed as inop in the MEL. ZZZ ops was not aware of the APU inop on arrival. Although we called ops on the ground in ZZZ to ensure power and air would be available at the gate (XX); they failed to have a jetway driver at the gate (so no ground power) and ground personnel were unaware that we would be leaving an engine running for en extended period of time; leading to an unsafe situation with the wing walker moving towards an operating engine and no control of vehicle traffic behind the aircraft.Report narrative of flight did not operate.Just prior to closing the aircraft door for departure out of ZZZ; the APU automatically shutdown. Maintenance accomplished a restart and the APU automatically shutdown a second time for high APU oil temperature. Maintenance informed me of their intentions to MEL the APU as inoperative for our next 2 legs through ZZZZ to ZZZ1. The temperature in ZZZZ was forecast to be 84 degrees; and I felt that would have caused uncomfortable cabin temperatures at the gate and on departure. In addition; my experience with issues of not having a gate agent/jetway driver upon arrival (for ground power from the jetway) as well as potential of having inexperienced ground personnel around a running engine; and language issues complicating communication; had me concerned about safety issues on arrival at these locations. For those reasons; I placed a flight did not operate entry in the logbook. Report narrative of Flight ABCD Day 0.Prior to boarding in ZZZZ1 with no ground power or conditioned air available at gate XY; the APU automatically shutdown. We accomplished the APU fault checklist and coordinated for maintenance; ground power; conditioned air for the cabin and for the potential need for pneumatic air cart. With coordination from maintenance and Maintenance Control we conducted an APU restart and the APU again automatically shutdown. The APU was MEL'd and we proceeded with appropriate supplemental procedures and coordination for departure. The weather in ZZZZ1 was 84 degrees and cloudy. We had conditioned air prior to boarding and all necessary ground equipment standing by. At the time; I felt ZZZ should be a competent station to safely receive an aircraft without an APU. The cabin temperature got uncomfortably warm during the crossbleed start but cooled relatively quickly in flight. The APU was in the MEL and we felt ZZZ should have been aware of the aircraft status for arrival. After an uneventful flight and landing on Runway XX in ZZZ; we called ZZZ ops on the short taxi to gate XX. The FO asked ops if power and electrics would be available immediately on arrival at [gate] XX. Ops said something like 'understand you are asking for power and air; does that mean you have an issue with your APU?' The FO responded that the APU was inop and we would need electrics and air conditioning at arrival. Ops told us power and air would be available but I don't recall their exact words.We taxied to the gate and set brakes. I looked towards the operating engine and saw the wing walker walking from the wing tip towards the operating engine. She took about four steps then stopped briefly before taking another step or two towards the running engine. I opened my window and motioned for her or someone on the ground to get her away from the left engine. I was prepared to shut the engine down if she continued moving towards it. A supervisor yelled in her direction and she moved outboard of and aft of the wing to stop traffic on the road behind us.I then looked at the jetway and realized we didn't have a jetway driver; and therefore had no ground power available. The FO called ops and asked for a jetway driver. The response was that an agent was on the way. The agent arrived at the gate a few minutes later and we waited for the jetway to be positioned before ground power could be provided to the plane.I felt the entire process of receiving an aircraft without an APU was handled without urgency or an understanding from ops or ground personnel of the potential dangers involved. I felt like we were communicating the situation but we weren't understood. To make matters worse; we had an FAA representative on the jump seat witnessing the entire event.

Maintenance Control was still on the radio and we told them what happened. At that moment we decided to head back to ZZZ. Knowing that we were going to be very overweight we requested priority handling and had personnel waiting for us. We briefed each other; the FAs and passengers of the situation. We got the airplane ready for landing in ZZZ and landed without any incident. We exited the runway and had personnel verify our brake temps before entering the terminal area. column121: There is a new landfill pit that garbage is being dumped into on a 1 mile final to Runway 36L. We cross that point at 500 feet RA. I've noticed excavating on previous flights but on Day 0 I saw that garbage was being dumped into this pit. Landfills create thermals and attract large birds like seagulls. Not a great idea just short of a runway. I again flew into AUS the next day; Day 1; and I saw more garbage being dumped into there. On the ground I mentioned to my FO that this new landfill pit will cause thermals and attract birds; so be wary on upcoming flights. column121: Headed to ZZZ with winter weather moving in. Weather at destination had been a bit variable over the time period we had been watching it prior to our arrival.340 to 360 5-8kts visibility was reporting 6-7 miles ceilings were 600+ temp just above freezing around 2-3c. Due to the high tail wind and decreasing weather conditions we were concerned with being able to land XX in ZZZ. Weather in ZZZ1 had been similar however wind had been reporting higher. There was a lot of discussion about the pros and cons of shooting the ILS to XX and landing with a tail wind vs LOC XX circle XY. We did run our EFB for both directions and they both worked with current conditions. However with the wind just below the limit at ZZZ1 made Captain nervous with conditions worsening. He called tower directly over the radio and got a weather report. I don't remember what that report was I believe higher winds from the north. He also mentioned tower hadn't had any traffic in a while so no runway condition report. Visibility was reporting plenty good so we opted for the LOC XX circle XY. On the approach we broke out higher than I was expecting however visibility was not what was reported. In particular on the south end of the field. We circled at the published MDA however we forgot about the NOTAM with a MDA 60ft higher. At the time we were both completely unaware we had made the mistake. Around the downwind to base leg tower gave us a low level alert which we confirmed our altitude. Shortly after we lost sight of the airport and went missed. Which leads to the second error. The turn away from the airport. Captain said I lost sight of the airport tell them we are going missed. I call tower and let them know; they acknowledged and told us to fly the published missed. Captian hits the go around button brings power up then makes no call outs. I query him about setting flaps to setting two. He replied flaps two. Then immediately calls gear up. I raised flaps to two and put the gear up. In the time period he started making a right turn away from the airport. I could tell he was behind the plane. I didn't want to cause more confusion or debate with correcting him at this point. So checked the chart for obstacles. When my eyes get back to the PFD (Primary Flight Display) I notice we are well beyond 30 degrees of bank so I called out bank angle. He corrects however is a little aggressive with the controls when he does. At this point we continue on with the missed and divert to ZZZ1.

column121: During pre-departure preparations for Flight ABCD (ZZZ-ZZZ1); maintenance personnel entered the flight deck approximately ten minutes before door closure to check oil levels and advised us they would service the No. 2 engine. We acknowledged and continued normal duties. After receiving matching passenger counts from the flight attendant and release; I authorized door closure. Both packs were operating at that time; and no abnormal odors were present.Seconds after the door closed; while awaiting the flight attendant's cabin secure" report; I detected an acrid; "old socks/burning" odor on the flight deck with no visible smoke. I immediately turned both packs off and opened the DV (direct vision) windows to ventilate. The flight attendant confirmed the odor was also present in the cabin. With windows open and recirculation fans on; the smell began to dissipate. I contacted Maintenance Control and described the situation. They requested that we turn each pack on individually to isolate the source. I expressed concern about reintroducing fumes; but they advised the effect should be minimal with ventilation.We briefed the flight attendant and instructed her to open the service door if the odor returned. Pack 1 produced no abnormal smell. Upon selecting Pack 2 on; the same strong acrid odor immediately returned; prompting us to turn Pack 2 off. The flight attendant opened the service door due to the intensity of the smell. At this point; I determined the aircraft was no longer safe for passengers or crew. I instructed the First Officer to contact Operations and request the jet bridge be reconnected for deplaning. I informed Maintenance Control that I was refusing the aircraft and contacted Dispatch to advise that a new aircraft would be required.After all passengers deplaned; the crew elected to seek medical evaluation out of caution. Vitals and blood samples were taken; no abnormalities were found. I experienced a scratchy throat; and medical staff advised it should resolve within 24 hours.Cause: I believe somehow the oil vapors or oil drippings got into the APU bleed system when they were servicing the engine number 2.Suggestions: Use O2 mask whenever it is needed. I didn't use it because I thought the ventilation with the windows open was enough. I ended up with a scratchy throat."

I agreed to to fly the legs and advised my dispatch that we can't go to ZZZ1 since it was suppose too be below the minimum weather; but we can do ZZZ3 that had better weather conditions at my ETA. Now the ZZZ3 should be the destination and ZZZ will be the starting point; but the airplane was already fueled for ZZZ3. I was told that the passengers are waiting for me at ZZZ; at the FBO. And I need to hurry up. I landed ZZZ walked inside the FBO and there were no passengers. I called the dispatch to report it and I told them to update the program. Since the destination was still showing as ZZZ1 instead of ZZZ3; dispatcher told me that I should try ZZZ1 first and then divert to ZZZ3.I immediately reacted and told her that ZZZ1 was well below minimums and most importantly the runway at ZZZ1 was closed since the morning of Day 0. Dispatch finally changed the destination as ZZZ3. 6 passengers showed up after 20 mins with 8 bags; 5 sets of ski and pole; one big black ski sleeve with skies in them; one pair of ski boot; 2 cool case with different liquor bottles in them and 1 full size dog. Passenger weights as follows 265+170+205+165+140+155LBS Cargo Estimated 200LBS. Fuel 2300LBS. Airplane was within weight and balance limits.I took off from ZZZ. I was told to turn to 030 by ZZZ Tower; Gears up/Lights off/YD On/Climbing right turn to 030 degree. Autopilot engaged/Airplane flew through 040 degree/AP Disconnect and YD Disconnect/Hand flying trying to turn the airplane back to 030 degree. Airplane won't turn left; it kept turning uncommanded to the right. Check trim panel. Rudder trim was all the way to the right. Reduced power. Lowered Nose. Fighting the rudder trim/super heavy controls. Cancelled IFR with departure; contacted ZZZ Tower selected runway XX right downwind. All turns to the right. Landed safely with all 6 passengers.Contacted chief pilot described the situation with directional control. I was advised to burn more gas on the ground and finish the flight. No de fueling available at ZZZ. I agreed. I asked the dispatch for a permission to fly the airplane for an hour by myself to burn gas. Permission denied by dispatch. Dispatch wanted me to burn the gas on the ground with passengers inside the airplane. I was burning the gas down at the runup area RWY XY. Dispatched called me again;asking about the fuel quantity. It was 2150LBS Indicated I reporterted over phone they estimated the cargo at 250LBS. With 5 set of skis I clearly saw there were more than 5 set of skis in the cargo plus other items. With all the passenger weights; fuel and cargo they told that I am within limits and I should fly the airplane right awayI rejected to fly the airplane until the fuel weight drops below 2000lbs. They were not happy about it. Dispatch told me to park the airplane at the ramp at ZZZ and put the passengers out and sent another airplane to do the trip. I was told that company had to face losses for my decision making and had to use another bigger airplane.

column121: I was flying under call sign X on Approach to ZZZ. I was flying the RNAV XX on an IFR flight plan. I was handed off from ZZZ app to tower. On the handoff I was advised of traffic in the pattern at ZZZ1. Checking on with ZZZ Tower they told me there was two in the pattern at ZZZ1 and I said I had both in sight (one on final and one on the go). Shortly my GPS alerted me to traffic 500 below. I had lost sight of the departing aircraft as it had gone under my nose; but at 500 below and based on the track presented to me it appeared to be in the pattern that I was overflying. Seconds later I saw an aircraft same altitude heading directly at me in a climb. This aircraft never leveled off or cleared the area. I took evasive action diving and braking away to the right to avoid the midair collision. I would estimate we were 100 ft or less. I let tower know I was maneuvering aggressively to avoid traffic and they told me they understood. No other issues on the flight.After landing I looked up the flight and found it to be Aircraft Y from Company.Looking at the departure of the aircraft they took off in a normal pattern; then climbed through downwind before departing. after following the highway for several miles. This was not a normal departure from that airport nor was it one following the AIM. It is also clear to me they never cleared the climb and I saw the aircraft take no action to avoid the conflict. This was a clear unsafe maneuver that almost ended the life of both myself and my daughter. I believe this could have been avoided with departing the airport per normal AIM procedures as the aircraft did on the next flight of the day. I believe there is an unsafe culture at ZZZ1 and more so out of the flight school that is operating there. This is not the first time I have heard of conflicts and I'm worried someone is going to get hurt.

column121: This is a follow up from my previous report regarding dual FMC failure. We lost both FMC while circumnavigating thunderstorms. ATC had just cleared us direct to ZZZZZ while we were climbing when both FMC locked up. It eventually returned back while we switched to HSEL and V/S and the PM reloaded the FMC. It appeared to be operating properly once everything was back inserted in the FMC. However; it turned out that the ILS was in PARK when we tried to shoot the ILS into ZZZZ. It would not allow us to delete it or put in another frequency. After we were on the ground; we researched this online as no checklist came up and when we did a search in our FM; nothing useful came up. Eventually I found the FMC checklist that should have popped up when all three FMC had failed but it did not come up. As a matter of fact; no EICAS message or STATUS message came up except for the 'Landing Altitude.' It turned out that in order to get it out of PARK; you have to go to ALT NAV; Page 2; Turn it ON; type the frequency in manually and the course and that should fix it. However; as we were close in; and that knowledge was not available with a quick search; we ended up flying more or less a visual approach on the PAPI. As a note; when we did the Descend checklist; the frequency for the ILS had not popped in yet; but that is not necessarily unusual if we are too far out. We just never got back to it again. I think we used to check it at 2500 but that has been out of the books SOP for awhile now.

column121: This is the third EXACT incident that has occurred during pushback from Gate XX in SFO. During pushback; four vehicles drove across the service road crossing between Taxiways 1 and 2 near 3 from terminal 1. The vehicles drove directly between the attached tug pushing the aircraft and the nose/forward marshaller positioned behind the tug(aircraft nose position).Our pushback instructions were 'cleared to push onto 1' from gate XX. A vehicle on the terminal 1 side adjacent to taxiway 1 turned on the service road near 3 between taxiway 1 and 2. The vehicle drove on the service road crossing between the tug attached to the aircraft and the nose marshaller. The vehicle driver ignored signals from the nose marshaller and continued to cross the service road. The vehicle was a small ramp tug. A second vehicle followed shortly after mirroring the actions of the first. The nose marshaller made several attempts to get the attention of the second vehicle driver which again was ignored. The second vehicle was a pickup truck.A third vehicle also followed; however the third vehicle came from the opposite direction on the service road traveling faster than normal. Third vehicle was a larger catering truck. The nose marshaller had no chance to reinforce his stop signal and regardless the catering truck was traveling to fast to acknowledge and yield to the stop signal.A fourth vehicle proceeded from terminal side 1 on the service road. This vehicle was the most dangerous as the nose marshaller walked towards the tug as the tug was disconnecting and backing up. The nose marshaller had to make a positive move to stay clear of the vehicle as it the vehicle manuveur The fourth vehicle was a van. This vehicle not only failed to yield to the nose marshaller; but continued and swerved around the nose marshaller causing a dangerous situation rendering the nose marshaller defenseless against a moving vehicle. The vehicle swerved and drove completely outside the service road markings onto unmarked taxiway areas. The push was finished with no additional issues and taxi was started down taxiway 1 East bound. Before disconnecting; I debriefed what happened with the tug driver and also discussed safety zone procedures concerning the perimeter of the aircraft. I contacted ZZZ ground and requested to have the video of the push saved and reported the incident. Also; Company #; a 737 ZZZ to ZZZ1 observed the incident and add the same safety concerns from a different perspective. It is extremely alarming the fourth vehicle's actions. I am very interested in viewing the video of all the vehicles; specifically the fourth. The actions of the fourth vehicle clearly demonstrate the driver's intentions were cross the service road by any means necessary disregarding any and all safety procedures.This is the third exact incident I have experienced pushing from XX onto taxiway 1 near this service road. I strongly believe the fourth driver was extremely reckless and put the nose marshaller in extreme danger. I also feel strongly the driver of the fourth vehicle should be identified.Please reference FO report # I submitted for a similar incident. I referenced our company manuals for direct guidance concerning marshaling and tug procedures. Unfortunately; I was unsuccessful. I am not sure exactly where to find any guidance concerning preventing this incident from happening in the future. My understanding is while being pushed no vehicle or object should come in between the attached tug and the nose marshaller(any marshaller to include wing marshallers). Again; I cannot find any guidance to support this theory however in the spirit of safety the most conservative action would be to acknowledge the signals of the marshaller which were ignored.I would like to highlight; again; the last vehicle; the van who deliberately did not yield and blatantly ignored the nose marshaller. I am confident the video will show the dangerous actions of the van driver being reckless and unacceptable. It is also disturbing the trend is it's ok and common to drive on the flight line between a nose marshaller and tug attached to an aircraft; and even worst ignore a ground marshaller.

column121: This morning I was having issues with my electrical system in the Arrow I was flying. My radio comms failed and I had talked with the tower over the phone about me receiving my takeoff clearance over the cell phone and using that as two way comms until I was out of the airspace.
