column121: Previous flight that we flew in for assigned (737 NG) aircraft Y had a pneumatic maintenance issue. I was unhappy with maintenance effort to rectify problem. They cleared the warning electronically and did a leak check of right ACM (Air Cycle Machine) bay. Basically; they turned on APU and told us to call them back if light came on again; but would not check the wing strut or leading edge despite our requests and explanation of system. After a discussion with Dispatch; she agreed it was a problem; and offered a solution of another aircraft; Aircraft X; that was scheduled to ferry to ZZZ with two pilots we had deadheaded in. This plan was put in motion. I was told the ferry paperwork needed to be changed to a revenue flight and aircraft brought from hangar. Deadheading crew was to fly back with us.While we waited; we reviewed the aircraft history. Apparently on Day 0 Aircraft X (737NG) experienced a #2 engine failure that tore up the turbine blades and sent debris into the horizontal stabilizer. The logbook documented that the engine was replaced at ZZZZ; ground run only; and horizontal tail holes speed taped. FO and I discussed concern on putting revenue pax on aircraft with new engine that had never been flown; and concluded this was indeed FAA approved company policy and all paperwork appeared in order.When we arrived at aircraft; it was clear it had never flown; and cockpit was in configuration of last single engine landing (flap inhibit up; trim adjusted). Duty day was beginning to become concern due to delays and it was brought to my attention that customs closing was an issue. At some time dispatch notified me that customs would stay open; but we needed to hurry up. The usual delays of switching aircraft (bags and catering) occurred; and I was notified some bags had to come off for pax that had not re-boarded. Start up and push was normal; but upon After Start check we discovered that EECs (electronic engine controls) were in ALTN. Called dispatch and conferenced in Maintenance Control to discuss (item is flight crew placardable). Discovered EEC were not on; FO said he must have missed on pre-flight flow (very easy to do). Maintenance Control could find no reason they were off; but I asked about ground run test card that was in logbook and on a hunch she got the actual mechanic that did the ground run (he was still in ZZZZ) who admitted it was part of the test and that he left them off. Maintenance Control then cleared us to turn them on and proceed and with concurrence with dispatch; FO did so. Dispatch then had to check to see if customs would still stay open at ZZZ for our late arrival; which they did and she gave clearance to proceed.Taxi; takeoff; and initial climbout was normal for night VMC at ZZZZ. We had just negotiated a isolated line of thunderstorms that were putting out a little light turbulence and FO as PF had slowed the aircraft for turbulence when he decided to speed up to ECON speed at about 31000 ft. I felt a rumbling vibration and a slight yaw as PM and asked 'did you feel that?' Before he could answer I felt more vibrations and looked over to the engine instruments to see #2 engine rolling back and 'ENG FAIL' displayed. He said 'MY Aircraft' at same time I said 'your aircraft' and clicked off autopilot as aircraft was slowing and yawing. I realized that we would immediately be drifting down; and requested priority handling with ZZZZ Control asking for lower and a return to ZZZZ (we were 20-30 min out and this was closest suitable airport). Immediately started getting calls from back of aircraft saying they had seen a flash and 'sparks'. Executed QRC Eng Severe Damage or Separation checklist due to prior vibrations; and subsequent One Eng Inop Landing and Nonroutine Landing checklist while FO navigated back through weather towards ZZZZ and I followed along with charts monitoring minimum safe altitudes (low chart and 20-1 page) as identified threat was also terrain. Communication was difficult dueto constant communication with cabin and language barriers with ATC. ATC told us to expect ILS Y XX which is a teardrop turn from ZZZ VOR to the ILS XX. Neither the FO nor I could get it to load without placing a discontinuity in the middle of the approach. We tried numerous techniques but it kept leaving a discontinuity in middle of approach. Normal checklists also completed sometime in here. I am familiar with ZZZZ and knew they vector on one side of the airport; so asked for vectors for the ILS Z which they approved. This removed a major distraction. FO flew the aircraft on FD1 (Flight Director) and AP1 (Autopilot) (CMD 1) to downwind as I briefed the approach; and set up for Flaps 15; brakes 3. I decided to fly the approach as I had just done a flaps 15 in there that morning and was more experienced in the aircraft. Took aircraft on base leg and intercepted LOC on vectors at 2;500 ft. For some unknown reason; I saw flight director disappear in HUD and looked down at PFD (Primary Flight Display) to see lateral disappear and shortly after vertical to disappear. Immediately transitioned to HUD raw data and continued hand flying while asking FO to troubleshoot by resetting FDs. Field was in sight and PAPIS operational.Flew overweight landing to a smooth touchdown about 1;500-1;700 ft down and stopped short of a taxiway (1 maybe) about 8;000 ft down 10;500 ft runway. FO moved flaps 40 and spoilers down while I spoke to people in back. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) rolled up to inspect aircraft. We quickly discovered we had no contact with ARFF and tower wanted to relay all communications to them which became really awkward as we relayed our condition; what we wanted checked; and tried to warn them to stay clear of operating #1 engine. Additionally; we checked brake energy and discovered for our weight and speed were in 'caution zone'. Through a series of awkward communications (language barrier and 'pass the message' barrier) we asked tower to have fire chief aware and eventually we got back info that one tire/brake was indeed smoking. I asked tower to have ARFF chock nose so I could release brakes with a plan of allowing brakes to cool some and eventually taxi to gate. This seemed to not be understood or confusing to those on ground. FO at this time was also trying to get hold of OPS for gate assignment and to notify maintenance. We attempted visual signals but mostly just got quizzical looks. At some point a random individual showed up on FO side and he believed this individual (which was not a uniformed fireman) was asking us to shutdown. Since we had not gotten hold of anyone at company yet and fire chief had not cleared us off; I was reluctant to do so. I told him to signal the fellow to come over to my side and tried to communicate to this very animated individual who was not responding to my chocks signal either. Had to shut down in order to hear him. Turns out he was company maintenance of some sorts and basically just took over from Fire Chief telling me he would get tug to tow us in. I told him we had hot brakes (assuming he might not want us immediately in a gate area) but he did not seem to care. Tug showed up and we towed to gate area. Once at gate and checklist complete; I sent FO down to ensure wheels were chocked twice and released brakes to cool. FO told me that maintenance got a bit aggressive downstairs stating he was in charge and how we should have listened to him immediately (even though we had no idea who he was or why he was there). My FO says he corrected him in the conversation as to who was in charge-us and ARFF at that point in the situation. Later I found out that they had run from hangar straight out to us; but had no headsets; radio; or chocks with them. I am not sure they were communicating at all with Fire Chief on ground. Ops never answered on radio. I called dispatcher; who had gone home; asked replacement for chief pilot; who could not be found; so called safety. Filled out logbookfor engine failure and overweight landing. After that; things seemed to move along. Through ops coordination and the app eventually secured 8 rooms for crew. Assigned to fly Aircraft Y (original aircraft) home next morning. My original refusal write-up as signed off with requested inspections when we showed up.Cause: What started out as a simple 'turn' ended up being very long day. The length of day and darkness exuberant the 'startle affect' for all involved; but front and back end of crew worked well together. Terrain; weather; and communication barriers were a constant distraction. FO and I reviewed/debriefed with safety software. I discovered a few errors and pointed that out for us both to learn. I found out that when I asked for flight directors to be reset; he did not turn his off (just mine) as he was afraid he would lose his flight director. I suspect had we recycled; that problem would have gone away. We are not sure why approach would not load. I suspect it was some combination of direct to IAF and constraints somewhere. The next day I was able to put in the FMS for Aircraft Y no problem.Maintenance in ZZZZ seems to have a bit of attitude working with aircrews and ARFF. If they are going to insert themselves with ARFF they really need comm gear (radio/headsets) and if planning on towing; chocks. ARFF at ZZZZ really needs comm capability with priority aircraft. Finally; I really don't think the first flight after an engine change needs to be with revenue pax on board.
column123: On climbout from ZZZZ approaching 31;000 ft MSL I felt and heard two distinct high frequency vibrations. I immediately looked at the engine gauges and saw the #2 engine N1 RPM rapidly winding down. The EGT maintained at this point. I verbalized this to the CA and called My Aircraft. We analyzed what was happening and I clicked off the Autopilot to fly the aircraft. My focus was to keep the aircraft in coordinated flight; maintain speed with minimal altitude loss. This was at night and I knew there was mountainous terrain underneath us. ZZZZ1 was to our left around 30 miles or so and my thoughts were that returning to ZZZZ was the best option since it was low altitude and was clear of terrain to the west and south. The #2 engine N1 wound down below idle and ENG FAIL showed on the EGT. Since we had engine failure with associated vibrations the CA pulled out the QRC for Engine Failure or Shutdown and followed the path for Airframe vibrations with abnormal engine indications. We followed the QRC and QRH and shut down the #2 engine. The CA requested priority handling and asked for a return to the ZZZZ airport. I maintained the flying role while the captain then ran thru the checklists and took care of the people and flight attendants. I turned the aircraft back to the airport; turned the autopilot back on and flew back to vectors to downwind for an ILS to runway XX. The CA had flown a flaps 15 into this airport that morning so he took that aircraft and flew the approach and landing. This return to the airport; approach and landing was mostly uneventful except for two minor avionics oddities which didn't affect our ability to safely return and landing the aircraft. The first was that we could not get the ILS Y Rwy XX to fully connect without discontinuities. We tried a couple different methods to fix this but to no avail. We simply executed vectors to the south of the airport and picked up the final portion of the ILS. We were able to get this approach to load the next day without issue on a different aircraft. The other issue was that when the localizer was captured the CA's flight directors (FD) disappeared. Everything else appeared normal - generators on the APU; radar altimeter reading correctly and the FO had normal FD and indications. This also didn't affect the approach and landing since we were VMC and had PAPIs; HUD; raw ILS data; etc but it is noteworthy. Landing was over max landing weight and after coming to a stop I set the flaps to 40 and we used the brake cooling tables to assess that we were in the caution zone. 'Wheel fuse plugs may melt.' 'Delay takeoff and inspect after 1 hour.'The fire trucks and emergency personnel were in position to check us over but the only way to communicate with them was with replay comm thru Tower. I was able to tell Tower what we needed from the emergency crews etc and they would relay that to the emergency crew. The crew would then relay what they see back to Tower and Tower would then tell us. Realize that there is a bit of a language barrier due to accents and terminology. I was able to clear the emergency crew; thru Tower; that they are cleared to inspect the plane. I informed Tower at least twice that the right engine was shutdown; the left engine was running and asked to tell the crews to look for damage; debris on the runway; damage to the engine; wing and tail and to stay clear of the running engine. This took a significant amount of time to relay to the emergency crew to get in there and inspect because there was no way to talk to the ground crews via direct radio contact.The CA and I were also concerned about the hot brakes. I asked Tower to get them to look assess the brakes as well. From what I remember there was indication from Tower that the brakes were hot or abnormal; and nothing else abnormal with the engine; FOD damage - so in the CA and my mind our priority now is to get the nose wheel chocked so we can release the brakes. I communicated this to the Tower numeroustimes and there was basically no action from what I could see from the crews to chock the plane. They were walking around but no chocks. At this point a new person to the scene was waving at me and trying to get my attention. He was not part of the emergency crews and he eventually yelled to the CA that he was a part of company maintenance. I opened my window to be able to yell or get my 'chocks in' signal more clear. He gave me the shut down the engine signal. I went back and forth with him a few different times trying to get him to confirm that the chocks were in. He held up his finger to indicate 'not yet - wait for it' I was trying to get Tower to give me confirmation that the chocks were indeed in but there was no winning comm at this point. Since it was dark and the crews were looking confused we couldn't tell what they accomplished or didn't accomplish. From what the Tower indicated was that the emergency crews were trying to find chocks somewhere. The maintenance person was telling us to shut down the #1 engine but was not part of the fire crew so I was confused on what exactly was happening. Again no radio comm available to anyone on the ground. The CA and my priority since we were told everything was fine by Tower was to get the plane chocked so we can release the brakes. Our overall plan was to let the brakes cool; have the fire crew inspect and then - as we are trained to do - decide to taxi or not single engine back to the gate. The maintenance person went to the CA's window and they were able to yell back and forth. He said we were to be towed in to the gate. I was also talking with Tower and they told me that our company was going to tow us back to the gate. During all this I had tried to call ops on their freq but no answer - late at night or out here at the jet - unknown. The CA and I were happy to be towed back to the gate but the big issue was that maintenance was aggressively trying to get us to shut down the other engine without understanding our situation. This was highly frustrating but we worked as a team to eventually get the plane chocked; shut down the engine and get towed back.The main issue we have is the lack of ability to communicate with the emergency crew. The second is that as far as we were concerned the emergency crew is the ones to be handling this aircraft especially considering the hot brakes situation. The maintenance person just popped in to the situation and tried to take command of what we were doing and it added negative value to this situation.I spoke with him on the ground at the gate and I explained that we had hot brakes and were not going to shut down the engine without being chocked. Additionally we were told by the emergency crew - thru Tower - that there was no danger so why was he trying to get us to shut down the #1 engine. He said that in order to inspect the aircraft we had to shut the engine down. I said we were never trained to do that and additionally if there wasn't a fire or some more severe issue that we weren't going to just shut down the engine without chocks or a signal from the emergency crew. I told him our plan was to chock the nose; assess the brakes and then taxi back; get towed back or evacuate if something bad occurred. He put himself in the middle of our standard game plan and caused confusion at the least. He said 'This is ZZZZ and we do things differently. We have to have both engines shut down to inspect.'Regardless I thanked him for having this debrief with me and he can discuss this with the captain once all the passengers are deboarded.Cause: Mechanical. We found out a couple days later that the engine experienced multiple compressor stalls and fuel starvation. The HMU (Hydro-Mechanical Unit) was the cause of these issues. The previous flight experienced the same #2 engine failure but with material failure and shredding of turbine blades which caused damage to the engine; wing and horizontal tail. The removed and replaced the engine; testedit on the ground; but never test flown. We were the first flight to fly this jet with passengers with a new engine.

column121: Approximately half an hour into the cruise; while resting in the cabin; I heard the master caution chime; and autopilot disconnect alert. Upon entering the cockpit and seating in the observers seat I saw the captain reading a QRH checklist and observed the EICAS Caution message 'HYD PRESS SYS 1' along with the lower EICAS displaying the HYD SD page; and the number 1 hydraulic tank indication empty. I then opened the HYD PREES SYS 1 checklist on my IPAD and monitored the actions of the PM and PF.  Following the selection of the alternate gear extension; the right hand wing gear indicated hashed/in transit; and an EICAS gear disagree message was displayed. The crew actioned the gear disagree checklist and that did not remedy the situation. I contacted Maintenance Control; Deputy chief Pilot and the Supervisor on the sat phone. I asked the question to the Supervisor if; (as we had used the alternate gear selection ) would there be any negative repercussions with selecting the landing gear handle down; as this was not a step that the gear disagree checklist advocated. Upon receiving the 'no objection' from the Supervisor the gear handle was selected down and the right wing gear indicated green. We then landed in accordance with the loss of hyd 1 system; and were towed to the ramp following shut down on the runway.I wish to commend the Captain on his excellent crew management and command handling of this malfunction.Suggestions: I suggest that the B744 QRH GEAR DISAGREE checklist be amended to direct the crew to step XX (Landing gear lever (if possible)…DN. Currently the checklist directs crew to step XY bypassing the gear lever down selection.

column121: Experienced a traffic conflict (TCAS TA) due to another airport's traffic while circling to land in PVU. Commenced a VMC circle maneuver from the RNAV Runway 13; to land Runway 31. Winds required landing Runway 31; and the RNAV Visual Runway 31 was not an option due to marginal ceiling that would have prevented us from maintaining required visual contact and cloud clearance. While maneuvering base-to-final for Runway 31; we received a TA; and the target appeared to be within 2 miles (possibly closer) and less than 700 feet below us. Shortly after the TA sounded; we heard a traffic call on the other airport's CTAF; which we were monitoring in accordance with company chart recommendations. As we were in a very high workload moment; I don't recall how close the target ultimately became. We never acquired visual contact with the conflicting traffic. Already in a turn away from the conflicting traffic; we continued the circling maneuver to landing. Cause: Spanish Fork Municipal (SPK) lies less than 5 NM from the approach end of PVU's Runway 31; with a similarly-aligned runway. PVU's Class D airspace has a cutout for this airport; such that the only way to keep a circling maneuver within the Class D would be to fly less than a 2.5 NM final to Runway 31. Utilizing the protected circling radius of 4 NM; we were well outside of PVU's Class D during the maneuver; placing our base-to-final nearly over the departure end of SPK's active runway. The layout of these two airports; especially with one being uncontrolled; presents a unique risk of midair collision.Suggestions: For my part; I would have made a traffic call on SPK's CTAF during the circling maneuver; though doing so would need to be carefully balanced with the need to manage the flight path during a high workload situation. Having monitored the CTAF since well before commencing the approach; I would have hoped for a traffic call from the other aircraft before they were airborne; but it seemed that their first CTAF call was made after departing. Besides mutual CTAF communication; I'm unsure how to mitigate the risk of midair collision between these two airports; but there must be an in-depth discussion of how to do so. Of all the places I operate; landing on PVU Runway 31; especially when the RNAV Visual 31 is unavailable; presents a unique risk. Enough repeats of this flight's circumstances; in my view; will eventually lead to an accident.

column121: In Month 2; while I was off duty; my peer ZZZ QC (Quality Control) Inspector Person A completed a borescope re-inspection on Aircraft X #1 engine; S/N XXXXXX. She determined that the previously deferred (Logbook Deferral Sheet XXXXXXX) burn holes had grown axially but remained on the same 150-hour re-inspection interval.Two days later; Maintenance Control Technician Person B forwarded an email to the List of the ZZZ QC shop. The email was between Person C a powerplant engineer and Person D; an engineer. The Email explained they did not agree with the axial measurements and the worst radial measurements appeared to be 0.177 inch and per the AMM (72-XX-XX-XXX-XXX-XXX-X) the item should be on a 750-hour re-inspection interval.Upon my return to work; I read the email and checked the online system to find that Maintenance Person B had changed the re-inspection interval to the 750-hour limit from the 150-hour re-inspection interval applied in ZZZ1 on Month 1due to power plant engineer Person E conferring with Person D. It is my understanding that Maintenance Control is not to change inspection department findings without an approved document. A review of the facts found that ZZZ2 had originally placed this deferral on a 300-hour re-inspection. However; under ZZZ2; deferral reference; dated Month 0; identified a 150 hour re-inspect but a 750-hour re-inspection per the engineer).In Month 1; ZZZ1 Inspector Person F dropped the original limit from its initial 300-hour re-inspection to a 150-hour inspection. He stated the helicopter came in and set down at their hanger; shut down for about thirty seconds; started back up and immediately took off. He said he heard our departure call on RWY XX as the helicopter left the ground and started flying north through the two rows of hangers and passed by the office at high speed and rooftop level.  He said he has never heard a helicopter take off that loud before.  He thought to himself that the helicopter was going to fly right through (our) departure path. column121: On Day 0; I departed ZZZ to ZZZ1 for the purpose of practicing tower operations at an unfamiliar airport. After two landings at ZZZ1 with a couple hours of leisure flight in between the landings; I departed ZZZ1 for my return to ZZZ. My eta at ZZZ was approximately XA:00; and; based on the weather data available through my EFB; my expectation was an arrival on RWY XX at ZZZ. The flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was unremarkable in all regards. Approximately 10 miles east of ZZZ; I obtained the weather via the ZZZ AWOS system; which indicated winds from 020 at 9 kts. As expected; the winds favored an arrival on RWY XX; so I set up for a slightly wider than normal righthand base entry for RWY XX. There was no local traffic in the pattern; and the only radio traffic was from a single inbound plane approximately 10 miles out for RWY XX.I descended to pattern altitude at approximately 5 miles from ZZZ; added 10 degrees of flaps; and entered the right base for RWY XX pitched to approximately 90 kts. Upon turning north for final; approximately 2-3 miles south of ZZZ; I noted the winds aloft at pattern altitude seemed brisker than the AWOS report and I felt slight gusting; which was consistent with my prior experience at altitude and generally unremarkable. Because of the ground level crosswind and the gusting at pattern altitude; I decided to make my landing with 20 degrees flaps; rather than my normal 30 degrees; and adjust my final approach speed up from my normal 65-70 kts to something in the low to mid 70 kts range.During final approach; I added the second 10 degrees of flaps approximately one mile from the threshold and I maintained a crab angle into the wind; which meant my heading was east of the runway heading; as expected. I adjusted my pitch after adding the second notch of flaps and was holding a pretty steady 72 kts airspeed with 20 degrees of flaps. Upon reaching short final; I added left rudder to transition from a crab heading to runway heading using a 'right wing low slip technique' and continued to hold approximately 72 kts. The slight gusting I had experienced at pattern altitude was no longer evident at short final altitude. Overall; the final approach felt stable and my airspeed and heading varied very little from the initial turn final until the threshold; except for the intentional airspeed adjustment associated with adding the second notch of flaps.As I crossed the threshold; I pulled power to idle; compensated for the slight nose down action associated with the 182 when power is brought to idle; and entered the ground effect. Flight in the ground effect was stable; and my runway placement was slightly left of center but certainly within the middle third of the runway.When my airspeed dissipated sufficiently; I began my flare for touchdown. At this point; I experienced a gust (presumably) that caused the plane to yaw noticeably and abruptly to the left; which resulted in me being in a 'right wing low' bank with the right main leading the left main. I was expecting to touchdown any moment; so my reaction was to correct the left yaw by adding right aileron to bring the nose to the right and toward the center of the runway. In doing so; I believe I overcorrected for the left yaw and ended up pointing too far to the right when I touched down; which occurred immediately after making my correction.The touchdown led with the right main; which would have been oriented farthest to the south at this point due to the overcorrection. After the right main touched down; the left main and nose gear followed; either at the same time or perhaps with the left main slightly ahead of the nose. The touchdown itself was not particularly hard; although I wouldn't hold it out as my smoothest landing by any means.At this point; elapsed time became a little difficult to judge; but it seems like within a second or two after touchdown; I felt a force acting on the plane that I hadn't experienced before; and that caused me to pause for another second or two in order to evaluate what I was experiencing. I determined the force was sideloading toward my left; and I also noticed the left wing of the plane was dipping and the right main had come off the runway; resulting in the plane rolling only on the left main and the nose gear. I responded to the side loading by adding what little remaining right aileron I had left and pressing the left rudder pedal aggressively. Unfortunately; neither control input seemed to help; and I believe the sideloading actually caused the nose wheel to turn to the right because the plane began rolling across the runway in a right arc. The tilt to the left gradually increased to the point where I actually leaned to the passenger side of the plane in an attempt to offset it. At some point; I heard a rubbing noise I didn't recognize; and my first reaction was to look out the left window to see if the left wingtip was dragging the ground. It did not seem to be close to dragging; so I assumed the rubbing noise was coming from the nose gear being in a bind or something along those lines (I later learned the noise was the prop contacting the runway surface).After arcing to the right across the runway for a couple seconds (which felt like an hour) with all the right aileron and left rudder I had to provide; the plane leaned back to the right and settled on all three gears. At this point; I engaged the brakes pretty aggressively and came to a stop about three feet from the right edge of RWY XX with the engine running smoothly at idle. I'm guessing at this point; but it seems the nose of the plane was pointing about 040 or 050 at the time. Suffice it to say; the rightward arc I traveled across the runway was significant in any event.I looked out the windows of the plane and noted a runway light less than a wing width away toward my left; and; based on my proximity to the runway edge; I didn't think I had enough room to attempt a left turn on the runway without risking an impact with the runway light. As a result; I elected to exit the runway to the east; make a lefthand arc through the RSA; and reenter the runway between the next set of runway lights; so that's how I proceeded. The exit and reentry of the runway was smooth and uneventful; so I proceeded north down RWY XX to the next taxiway intersection and exited the runway. While taxiing down the runway; I heard the plane behind me call a five-mile final; so I announced myself upon exiting the runway and noted the traffic was on short final at that point.I taxied uneventfully back to the hangar and shut down the engine; and when the propeller came to a stop; I realized the tips were all curled; hence the unexplained noise I heard while arcing across the runway. This was the first time I realized a prop strike had occurred.At the time of the occurrence; I held a private pilot license with an instrument rating; as well as high performance and complex endorsements. I had 314.9 hours of total time; with 287.2 as PIC. Specific to C182 time; I had a total of 81.0 hours and 100 landings; 40 of which were night landings. In the last 180 days; I had 20.8 hours in a C182 and 18 landings; 7 of which were night landings. In the last 90 days; I had 5.6 hours in a C182 and 11 landings; 6 of which were night landings. Eight of the eleven landings in the prior 90 days; including all six of the night landings; took place one week before the occurrence; and those practice landings took place at ZZZ in nighttime crosswind conditions comparable to the date of the occurrence.I believe the occurrence was ultimately caused by pilot error; and better pilot actions at a couple different points in time could have potentially avoided the outcome. The initial opportunity could have been when I first experienced the gust (if it was a gust) and the resulting left yaw immediately before touchdown. Had my reaction been to add full power at that point; rather than attempt to correct the heading; the outcome might have been avoided. Likewise; had I not overcorrected with right aileron / under corrected with left rudder during the correction; I may have touched down aligned with the runway and avoided the sideloading upon touchdown. Additionally; had I immediately recognized the side loading force when it occurred and added the remaining available right aileron and left rudder without a couple seconds of delay; I may have timely offset the force and corrected the track of the rollout before the side loading became so strong that the right main gear left the runway pavement. In terms of future corrective actions; I plan to schedule some instructor time under crosswind conditions so the instructor can make a fresh evaluation of my crosswind landing technique to see if there are deficiencies I haven't recognized. As an additional step; I believe I'm going to obtain a tail wheel endorsement because I've heard and read that tailwheel training really enhances rudder skills during landing and taxi operations.

By about 6 miles away the engine began losing more rpms but by then I had a good feeling we'll make the runway but it'll have to be a tailwind landing. There wasn't enough power to get into the pattern so I just elected for a straight in runway XX at ZZZ. After we landed we still had some power to roll off the runway and started rolling towards the ramp by then temps were really hot so I shutoff the engine and continued rolling on to the ramp. column121: Leveling off at 36000 feet; I made a PA to the passengers; and turned off the seatbelt sign. A few minutes later we heard the CABIN ALTITUDE horn going off. After speaking with the flight attendants; I made a PA to the passengers updating them on the situation. I let dispatch know through ACARS of our situation and that we would be diverting to ZZZ. The FO as pilot flying did an excellent job coordinating with ATC and setting up for our approach to XXL in ZZZ. column123: On the arrival for runway 30 visual approach into HTS; the winds were stronger than previously reported. While flying the approach with autopilot; I adjusted power settings which made the aircraft chase the glide slope and momentarily put the nose of the aircraft in a pitch down attitude which activated the terrain alert due to the mountainous terrain.  We TCSs the aircraft pulling the nose up and putting the aircraft back onto a stable approach.  We continued for landing since it was a visual and had the runway in sight. column121: Day 0; Learjet 60; departed ZZZ1 for ZZZ. The forecast for ZZZ indicated ¼ mile in FZFG which caused the crew to delay takeoff for 1 hour to allow our arrival at ZZZ for the estimated forecast at XA:00z to be 200 and ½ mile visibility. The crew departed ZZZ1 at XB:51z and arrived in the area at approximately XC:06z just after the control tower opened. The crew acknowledged the new ATIS '1' indicating winds Calm; ¼ FG; Ceiling 100; Temp -1C/Dewpoint -1C; and Altimeter 30.17. There was no mention of Freezing Fog. RNAV (GPS) Rwy XX was in use. The ILS Rwy XX Glidepath is NOTAM'd out of service. As a crew; we decided to 'take a look' and performed the approach. At minimums; the approach lights came into sight and then the runway was in sight. However; due to a loss of visual to the runway missed approach was conducted. During the missed approach the crew noticed the weather seemed to be improving. We talked about it and thought that we would be able to complete an approach and land. After being vectored to the final approach course by ZZZ Approach Control; we performed a second RNAV (GPS Rwy XX approach. On this approach; we again had the approach light system in sight at minimums and then the runway in sight. The Flying Pilot maintained a stabilized approach speed of approximately 140 Knots based on a calculated VREF speed of 137 Knots. During the landing flare the plane floated for about 2 to 3 seconds before touching down. The flying pilot immediately deployed the thrust reverser system and began braking. The Pilot Monitoring noticed the 1000 foot marker quickly approaching and made the callout. The Pilot Flying went to maximum braking and the aircraft overran the end of the runway approximately 20 feet in soft mud.The calculations from the aircrafts Aircraft Performance Program  indicated that based on the criteria of a wet runway and flaps 40° and using 115% performance numbers; our landing distance based on a 18;361 pounds was 3794 feet. Unfortunately; because of the 3 second of floating time; much of the runway was used up during the landing.After shutting down the engines and notifying the tower of the incident; we exited the runway to assess any damage and coordinate with our company to recover the aircraft. I noticed that the runway was very slick in spite of being grooved which I believed contributed to the overrun. No obvious damage was noticed and recovery efforts were accomplished with no further problems.

column121: Potential electrical hazard in the BK117C2/C2e. While checking aircraft battery voltage; I noticed the Caution and Advisory Display (CAD) had asymmetrical caution lights with the left side BUS TIE OPN caution not illuminated. After troubleshooting; I was able to determine the #1 Main Bus was hot when it should have been cold in this state. The cause was determined by Maintenance after extensive troubleshooting and effort to be a failure of the Bus Tie Control Relay in the Overhead Panel as it was generating power at all times causing the Bus Tie Relay to be closed at all times and rendering the BUS TIE switch inoperative. My concern is that our base pilots operating per the checklist for everyday operations close both bus ties and never noticed; nor should they have noticed; the anomaly with the aircraft. There are multiple electrical emergency procedures that would be affected by such an anomaly and I feel Airbus should consult as to whether or not they wish to change their guidance for preflight procedures as they did when they added the DC System Check" to the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the EC135 in the early 2000's. They should add a step in the normal procedures section of the RFM to pause when turning power on via the BAT MSTR switch in the "ON" position until the Central Panel Display System (CPDS) self-test is complete and ensure both BUS TIE OPN caution lights are illuminated before cycling the switch to the "Engage" position."

column121: At ZZZ; I was attempting to Taxi to Runway XX at ZZZ for a cross country flight when winds caused the plane to drift off the runway to the left when perpendicular to the runway prior to lining up with the centerlines. Of note; the flight had been delayed one hour due to gusting winds. Winds had reduced prior to taxi and were predicting to continue to decrease according to regulated weather sources. The rate of drift was slow; but rudder control was reduced; leading the tires of the plane to be slightly to the left off of the runway when control was re-established. Due to the position; the tire was stuck and the plane was unable to move forward to be re-established on the runway. The pilot communicated the issue to ATC; who directed upcoming landing traffic to go around. Due to the plane's inability to move backways (due to the manufacturing limits of the plane); I communicated with ATC that I would need to physically push the plane backways. I then turned off the plane; pushed the plane backward and then in line with the runway. After starting up the plane; I regained contact with ATC and let them know that the plane was now in line for takeoff. I was able to takeoff without any issues with winds or gusts. The plane was landed without incident at ZZZ1. There was no damage to person or aircraft during the incident. Incident occurred due to wind gusts and the pilot underestimating the extent of the effects of the gusts when perpendicular to the runway prior to lining up on centerline. Corrective action includes further training on effects of wind; especially in Cessna 152. In addition; although the flight was delayed due to the wind; further delay or cancellation would have avoided the incident completely.

column121: Date: Day 0Location: Practice area east/northeast of ZZZ near the ZZZZZ fixAircraft: Aircraft X; Aircraft YOther Aircraft Involved: RV-4 On Day 0; during a training flight operating in the practice area northeast of ZZZ; a near midair collision occurred between our aircraft and an RV-4  near the ZZZZZ fix. The conflict developed as both aircraft converged while climbing and maneuvering in the same airspace. Evasive action was required to avoid the other aircraft.During a training flight on Day 0; I was instructing my student pilot departing from ZZZ. They are working on their Private Pilot Airplane Single Engine Land training in the Cessna 172 Skyhawk. They have nearly 100 hours and was doing one last flight to prepare for their end-of-course progress check. After departure; we transitioned northbound from ZZZ and proceeded into the local practice areas commonly referred to as City X and City Y at 7;500 MSL. These practice boxes are below ZZZ1 class Bravo.We remained in the practice area for a short while; conducting normal training maneuvers for a private pilot. After completing those maneuvers; we transitioned eastbound; positioning ourselves slightly south of ZZZ2.While in this area; we conducted two ground reference maneuvers: turns around a point and S-turns across a road. These maneuvers were performed at approximately 1;000 feet above ground level. Which; for this given area; was roughly 5;900 MSL. We were making routine traffic calls on the North Practice area frequency of XXX.XXX throughout the entire flight. We made sure to comply with 91.119 and maintain an altitude allowing for an emergency landing without power; without undue hazards to person or property on the surface. This is a sparsely populated area consisting mostly farmlands underneath the ZZZ1 class bravo.Upon completion of the ground reference maneuvers; we began a climb to 6;500 feet MSL while turning westbound to return to ZZZ. This put us roughly 1;500 ft AGL.While en route westbound at approximately 6;500 feet MSL; shortly after; I observed a traffic advisory on the aircraft's MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) indicating traffic off our right side. The traffic was identified on ADS-B; an RV-4; and was initially displayed approximately 500 feet below our altitude.Because I did not yet have visual contact with the aircraft; I instructed my student to initiate a climb to 7;000 feet MSL in order to increase vertical separation. The student began the climb; and the aircraft reached approximately 6;770 feet MSL when I observed the aircraft passing below. I pointed out the traffic to my student and notified them that it should soon be passing under the nose and appearing on their side (left) of the aircraft. We continued climbing to increase separation. I monitored the traffic information on the MFD and observed the altitude separation decreasing rapidly. The traffic indication changed from 500 feet below to 400 feet below; then 200 feet below; and eventually indicated the same altitude and the same position.At that point; it became clear the other aircraft was climbing directly toward our altitude. I immediately took control of the aircraft and initiated a right-hand evasive turn to the north.As I initiated the right turn; the RV-4 also began a right-hand turn toward the north; indicating the same altitude the whole time; further reducing the lateral separation between the aircraft.Based on the maneuvering and flight profile; it appeared the RV-4 was performing aerobatic maneuvering in the area and was likely unaware that we were operating nearby.I personally did not obtain visual contact with the RV-4 during the conflict. However; my student; who was seated in the left seat; did acquire visual contact and estimated the aircraft passed approximately '3-5 feet off our wing'. They told me; 'They are right next to us and turning into us'. I then steepened the bank to roughly 50 degrees and pushed the nose forward to accelerate us to 129 KIAS.We lost roughly 1;000 ft attempting to break away from this aircraft and were still indicating the same altitude throughout the evasive action. This lasted almost a minute.Following the evasive maneuver; we successfully separated from the traffic. We then continued east briefly before turning northbound to reestablish our route back toward ZZZ while maintaining separation from the other aircraft. We then went north of the class Bravo and climbed up to 8;000 MSL. The aircraft continued to the south. We attempted to contact the aircraft on both practice area frequencies of XXX.XXX and XXX.Y. We received no communication back from the traffic. No further traffic conflicts occurred during the remainder of the flight.This event is concerning because the practice areas northeast of ZZZ are routinely used by student pilots from multiple training organizations. Many students conduct solo operations in these areas and routinely transition through the same airspace.The behavior and maneuvering of the RV-4 suggested the pilot was likely conducting aerobatic maneuvers and may not have been aware of other aircraft operating nearby. The lack of apparent situational awareness by the RV-4 created a hazardous situation in an area that regularly contains high volumes of training traffic.Given the frequency of student pilot operations in this region; this type of maneuvering presents a significant risk for future conflicts. Given the maneuverability of the RV-4 and the spontaneous maneuvering; it was extremely difficult to decipher which direction/altitude would clear us of traffic. No contact was made with the aircraft.

The lack of apparent situational awareness by the RV-4 created a hazardous situation in an area that regularly contains high volumes of training traffic.Given the frequency of student pilot operations in this region; this type of maneuvering presents a significant risk for future conflicts. Given the maneuverability of the RV-4 and the spontaneous maneuvering; it was extremely difficult to decipher which direction/altitude would clear us of traffic. No contact was made with the aircraft.

column121: I arrived and began preflight planning for a maintenance flight to test a diode on the right engine. I conducted a weight and balance form; a dispatch sheet and spoke with maintenance about what had been done to the aircraft in order to plan accordingly. I planned to travel to the midway practice area and perform basic maneuvers to include steep turns; slow flight; and stalls at 3;000 feet over water southeast of ZZZ. I conducted a preflight and noted no defects with the airplane; all fluids were filled to an acceptable level and no notable damage was found. I got into the airplane and started the engines; taxied to the runup; completed the before takeoff check checklist and taxied to the runway without any issues. I did a normal takeoff from runway XX full length at ZZZ and noted no issues on the takeoff roll. Approach let me know that there were two other airplanes in the practice area so I talked to them and determined I would work the east side north south at 3;000 ft. I got into the practice area; got set up for maneuvers and started with steep turns. No issues with steep turns so I moved on to slow flight. Once I began slow flight I pulled the power to 25% load on each engine and lowered the landing gear handle. Upon landing gear extension I noticed a strange yaw to the left and looked down and noticed my right main landing gear position indicator light was not illuminated and my gear unsafe light was illuminated.I continued to fly south and I began to trouble shoot starting with the gear fire test button which illuminated all landing gear position indicator lights and proved that all lights were working. I then called Aircraft Y and asked if they could fly below me and check if my gear was down. They did and confirmed the right main was in the wheel well. I then asked if they noted any change as I ran the manual extension of landing gear checklist and pulled the manual extension handle. The pilot of Aircraft Y confirmed that the landing gear was still stuck in the up position. This confirmed that there was a real problem and I began to maneuver with the gear handle down in an effort to try to pull the landing gear out of the wheel well. Once I had tried this a few times I determined that it was not working and wanted an official answer from the tower confirming that the right main landing gear was stuck up. I swapped frequencies to approach control and requested priority handling requesting to return to ZZZ for a low pass. I did and the tower confirmed that the right main appeared to be in the wheel well.I responded to the tower that I would return to the midway practice area to troubleshoot and burn off fuel. I returned to the midway practice area; continued to maneuver the aircraft and asked over our company frequency if anyone could get maintenance on the radio. Maintenance had me try a few different methods to lower the gear including going 180 kts and lowering the landing gear; pushing the manual gear extension handle back in and cycling the gear a few different times and adding constant G forces in a 60 degree banked steep turn. None of these methods worked. Eventually Aircraft Z; containing a representative of the FSDO and my Chief Pilot; departed ZZZ and flew close to me while I troubleshot the problem. Once I had tried everything and burned 10 or more gallons of fuel; I determined that the gear was not going to come down. I then returned to ZZZ. I entered left traffic XX. On short final for XX ~100' I pulled the power to idle and turned off the left then right engine masters and landed. I opened the canopy as I was coming to a stop. Once stopped I turned off the electric master and departed the aircraft.

column121: On a VFR flight returning from near ZZZ1 (flight originated from ZZZ; overflew ZZZ1 then returned to ZZZ).  Using VFR flight following in contact with ZZZ Approach.  Approximately 20NM north north West of ZZZ at 5;225 MSL I noted traffic enter the 4NM ring in the app on my IPad +300 ft above and slightly ahead on my right on a course crossing mine at approx 90 degrees from mine.  I asked my passenger if he heard a traffic alert from ATC that I missed but he had not.  I looked for the traffic but could not see it.  I noted that the traffic was descending to within 200 ft above and now approx 3MN and still slightly ahead intersecting my course.  I called ATC and notified them that I was descending to avoid traffic.  I did not hear a reply. I could not yet see the traffic.  When I did see the traffic it was approx 200 ft above nearly even with my right wingtip and approx 250 feet away.  I continued my decent and the traffic passed barely above and slightly behind me.  I noted that the traffic continued descending toward ZZZ2.  ADS-B showed the traffic ID as Aircraft Y.  At that time I recalled that a couple minutes before this incident I heard a pilot discuss an instrument approach to ZZZ2 and connected that this might be the same plane.  Moments later ATC asked me if I had ZZZ ATIS information.  I told him that I did not.  I tuned ZZZ ATIS for their information then informed ATC that I had ZZZ information 1. ATC then instructed me to squack VFR and contact ZZZ Tower.  I waited a couple of minutes to all as I was still 19 miles from ZZZ and well away from their airspace recalling that in the past ZZZ Tower has requested that I contact them again when I was closer.  The rest of the flight to ZZZ was without incident.

column121: Who; What; Where; When; Why?On Day 0; at approximately XA:40 local time; I operated a Small UAS (under 250g) at a park in Layton; UT. The location is within a 0ft LAANC grid for Hill AFB. My intent was a short local flight in a public park. Shortly after I had finished the flight and the drone was secured; I observed a military aircraft taking off from Hill AFB. I immediately realized the proximity of my flight to active military operations and the potential safety risk I had inadvertently created. At no point was the drone in the air while manned military aircraft were operating.Contributing Factors:I am a new hobbyist and misunderstood that even micro-drones require LAANC in a 0ft grid. I incorrectly assumed that recreational flight in a city park was permitted without checking the specific UAS Facility Map (UASFM) for that GPS location.Corrective Action:Immediately following the event; I researched FAA regulations and successfully completed the TRUST Completion Certificate (The Recreational UAS Safety Test) to ensure full compliance with hobbyist rules. I have downloaded a LAANC-integrated app (B4UFLY) and will ensure all future flights are conducted in permitted airspace with proper authorization.I am filing this report to document the incident and demonstrate my commitment to following all FAA safety guidelines and respecting National Defense Airspace in the future.

column121: On decent into El Paso International Airport; we were cleared to descend VIA the BEAHR3 for the RNAV 26L Y approach. Captain set the bottom Altitude on the altitude selector for the RNAV 26LY approach 5700 ft and set 7000 ft in the FMS for BUSEY and activated the hard altitude for BUSEY crossing restriction. We were descending in PATH mode at around 3200 FTM; nearing 10000 ft I called for speed check as the aircraft was descending at high rate in Manual speed mode; trying to make the crossing restriction. The Captain told me to let Approach control know we will not make crossing restriction; and the Captain change the decent mode to Vertical speed. I informed Approach control of the unable to make restriction; Approach control asked us to cross BUSEY at or above 8000ft. I asked if we ate still cleared for the approach; ATC confirmed cleared; I called for speed check again and mentioned our FMA vertical mode change and reminded Captain we are cleared for the approach. I asked the Captain do you want me to set the new hard altitude crossing 8000 ft at BUSEY. Captain mentioned not necessary but go head; I bugged 8000 ft at BUSEY and activated; our (altitude selector was still selected for our bottom RNAV 27 approach altitude 5700 ft ) after inserting new information into FMS below 10000 ft; I looked up called check speed and altitude and mentioned cleared for approach as the vertical mode was still in Vertical Speed and decent rate was excessive. At that time ATC mentioned low altitude alert and to climb to 6500 ft we started the climb; ATC then asked us to climb to 6700 ft; I asked if we were cleared for the approach; they confirmed cleared and transferred us to tower.Suggestions: As a crew we could have asked for a decent sooner as it's known for El Paso approach to bring aircraft in high then descend fast to meet a restriction. Better awareness during heavy workload; with last minute changes below 10000 ft with head down; While bugging new information not noticing new FMA changes made by Pilot flying. Being more assertive with altitude and speed restriction callouts.Less talking on the radio with ATC during critical phases; Captain mentioned couldn't hear or understand ATC instructions so I pilot monitoring had to keep confirming instructions; which increased workload during critical phases.
column123: ATC instructed at FL200; cleared to descend via the BEAHR3. At FL200 I set 8000 for BEARH and armed vnav. As we were descending ATC then said cleared direct FABAN cross FABAN at 8000; we vertical direct to FABAN but we were high; so I pulled the boards to get down; so we could make the new fix with the altitude restriction. ATC then said cross FABAN at 7000; cleared for the RNAV Y 26L; I set the final approach fix altitude; as we were cleared for the approach; I asked the FO to let ATC know we were not going to make that altitude restriction at 7000; I put it in VS to try to get down and slow down; somehow I missed ATCs response to now cross FABAN at or above 7000; I never put it back in path; or set the alt back to 7000; the alt was set for 5200 for the final approach fix; as I caught it we were already descending below the appropriate altitude; leading to an altitude deviation. We corrected the altitude deviation and completed a stabilized approach and landing. Suggestions: There was a lot going on in this phase of the flight; several things could have made this better; setting the altitude back to 7000; so we didn't blow through it; until me met that restriction then resetting the final approach fix; and/or putting the aircraft back in VNAV. Both would have prevented the deviation. The big one is I thought it was cross it at; not at or above; my misinterpretation of the clearance. Because we were given direct FABAN while we were high; I was distracted by trying to get down and slow down. Our CRM could have been a lot better also.

column121: On Day 2 at approximately XA:00 prior to aircraft door closure I was informed by the ground crew that they had observed an uncontrolled fuel leak coming from the right main wing tank on the outer edge of the tank towards the winglet.Immediately I grabbed my safety vest and air protection; exited the flight deck; and went out to the ramp to confirm that yes indeed there is a pencil width sized leak coming from the vent hole on the fuel tank. This leak was uncontrolled; could not be stopped; and required immediate attention. I returned to the flight deck and made a PA and told the passengers the situation and mentioned that because it was a fuel spill that had not been contained yet it was advantageous for everyone to grab their belongings and exit the aircraft as soon as possible. I then called my dispatcher and told them exactly what I had done and the event that had occurred outside. He was in agreement; deplaning the aircraft was a good idea. In the meantime; the ZZZ Ground crew flawlessly contain the spill so that there is minimal impact to ramp safety.I got off the phone with the dispatcher so that I can make the appropriate entries into the aircraft electronic logbook. My first entry into the logbook; stated that there was a new leak coming from the main wing tank. This issue had previously been written up and addressed on Day 0.After making the logbook entry; I called back dispatch and asked to be connected with the maintenance desk. The tone of the maintenance technician on the phone sounded frustrated; but eager to help. They simply said without any investigation or asking me any questions that I had just been over fueled and the situation was normal. The situation was not normal. We were already at our recommended fuel release load. Between us inspecting the leak and approximately 10 minutes later we had lost almost 200 pounds of gas due to a leak. When I advised the technician of this they did not change their judgment. They simply said yes that happened because you were over fueled; even though we are at the correct fuel load given our flight conditions as a matter of fact; we took off out of ZZZ1 with a higher fuel load on the previous flight and never encountered a leak.Once I was finally able to make my point across the technician on the other end of the phone; they decided it would be worth calling contract maintenance to come out and look at the aircraft.Roughly about an hour later maintenance arrived to the aircraft and began inspecting the wing for leaks . Maintenance personnel asked me to fully extend the flaps and slats so that they can fully inspect the wing to find other leaks. The contract maintenance technician then asked me to move fuel from the fuel control panel inside the aircraft to different tanks. I told him I was not comfortable doing that because it violated our SOP's. And I was not fully taught how to do this. Less than one month prior to this incident I remember an email being sent to all pilots asking us not to perform maintenance functions on the aircraft.The contract maintenance person was frustrated with me after I politely told him that I would not be able to comply with that request. I offered him my seat so that he could do it himself. The contract maintenance personnel moved roughly 1000 pounds from the right main wing tank to the left main wing tank and told me that the leak has stopped and that we were good to go. He became very frustrated with me when I told him that that doesn't comply with Company SOPs. And that we are not allowed to take off with a 1000 pound and balance between the wings. I also informed him that both main tanks had to be full of fuel before the center tank could be filled. The leak simply stopped because we moved gas away from the hole not that we did not actually solve the problem or find the source of the leak.After this diagnosis and attempt to fix the problem; I refused the aircraft and made a corresponding info item notation in theelectronic logic book. I had lost faith that this problem was gonna be solved to a satisfactory and safe nature and I elected that it would be best to remove myself from the situation. And not fly an unsafe aircraft.I then received a call from the chief pilot. The chief pilot did not give me their name and immediately became a line of questioning that seem to escalate and tone and speed; spinning a tighter and tighter web trying to find a fault in my story and trying to find a weakness in the narrative that I had told them. The told me not worry; the aircraft was actually fine and I was being overly cautious. I was told we had just been over fueled and it happens sometimes. For the record; I have almost 6;000 hours in this aircraft and that has never happened. I also informed them that we were at the correct few release number. This fuel release number is also not very large and it's very normal for this route and altitude.Their line of questioning seemed to invalidate my concerns for safety. Had I not been so confident in my judgment and prior experience; I could've easily been manipulated into making an unsafe decision that merely would've only benefited the company by moving an aircraft. This line and reasoning for questioning is very concerning to me. It seems unsafe; unprofessional; and against the norms that I had become to expect from Company.Thankfully; the first officer had taken a video of us finding the leak. I sent the video to a number that texted me saying that they were with the management team and they needed to talk to me immediately. I wanted to also let it be known that every contact attempt by the company did not include the dispatcher. I found that very concerning because any communication with the dispatcher is on a recorded line.I talked to a new maintenance control supervisor named Person A. He told me that the contract maintenance personnel also found a fuel leak coming from the fuel service panel on the right wing. Person A then asked me to perform more function checks on the aircraft. I told him I did not feel comfortable doing that. Although Person A seem frustrated; he did not seem frustrated with me. Merely just at the situation. I fully understand the inconvenience and impact this maintenance issue caused; but unfortunately the facts are undeniable. Taking an aircraft off the ground full of people that is leaking fuel is unsafe.A new contract maintenance personnel member came out to the aircraft approximately 2 1/2 hours after our initial report of the fuel leak at this point the leak had stopped; but we had lost approximately 400 pounds of fuel. The maintenance technician went to the flight deck; asked to sit in my seat and begin working with the fuel panel. The technician moved fuel from both wing tanks into the center tank and claimed that he had fixed the leak and that everything was good to go. I asked him how he fixed the leak and he said he had moved fuel from the wing tank to the center tank and you should be fine while both tanks were balanced. The center tank was grossly overloaded. This goes against Company standard operating procedure of fueling the wing tanks first then fueling the center. I asked if the hole and leak had been located and fixed he said no.Despite and obviously known outcome; I remained on duty to ensure that the maintenance situation was dealt with accordingly; I was fearful that another pilot would be given this aircraft with it fully not fixed and have an issue. At approximately XE:45 the dispatcher working my flight had called me and said 'hey; I am at shift change. I just wanted to call and see why things were and how things were going.'I informed him that nothing really changed. There is still a leak. There is fuel moved away from it; which is simply why it stopped leaking. I still don't fully understand how this is deemed a reliable and practical fix. I then told him for a third time I am still refusing the aircraft. I will not go into crew rest only to come back out to the airport and fly the same aircraft home if nothing had been fixed. I noted that I had said this for three times; and put it according info item in the electronic logbook hours ago. It was at that point we were finally released from duty given a min rest overnight and a new aircraft to fly home the following morning. Cause: Safety can at times be inconvenient; however should not cut corners to find a substandard resolution.

column121: During the pushback sequence from gate XX; engines 4 and 3 were started in accordance with approved company procedures. Ground handling personnel failed to adhere to standard operating procedures in several critical respects:-They did not issue any verbal instruction to the flight crew to set the parking brake prior to initiating disconnection of the tow bar and tug.-Without prior authorization from the Pilot in Command (PIC); and while engines 1 and 2 had not yet been started; they proceeded with disconnection of the towing equipment.With the parking brake unset and the nose wheel steering bypass pin installed (disabling hydraulic steering); as engines 4 and 3 stabilized at idle thrust; the aircraft began to move forward and yaw uncontrollably to the left.Ground personnel immediately shouted instructions to 'release the parking brake;' to which the PIC promptly responded; 'parking brake is released.' Shortly thereafter; ground personnel urgently directed the crew to 'set parking brake.' The PIC applied the brakes without hesitation upon observing the aircraft's forward and leftward movement.Despite the immediate brake application; the aircraft's residual momentum caused the nose landing gear to strike the tow bar; resulting in damage to the scissor link (torque link).Immediately following the incident; the flight crew overheard; via the interphone; the headset operator (ground personnel) state: 'I [expletive] up.'Upon return to the gate and subsequent opening of the aircraft door; the flight crew promptly disembarked to inspect the damage and assess the situation. The headset operator involved in the pushback was no longer present in the vicinity.The root cause of the incident was procedural non-compliance by ground handling personnel; specifically:Failure to follow the standard pushback sequence; including the omission of any instruction to the flight crew to set the parking brake.Initiation of towing equipment disconnection without clearance from the PIC.Premature disconnection attempt while two engines (1 and 2) remained unstarted.No injuries were reported.Suggestions: Reinforce ground personnel procedures and communications.
column123: After completing all ground checks on either; crew side and ground crew side; we started the push back procedure from gate XX in ZZZ; first by the broadcast where aircraft Y behind us was pushing back first. We meanwhile once cleared by the ground staff; pressurised the hydraulic and ran our before start checklist. After aircraft Y started taxiing; we then proceeded to make another call on the broadcast frequency and receiving no reply; determined it was safe for us to initiate the pushback. The ground crew initiated the pushback at XA:00. During the pushback; the PIC; using standard phraseology at all times; requested from the ground crew the authorisation to start engines; after an initial 'stanby by;' the clearance to start came while the aircraft was still in towing motion. While starting engine 3 and 4 on autostart; the plane came to a stop in what appeared to be an intermediate position; far from aligned with the taxiway 'aircraft offset on the left of the taxi lane with nose in by 20 to 30 degrees.' While monitoring the engine start; we heard nothing from the ground personnel nor any commands from them prompting us to think that the tow was still in progress to the final start stop 'E2 in that case.' The crew then felt a motion forward that would be similar to a tow then came again to a stop. Still awaiting any commands from the ground staff; we then finished to monitor engine 3 and 4 starts. The aircraft then sustained a mid to strong shake; again happening sometimes during a tow; came to a stop; to then a violent shock and a stop followed by a motion forward and yaw to the left.The ground personnel then eventually start talking ;shouting on the headset 'realease the brakes; release the brakes;' command that both startled us as not being able to have any idea of what was happening downstairs. Looking at the EICAS showing no 'parking brake set and the PIC feet that were not commanding any brakes; we asked the ground staff to confirm if he wanted the brakes to be set; where he simply yelled back "Brakes; brakes.'The PIC then set the parking brake and seeing the motion stopping; we realized that the ground personnel disconnected the equipment and the motion forward was induced by the engines and not commanded by the tug. During all that time; the mic of the ground staff remained open and we could eventually hear the staff on the headset verbally confirming 'I [expletive] up man; i [expletive] up' to his co-worker driving the tug. Following this; the ground supervisor came to take charge of the tow; assess the situation and tow us back to the gate. It is important to note that at this moment while we are still waiting in the cockpit to clearly understand what happened; that the towing personal in charge of the headset left the scene; and the tug and tow bar involved in the incident also were removed and swapped from the scene. After confirming damages to the NLDG; the new staff then proceeded to tow us safely back to the gate to asses damages. Notes : - After confirming that a report on their end will be completed; the ground supervisor 'who promised to come back with the involved staff;' never came back to the aircraft. - The crew nor the onboard mechanics; never had a chance to see the involved tow bar. - Nor the crew or the onboard mechanics had a chance to see or talk to the involved personal.Potential causing factors. - Lack of standardization from the ground personal using wrong phraseology in normal and under pressure situation. - Heavy breach of SOPs on the ground crew side that did not respect the standard actions and calls on the following :     - Never asked for the parking brake to be set nor confirmed or established communication about this subject with the flight crew.    - Initiated a disconnection of the tug and tow bar; during engine start while SOPs assert that a disconnection cannot be initiated without consent and positive contact from a flight crew member after the parking brakeis set and all engines are started and stabilized; with parking brake confirmed by the PIC 'verbally and on the EICAS' and visually confirmed by a light on the NLDG.    - Used under panic; incorrect terminology; making the situation worse.    - ultimately damaged the equipment by incorrect actions.It is important and fortunate to note in this situation that nobody on the ground got injured by what could have been; really fast; a life threatening situation and/or causing further damages to neighboring aircraft's or equipment. Reinforce the strict adherence to SOPs and sequences at all times and circumstances to mitigate potential risks. While it is impossible to judge at that precise time in the process; if a motion of the aircraft is provoked or unwanted; the only solution would have been a clear communication from the ground staff.Suggestions: Review and reinforcement of SOPs and safety procedures for all ground personnel during towing operations; with an emphasis given to the fact that flight crew on specific aircraft cannot see the ground crew operate."

At approving 15000-16000' we received the aural warning for cabin pressure and noticed the cabin pressure illuminating red indicating 10400' and holding maybe slowling increasing; we immediately requested a descent to 10000'; center gave us and initial descent to 13000' then followed by 10000'. The PM went to the QRC followed by the QRH to lookup the procedure. As PF I noticed the #1 & #2 packs closed advisory message on the EICAS; I looked to check if the buttons for the valves were in the closed position but they were in the open position. I asked the PM if he reset the #1 & #2 packs on the after takeoff flow since we did a TO-1 takeoff due to weather; and said they couldn't remember. I further noticed that none of the after takeoff flow/checklist was completed. We reset the #1 & #2 packs valves and the aircraft pressurized as designed with no further issues. Flight was continued as normal.
column123: We completed an immediate turnout after takeoff for thunderstorm avoidance. We were light and climbing at a higher than usual rate. Prior to level off at 5000 feet my FO disengaged the autopilot. I warned him that the level off was coming soon. He reduced the power slightly and pushed the nose down but not enough. I warned him again several times. As he shot through the altitude I got on the controls with him and we got the aircraft back on assigned altitude. The deviation exceeded 400 feet. Later while climbing through about 16;800 feet we received a cabin altitude warning as the cabin altitude exceeded 10;000 feet. We stopped our climb and received clearance back down to 10;000 feet. I changed from auto to manual pressurization mode. It did not correct the problem. We then noticed that the AC Packs were offline. we reset the packs and returned the pressurization system to auto mode. We we then able to resume our climb back to cruise altitude and continue as normal. Neither of us recalled seeing that the packs were offline on the EICAS when we received the altitude warning on the EICAS which one warning would have been one right on top of the other on the screen. However; it is possible that I missed it after takeoff. We did a TO-1 (max power) takeoff due to approaching storms which often kicks the packs offline.  I may have failed to complete the after takeoff checklist on initial departure as we were distracted by the weather avoidance and then the level off deviation. So it may have been a pack malfunction or it could have been missed on the after takeoff checklist. In any case once they were reset they performed normally."

The (pm) stated this is the wrong airport. Immediately at 1000 agl we executed a go around; began climbing and simultaneously-atc called us; announcing a low altitude warning which the atc's aural warning could be heard in the transmission. The PM announced to ATC we had lined up on the wrong airport. No landing at POC was executed. We continued climbing to 4000 msl and proceeded direct to ont without incident or further comment from atc.PIC relied on the PM statements and this action caused an inaccurate decision identifying the wrong airport.Corrective action would be to have distance of destination airport prominently displayed for situational awareness. Double check the PM by the PIC.Turbulence and forecasted windshear affected flight comfort.At the end of the previous day of flying certainly had affected the PIC. The actions of an irate and verbal abusive passenger was experienced by the PIC due to a customer service issue. column121: Immediately after executing a base leg turn from downwind for RWY XX; inside long downwind base traffic; at approximately 400-500ft AGL; I observed Helicopter final traffic to my immediate right; west of the field at approximately 300ft AGL.  Last I saw this traffic I was ahead of them and from my sight view there would be no traffic conflict caused by my early base turn to final.  I did not hear the helicopter traffic's base and final radio calls for the midfield grass area for landing; due to my passenger stepping on the radio call over Intercommunications Systems (ICS).My early turn to base/final; coupled with the missed radio calls created the potential for a midair collision between my aircraft and the helicopter final traffic. Early turns to final with potential conflicting traffic should be avoided at all times if traffic is not seen.  Additionally; no turn to base should be initiated until final traffic is clear.  It is better to avoid the early turn to final and extend the downwind than risk a potential for midair collision.Enhance lookout doctrine for traffic closer into to the field; especially helicopter traffic routinely operating at the field; not just the traffic you are attempting to turn inside of.  Additionally; avoid turns inside of other traffic; even if sufficient space is available.Brief the importance of a sterile cockpit for ICS communications with passengers to avoid blocked radio calls from other traffic; Emergency calls only.Even though in the landing phase minimize overflight of airport hangars and buildings.  To minimize risk for other personnel and equipment in the event of unexpected aircraft emergencies.

column121: During a private pilot training flight I guided the student over the Petaluma airport. I was monitoring the CTAF and verified there was no traffic in the area. I gave the student an engine failure and the student determined the Petaluma airport would be a good place to land. We entered a downwind for runway 29 and I made the appropriate radio call on the CTAF. I verified visually that there was no traffic in the area. The student was on a high and close downwind and turned base at 1300 feet MSL. The student determined that we were too high on the approach and we wouldn't make the field. I scanned the area to confirm no traffic was present and I took the flight controls. The altitude was 1100 feet. I started a right 360 turn to lose altitude. I verified we were not over any houses or people before performing the turn. While in the turn we lost more altitude then expected and exited on final around 500 feet. In the debrief I discussed that this maneuver was a nonstandard maneuver and shouldn't have been done unless we had actually had an engine failure. This maneuver could have been dangerous given how low we were. In the future I will advise students that the 360 could be an option but I won't demonstrate it at those altitudes. I got too low because I started the 360 from too low of an altitude initially. This discussion was caused by my fixation on demonstrating the importance of flying the aircraft; setting up for a good approach; and hitting your desired touchdown area under positive control during an emergency scenario. I also felt that the student had resignation over being high and I wanted to prove that there were still things we could do to get a positive outcome.
