Following this they asked the other aircraft (supposedly #2) to abort landing clearance and make and immediate left turn to 090. At this moment; that Aircraft Y came into view as it flew out from right under us; approximately 300 feet below. It's concerning that two planes were turned on base from opposite directions at the same time and that we did not have adequate spacing here. I believe the handoff from Approach to Tower created the problem and that Tower confused some of the planes since it was a busy afternoon with 4 aircraft in the pattern. In the future; pilots should not accept the base turn until the other traffic is in sight.

A radio call including approximate position; altitude; direction of flight; and type of maneuver to be performed was made approximately 50-60 seconds before occurrence. As the stall was about to become fully developed; a traffic conflict with another GA airplane heading Southeast was detected. I immediately assumed control of the aircraft and began the stall recovery procedure. The conflicting aircraft passed underneath; and the conflict was over at that point. I did not observe evasive action or alteration of flight path or altitude from the other aircraft. I find contributing human factors to be inadequate scan of the maneuver area; failure of other aircraft to announce position and intentions on relevant CTAF; distraction during observation of the learner pilot performing the maneuver leading to decayed traffic scan. It is worth mentioning that I did not have access to an ADS-B in receiver; which I believe would have provided an early warning of traffic conflict; which would have prevented the NMAC. ATC had also issued a traffic advisory to Aircraft Y calling traffic at their 6 o'clock low; Aircraft X overtaking; confirming awareness of the proximity of both aircraft. Climbing as cleared would have created an immediate collision hazard. I exercised my authority as PIC under 14 CFR 91.3 to maintain 1;000 feet MSL to ensure safe separation. I reported to ATC that I had traffic directly above me and requested an amended heading. ATC responded that my altitude was unacceptable and instructed me to climb immediately. I began climbing. ATC then issued a low altitude alert and instructed me to turn right to heading 300 immediately. Shortly after; ATC questioned why I was turning despite having just issued the heading change. I again reported I was avoiding traffic. The primary contributing factor was conflicting VFR traffic in the climb corridor during the VFR-to-IFR transition; combined with contradictory ATC instructions during the traffic avoidance. Improved traffic sequencing and coordination during VFR-to-IFR transitions at SQL could help prevent recurrence.

column121: The flight diverted to ZZZ1 due to increasing crosswind gusts at the destination and a developing fuel margin concern.During preflight planning; a threat-forward approach was used. The First Officer; dispatcher; and I evaluated the original flight plan; which had us landing near maximum gross weight with no alternate listed. Additionally; forecast gusts at the destination were near the aircraft's Flight Manual maximum crosswind limits. Given these conditions; we coordinated with dispatch to revise the plan to include a suitable alternate with improved margins. A thorough fuel and performance discussion was conducted during the approach briefing; including crosswind limits; landing performance with gust factors; and contingency planning should a go-around become necessary.The approach was conducted in high velocity; gusty crosswind conditions. The approach was primarily in IMC. Appropriate precautions were taken to balance gust additives with stopping distance considerations. The approach was turbulent; careful automation management was utilized to maximize pilot Situational Awareness. Below approximately 500 feet AGL; high crosswind gusts appeared to increase significantly and momentarily; requiring large control inputs; to maintain the desired flight path while remaining within stabilized approach criteria. During the flare; at approximately 20-10 feet AGL; with thrust just brought to idle; the aircraft encountered a strong sustained lateral gust that required substantial control inputs to maintain runway centerline. Simultaneously; the gust produced a noticeable performance increase; resulting in altitude gain of 20-30 feet. Based on recent performance training and anticipating the potential for an equally rapid loss of performance as the gust potentially subsided; along with the risk of airspeed decreasing below Lowest Selectable Speed; I immediately initiated a go-around. The gust began to subside and the aircraft did appear to momentarily descend.During the maneuver; careful attention was paid to pitch attitude to mitigate tail strike risk. Flap retraction and pitch changes were managed deliberately; ensuring a positive rate of climb prior to significant changes.Given that a possible go-around scenario had been thoroughly briefed in the context of our general fuel state; the wind conditions; and considering the largely IMC conditions associated with lower ceilings on the approach end of the field; the crew recognized that a second attempt (if unsuccessful) would introduce downstream fuel concerns. After coordinating and assessing the situation; we elected to divert to ZZZ1.The diversion was conducted in a smooth and controlled manner. The FOM diversion guide was utilized. Dispatch was notified. The crew was very efficient; having thoroughly discussed and prepared for this possibility during the threat forward departure and approach briefing. Threat forward briefings; and recent performance training were pillars in insuring a safe outcome. The diversion recovery guide was utilized upon landing. We departed ZZZ1 with additional fuel; and landed in ZZZ uneventfully.

column121: The crew of Aircraft X flight to MTJ descended from their cleared altitude after being cleared to fly the MTJ ILS 17 approach from GEJYU but before being established at GEJYU.This was the crew's first flight of the day; both pilots were well rested; and the approach was briefed; loaded; and checked in the flight computer.  The CA was flying and the FO was monitoring.  Conditions were VMC and the flight was under IFR control by Denver Center.  The crew had been working well together over the previous days and continued to after this event.On extended vectors after the previous aircraft had not canceled their clearance upon landing; Aircraft X was level at 14;000 feet to the north west of GEJYU flying direct to GEJYU when cleared the approach ILS 17.  Not expecting to be vectored as far north as they were; the crew had loaded the approach starting at MEYRS which included a crossing restriction at GEJYU of +12;300.  About 6NM prior to reaching GEJYU the crew initiated a descent to cross GEJYU at 12;300 in approach mode with 8100 selected in the altitude window.  About 3NM prior to GEJYU Center asked if the crew was established on the approach.  The CA matched the aircraft's course to the course on the approach plate and believed the aircraft to be within the RNP 1 bounds of the DIRDY to GEYJU leg and its lower +11;000 restriction.  The CA replied in the affirmative and confirmed that terrain was in sight; which the FO relayed to Center.  Center then directed the crew to maintain 14;000 until reaching GEJYU.  The crew immediately commanded a level-off passing 12;800 and was level at 12;500.  The CA momentarily selected a positive VSI to initiate a climb before canceling it as the plane neared GEJYU where a further descent would be required to fly the approach.  The approach and landing was conducted without event after GEJYU.After parking the aircraft the crew discussed the event and concluded that; even if the aircraft was on the DIRDY-GEJYU leg; the approach clearance began at GEJYU and so they should not have descended until crossing GEJYU (as required by FAR 121.659(a) and FOM.  Moreover; even if they had been cleared the approach from DIRDY; the flight computer was not loaded with DIRDY as the feeder fix so determining when established on the RNAV portion of the approach would be; at best; difficult and counter to the FOM which directs that RNAV procedures be selectable in the FMC and flown using autopilot or flight director guidance.  In heat of the moment; while monitoring area traffic at a non-towered airport; with the field and terrain well in sight the crew inadvertently got head of themselves did not comply the IFR established approach requirements.
column123: I was the First Officer (PM) for flight flying to MTJ; monitoring on both frequencies with Denver Center as well as monitoring CTAF Montrose Regional. There was at least one aircraft in the pattern at MTJ. At one point while flying Direct MEYRS for the ILS 17 at MTJ; another aircraft landed at MTJ and failed to cancel their IFR flight plan on the ground. ATC then gave a third aircraft; who was behind our flight into MTJ; holding instructions due to the non-canceled flight plan. Captain (PF) on our flight was on CTAF and contacted the aircraft on the ground and advised of the situation. Simultaneously; ATC gave us radar vectors due to the non-canceled flight plan. Aircraft on the ground then cued up on the radio and canceled IFR. ATC then provided us with additional radar vectors to return back onto the Approach. While on radar vectors for the Approach; ATC gave instructions to maintain 14;000 until GEJYU and cleared us for the Approach ILS 17. It was the afternoon on a clear VMC day. Captain (PF) called for 8;100 in the altitude box. I believe I then changed the altitude to 8;100. Captain then armed the Approach and we began our descent. ATC reports he received an altitude alert and asked if we were on the Approach. I did not understand the first part of what ATC said (I was still monitoring CTAF and the VFR traffic) and asked the Captain. Captain responded and said he (meaning ATC) got an altitude alert and tell him yes; we are on the Approach. I responded as such. Captain then immediately pulled for 0 VSI to stop the descent. I recall seeing our altitude at 12;800 when Captain pulled for 0 VSI. I believe we may have been 1nm prior to GEJYU at this time. ATC then asked do we have terrain in sight. Captain says; yes. I also had terrain in sight and reported 'in sight' to ATC. ATC then clears us for the Approach again. Passing GEJYU; the remainder of the Approach was uneventful and went as planned.

column121: After climbing through FL200 we were checking our systems pages and noticed there were xx in place of the volts reading for both generators. With Anti Ice on we received a bleed air 1 fault. We were able to reset the fault. Shortly after in cruise the Yaw damp 2 paddle tripped off and we were unable to reset it. Shortly after; the First Officer noticed his flight director had failed as well as some data on the PFD and ND. We came to the conclusion that it could be an ADC fault even though it was unannounced. He selected the FD and ADC switches on the switching panel to recover data. Having lost the ADC; we found we were unable RVSM and began a descent to FL270. During descent we heard a boom and looked at each other thinking it could be a load shift; however; the lower forward cargo door light came on as well as the Lower Forward Cargo Door ECAM message. We felt an irregular cabin pressure. We also received a pack 1 fault and Bleed air fault with the cargo door ECAM message. We donned our oxygen masks and requested priority handling and diverted to ZZZ where we landed uneventfully. We performed all required checklists and my decision was the cargo door was not safe. Per the checklist one of two choices; abnormal cabin rate; with accompanying door light confirmed diverting was the safest option.
column123: I was pilot monitoring during this flight.  As we climbed through FL200 we scanned the systems pages and noticed XX in place where the generator volts should read.  Shortly after we required anti-ice and got the #1 Air Bleed fault ECAM message and followed the checklist reseting the switch.  The fault reset and we continued to climb to FL300.  After level off we were no longer using anti-ice and got the #1 Air Bleed fault a second time and again it reset.  The FO then noticed multiple data missing on the Navigation Display and the Primary Flight Display.  The Captain took the radios while flying as the FO connected the dots of the data lost in the AOM to a possible Air Data Computer #2 fault that was not annunciated on ECAM.  Following the recommendations in the QRH the FO was able to get the Flight Director and ADC instruments back switching to the Captains side.  After discussion on RVSM compliance we notified ATC we were no longer compliant and were given a descent to FL270.  Around this time while descending and still working clean up on checklists we both heard a loud bang and immediately thought a possible load shift of cargo possible.  We noticed a shift in pressure in the cockpit and received a new message on ECAM for Lower Fwd Cabin Cargo Door open with an accompanying #1 Air Bleed fault and Pack #1 fault message.  The Captain maintained flying and the radios while the FO continued running checklists.  With the change in pressure we felt and confirmation from the sound we heard we donned oxygen masks; requested priority handling; and followed the checklist to descend to 10;000ft.  We were over ZZZ at the time and elected the safest course of action to divert into ZZZ.  The approach and landing into the airport was uneventful and we were met with the EMTs to confirm we didnt have any effects of decompression.

column121: Arriving in darkness after tower closed into ZZZ we were cleared for the RNAV Visual XXR as we requested direct ZZZZZ. This to avoid the no transgression upwind runway XX/R area. 2 things happened that could have been done better. We approached a bit fast for being under the Class B shelf of 5000 and this contributed to a steeper than normal descent rate to get down to at or above 4500 at ZZZZZ to establish on the glide path for the approach. Not exactly sure what transpired with the mode control as I was more concerned with being outside the aircraft for terrain and traffic avoidance and my co-pilot was flying. Additionally I was canceling with Approach; getting a phone number to contact them for clearance/cancellation on the ground and preparing to switch to  CTAF. My co-pilot was being proactive to get us down and capture the glide path and get us slowed down. At one point the descent angle and rate increased to a steeper than stabilized value which; to no surprise to both of us; activated the EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) SINK RATE; TOO LOW; PULL UP; to correct; which my co-pilot disconnected the Autopilot. We were still on the Downwind so we elected to continue the approach; which we completed without incident. However; with the APPR armed VNAV armed FMS showing captured we could not get a capture of the glidepath until 700 or so AGL. And we think this was also a contributing factor to why the plane did not arrest the rapid descent rate that set off the EGPWS previously. Again FMS was capture on the mode selector scoreboard; but perhaps we were not close enough to the course to capture the vertical guidance. Either way; VMC prevailed and there was never the perception that there was a CFIT risk. However we could have done better not to set off the EGPWS and that our speed may have been slightly above 200 under the class B at one point or another during the descent. And we were a bit confused as to why the plane did not capture the vertical guidance and why it steepened its descent rate right before the EGPWS warning.Suggestions: We will endeavor to approach ZZZ from the south at a slower speed for the Class B shelfs and to allow for more time to descend and capture. Additionally; we tried to adhere to the attention all users guidance to avoid the XXR/L Upwind. But I couldn't help thinking that it might have been better to track the course completely from ZZZZZ1 off the arrival and cut through this non transgression zone; especially since it was after tower was closed with little to no traffic. That way we could have been flying a prescribed course and altitude from the get go ; giving us more time to concentrate on configuring etc. As it was my primary focus was CFIT awareness given the fact that we were maneuvering visually to the direct ZZZZZ to avoid the no transgression zone. We were on frequency and the EGPWS occurred around XA:29. Incidentally we offered to to preposition earlier than scheduled during daylight and prior to the 3 hour sit in ZZZ; but we were backing up trips on the coast and it was determined best to wait to ferry from ZZZ to avoid possible double ferry legs.
column123: On Day 0 around XA:32 local time in Aircraft X we experienced a GPWS event where the PULL UP" command was annunciated. We were transitioning from the ZZZZZX arrival to the RNAV VISUAL XXR into ZZZ. We were instructed to depart the arrival structure and proceed direct to ZZZZZ waypoint on the RNAV VISUAL approach.  NAV with FMS; VNAV; APPROACH; along with AUTO THROTTLES and AUTOPILOT were armed.  When we were issued the direct to ZZZZZ; VERTICAL SPEED was added so that we could increase our rate of decent to be a little closer to the 4500' at ZZZZZ.  I recall the captain was on com2 when the instruction to fly direct ZZZZZ and cleared the visual approach was issued.  Lateral navigation and vertical navigation were stable; but as we approached ZZZZZ the aircraft increased its descent rate significantly.  I was monitoring the instruments trying understand what the avionics were trying to do.  The captain then indicated that I need to arrest the descent as to prevent a GWPS event; as I reached up to disconnect the autopilot and correct the pitch we got the PULL UP annunciation; and responded in kind; and the annunciation quickly went away.  We were in VMC and continued the downwind and approach via raw data and reference to the approach plate.  As we turned base I noticed the command bars on the Flight director were indicating an extreme pitch down and turn to the left.  Prior to departure from ZZZ1; we did a full departure and arrival brief with a focus on the "all users page" for the RNAV visual to XXR  and discussed FQOA concerns.  One of the biggest factors that lead to this event was my low experience in this aircraft.  Normally; when an aircraft responds in an unexpected expected manner I immediately disconnect the autopilot and hand fly; but in this case I wanted to gain insight to what the jet was doing in this situation.  The initial sensation of the event mimicked a configuration change from flaps 2 to full flaps and then progressed to a steeper descent.  There was no configuration change taking place.  Another contributing factor was speed.  We were in excess of 200 knots approaching ZZZZZ waypoint requiring a steeper descent; but not the rate which triggered the GPWS response.Also; when cleared to descend from our last assigned altitude to commence the approach; I just spun the Altitude select down to an arbitrary altitude; just to start the descent.  I will never do that again.  The Captain was on Com 2 when this happened.My main concern is; although I am aware that this can happen; I still do not know why this situation developed.Suggestions include improvements on my performance; which include slowing the aircraft down sooner; being proactively particular on setting the AAD in all situations; and quicker response to unexpected flight path situations."

column121: Taxiing on inner line to spot XX at CLT west ramp our clearance was spot XX to join the line to 5W. Approaching the spot I looked left and didn't see anything. We were slowing to make a right turn and the FO said clear right. I looked left to say clear left and saw a jet approaching which appeared close and I applied brakes. Firm at first then eased off. We sat at the spot for a minute and the jet pilot asked ramp controller what going on. Who was giving way and why weren't they notified. Ramp controller said that she didn't think the jet was going to turn the corner that fast and it wasn't going to be an issue. Well it was. The ramp controller told to Aircraft Y to give way to us and we proceeded to take off. I didn't call the cabin to see if everyone was ok. I thought they would call us if something was wrong. We flew to ZZZ without incident and had normal communications with the cabin. After shut down and leaving the flight deck a couple of F/A's asked what happened taxiing in CLT. When we got to the top of the bridge by the gate we told them what happened. The number 1 said she bumped her arm in the galley and the number 3 bumped her head. The number 2 said her back hit the galley wall. I asked why they didn't call us in CLT. They were preparing for takeoff was the answer I got. I asked if anyone needed medical attention and was told not yet. I called dispatch per the FOM for a follow up since everyone was able to preform their duties.Cause: Ramp control to give specific instructions as to who is following who. Communication from the cabin telling us they were injured before we depart. Not after completing the flight.
column123: When departing the west ramp from the gate in Charlotte we received instructions to taxi to spot XX; then join the line to 5W and contact ground. As we approached spot XX I looked out the right windows to make sure we were clear for the turn on to the line. After I said clear right" the captain applied the brakes as there was a jet coming from our left. The braking was firm but did not seem like it was an aggressive or instantaneous stop; especially as it appeared we were at an appropriate speed to begin the turn on to the line. There was confusion as to which aircraft was to proceed. The jet was first to ask; and ramp told the jet to let us go first; and ramp admitted that they didn't expect the jet to have caught up to us so quickly. We continued our taxi and the flight resumed as normal. Only after landing did the flight attendants ask about the firm braking in CLT; and then explained that the 1; 2; and 3 FAs had potential injuries. The captain asked if anyone needed medical attention; and none of the FAs said they did at that time. The FAs did not mention any issues or injuries during the flight; even during cruise communications to discuss en-route turbulence. Cause: If ramp had given instruction to either us or the jet to clarify which aircraft would be first then we could have avoided any confusion. The braking did not feel hard enough that I would have thought any injuries would have occurred; otherwise we would have called back to check if everyone was ok. It would have also been helpful to have had a call from the flight attendants if there were any concerns until waiting after landing."

column121: Flight was dispatched with MEL 24-XXX (inoperative IDG (Integrated Drive Generator)) configuration requiring use of APU during flight as a secondary electrical power source. Approx 120 West of ZZZ APU failed in flight. QRH requires land ASAP with one power source; several attempts to restart APU were unsuccessful. While discussing our diversion a ACARS was sent to our dispatcher to coordinate/discuss our intentions. After receiving an additional ECAM (ECAM IDG 1 OIL OVERHEAT) and noted IDG#1 temperature increasing; IDG#1 was disconnected per the second ECAM and we requested priority handling with the decision that we would be diverting to ZZZ. During the descent dispatch acknowledged our status and suggested a diversion to ZZZ but in the interest of safety (after the overheat msg) we decided to not fly further than required. A normal precautionary landing was made with a taxi to the gate. FO was the flying pilot and did an excellent job having the diversion airport/approach and a few ATC calls handled during time period I briefed the Flight Attendants and advised the passengers about our diversion; his efficiency was very much appreciated and he completely reduced my workload during a very short time frame from cruise at altitude to landing.
column123: We were dispatched that day with MEL 24-XXX which was an imperative #1 IDG (Integrated Drive Generator). Per the MEL we were able to depart with the APU continuously running to provide backup electrical power and generator. While in cruise flight at FL330 (max altitude per the MEL) and approx 120 miles west of ZZZ the APU  performed an auto shutdown. The FO announced my aircraft and took over radio communication with ATC while the CA ran the ECAM and subsequent QRH. The QRH led him to attempt a restart of the APU which was momentarily successful (less than a minute). The FO then began to look for nearest suitable airport to divert to per the QRH. At that time ZZZ was directly in front of the flight path and less than 200nm away. The FO asked for a decent to FL270 and was granted this by ATC whom was then notified by the FO that the flight was requesting priority handling and likely diverting to ZZZ. The CA agreed that was the nearest suitable airport and related this information to dispatch via ACARS message. At FL270 the CA attempted another APU restart which was unsuccessful. While descending out of FL240 a third and final APU restart attempt was made but unsuccessful. The FO continued to fly to ZZZ via new ATC clearance of direct and set up the MCDU (Multi-purpose Control Display Unit) for an ILS to runway XXR and entered the performance information for arriving at ZZZ. The CA made a call the inform the FAs of the diversion and made an announcement to the pax regarding the diversion. At this time the FO noticed IDG temperature of the #1 IDG began rising continuously until an ECAM message alerted the crew of IDG #1 OILOVRHEAT. The FO checked the reference sheet to ensure this was not a quick action item and not an ECAM exception. After verifying the ECAM was nether; he ran the ECAM procedures while conferring with the CA on each item. This led to a disconnection of IDG #1. After ECAM actions were complete a decent checklist was initiated by the CA and a normal precautionary landing was made at ZZZ runway XXR. We were able to taxi on our own power to the gate where we parked; shutdown; and all pax got off the aircraft for rebooking.Cause: APU failure caused our aircraft to be reduced to sickle stage electrical system. Increasing IDG temp on the #1 IDG resulted in ECAM that directed us to disconnect the #1 IDG. Mitigation suggestion would have been to shut down the APU whole on the ground in ZZZ1 to reduce its workload.

ATC then assigned us 180 knots. I acknowledged the clearance then got distracted by something. The FO slowed to 180 knots which was about 5 knots below flaps 1 maneuvering speed. column123: We were flying the ZZZZZ2 arrival from ZZZ. Prior to commencing the STAR; multiple ATIS updates indicated rain conditions at the airport.At approximately 12;000 FT; ATC began providing radar vectors and advised that two preceding aircraft had executed go-arounds due to wind shear. We were assigned a heading of 065°; which positioned us between two lines of weather. We subsequently received vectors to intercept the ILS for runway XXL.While descending through 8;000 FT; ATC instructed us to reduce speed to 200 knots. I had already requested Flaps 1 in anticipation of slowing below 220 knots. At that point; I observed significant airspeed fluctuations caused by a tailwind component in excess of 45 knots that continued to increase. I was required to make multiple vertical speed (V/S) interventions because the speed brakes alone were insufficient to achieve and maintain the assigned speed.ATC was delayed several times in issuing further descent clearances due to multiple aircraft ahead executing go-arounds; resulting in us being slightly high on the approach. When ATC subsequently directed a reduction to 180 knots; the airspeed oscillations remained pronounced; and the stick shaker activated for approximately one second. Flaps 5 were promptly selected; and the remainder of the approach was flown in accordance with standard operating procedures.The aircraft was landed safely on runway XXL despite the challenging weather conditions. No further anomalies were noted.I am submitting this report to document the event and support any safety review or analysis.

column123: On Day 0 at approximately XA00 we were operating flight XXXX ZZZ to ZZZ1. Maintenance had signed off the aircraft for an intermittent pax (Passenger) door indication written up by the previous crew. On the climb out we started to feel pressure that didn't seem normal and I asked my FO who was the pilot flying to reduce her climb. We were cleared to I believe 18;000 but at 10;000 we got the cabin alt" caution message. I advised ATC we needed to level off and we did at 10;000 feet. I took control of the aircraft and we ran the QRH for the "cabin alt". We advised ATC that we would be returning to ZZZ but we needed a few minutes to get ready. We entered a hold and ran all of our checks and briefings. Since we caught the issue early and didn't continue climbing; which would have created a bigger problem; we did not declare an emergency. Then we advised ATC we were ready to return to ZZZ where we landed without further incident. ATC did a great job handling us and my FO and FAs did terrific dealing with the situation. After maintenance corrected the issue several hours later we were able to board back up and complete the flight.Cause: The aircraft did not pressurize as it should have during climb out.Suggestion: After we returned to the gate the maintenance crew did a pressurization check. They saw the aircraft was not pressurizing. They corrected the issue after several hours."

column121: A routine instructional flight was being conducted to practice airwork and maneuvers in a multi-engine training aircraft. While maneuvering in an area of moderate turbulence; we experienced erratic RPM indications on the left engine. The tachometer rapidly fluctuated; momentarily indicating approximately 4000 RPM (overspeed) before dropping to zero RPM and then returning to a normal reading. The indications continued to fluctuate unpredictably. Simultaneously; the manifold pressure indication decreased to approximately 3 inches and fuel flow reduced significantly. At the time the anomaly first occurred; my student had the controls and the aircraft was in a bank while exiting moderate turbulence. Due to the turbulence and aircraft attitude; it was initially difficult to determine whether the aircraft itself was responding abnormally. Aurally; the engine did not sound significantly different from normal operation. I took control of the aircraft and began running the appropriate checklist procedures with the student. We verified each step and monitored engine indications. Due to the continued erratic indications and the possibility of an engine malfunction; I made the decision to secure the left engine. After completing the engine shutdown procedure; I contacted ZZZ Approach and advised them that we had secured the left engine and would be returning to ZZZ. An emergency was not declared. The aircraft was configured for single-engine operation and we conducted a precautionary return to the airport.The remainder of the flight was uneventful and we landed safely at ZZZ.

column123: Landed Runway 18; Tallahassee International Airport; at XA:21 on Day 0 in VFR conditions with slight mist forming in calm winds. Tower was closed as was Runway 9/27 per NOTAMs. Noted numerous vehicular warning lights at the approach end of Runway 09. Called the approach and exiting the runway on CTAF (118.7). Taxied to ramp; refueled and filed IFR flight plan utilizing Foreflight. Originally filed: ZZZZZ VXX ZZZ VXY ZZZZZ1. Foreflight notified that the flight plan had been alter to: ZZZZZ2 ZZZZZ3 TXXX ZZZZZ4 which I acknowledge and received notification that the later routing had been filed with an ETD of XB:30 and altitude of 11;000 MSL. Started aircraft and typed in my expected flight plan in my Garmin 430W and autopilot. Announced on CTAF that I was taxing from the ramp to Runway 18 and activated runway/taxiway lighting. Taxied via taxiway A11 then A to A1 - holding short of the runway in such a manner that I could clear taxiway A. Still calm winds and increasing mist - but could see the lit taxiway and runway lights to end. Accomplished engine runup and tried to contact clearance on 126.65 - was unsuccessful as tower was closed. Then attempted to contact Tallahassee Approach via phone as per the Chart Supplement at XA:23. This too was unsuccessful; Then tried to reach Jacksonville ARTCC - but failed as I had misdialed the number. I the dialed the FSS Clearance Delivery at - directed me to contact Jacksonville Center on 128.625. I attempted contact; but received no answer nor did I hear any radio traffic on that frequency. I again contacted FSS Clearance Delivery who instructed me to try again and then was able to hear radio traffic but had considerable trouble contacting the controller. The net result was that I was off the Tallahassee CTAF from XA:23 until XA:52 until I got my clearance. The clearance received was not that which Foreflight had said was filed. More scrambling to enter the data to this revision of my flight plan. I finally received clearance to take off at XA:56; called on CTAF that I was taking Runway 18 for takeoff; lined up and started rolling. After some 2500 plus feet of takeoff roll I noted white lights on the east side of the runway which I determined to be another aircraft back taxiing on Runway 18. These lights blended in with the runway lights and the lights at the approach end of Runway 09. There was insufficient time/space to do anything except maneuver to the west side to the runway - thereby avoiding a collision. I never heard any call from that aircraft - either before or after we passed each other.Being off the CTAF for some 30 minutes contributed to this almost mishap. During this time I probably missed the call from the other aircraft that he was taxiing - as he probably turned his radios on during that 30 minute period and; not hearing any conversation from me on the CTAF was not aware there was another aircraft moving on the airdrome. Possibly we both assumed we were the only aircraft active at TLH.I am not aware to the RCO situation at TLH; but it appeared that initially; no one was monitoring/transmitting through the local RCO until a second phone call from my cockpit got Jacksonville Center to start transmitting through whatever RCO was being used at THL. This might be an equipment or manning issue - and I am definitely not blameless in obtaining my clearance (though I have done it successfully many times before).Pilot controlled situations (like tower closed and with only CTAF to control aircraft actions with reduce visibility at night) demand the participating pilots adhere to set procedures. Back taxiing on a runway when a well lit taxiway is available to move to the number one position incurs additional; unnecessary risks. If the other aircraft had used taxiway A the entire conflict could have been avoided. If one is in a back taxi situation under pilot controlled conditions; one must monitor the CTAF for any unexpectedincursion or use of the runway. I never heard a call fromthe other aircraft when I announced my departure on Runway 18 nor when I passed close by the other aircraft. If the crew was using the back taxi to coordinate their departure - it was the wrong time.

column121: I was conducting a UAV flight to capture images of a residential property at Location X around XA00 hours on Day 0. The flight path remained directly over or in close proximity of the property's boundaries. Prior to the mission; I received LAANC approval to fly up to 100' (within the boundaries of ZZZ Class C airspace). I maintained an altitude below 100' during the duration of the flight; and was at approximately 70-80' directly over the structure when a battery alert began to annunciate. Knowing I had ample battery power to complete the mission; I chose to capture my last image prior to manually landing the aircraft. When the battery power reached a pre-determined level; the UAV software initiated an automatic 'return to home' sequence I was not expecting. At this time; the aircraft automatically began a rapid climb to begin the sequence. Knowing I was relatively close to the 100' approval ceiling; I manually overrode the sequence; which I had to accomplish twice within an approximately 15 second window. For approximately 2 seconds; the aircraft traveled up to approximately 112' before I could manually lower it; then again; for approximately 3 seconds; it traveled up to approximately 119' before I could manually lower it. It was at these maximum altitudes for approximately 1 second each prior to being manually flown lower; below the 100' approval ceiling. I landed the aircraft without further issue. No injuries or aircraft damage resulted from this incident. In the future; I will consider landing the aircraft prior to the initiation of the 'return to home' sequence; and will maintain increased situation awareness regarding the return to home sequence/ altitude and the aircraft's remaining battery power.

The CA told them everything was functioning normally and to let him know if they saw any other visual indications. The CA and I discussed the situation and determined it was most likely a single compressor stall on the number one engine and I began coordination with Air Traffic Control to return to ZZZ. The CA ran the Non Routine Landing Considerations Checklist in the QRH along with the Overweight Landing Checklist; which included sending a company message about the air interrupt and briefing the flight attendants on a precautionary landing. We were vectored for an ILS to XXC and requested thru ATC for ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) equipment to meet us after landing in order to inspect the aircraft. The approach and landing were uneventful and we cleared the runway with light braking due to our weight and stopped on the parallel taxiway to be inspected. No damage was noted and we then taxiied to the gate uneventfully. ZZZ ATC was great in helping coordinate our return and any assistance we needed.Cause: Unsure of the cause as it appears to be a mechanical issue. Of note it was a pretty quick return to ZZZ as we were only about 15-20 nm from the airport when the event happened. While we made everything happen that was required; in the future I would not hesitate to ask for extended vectors or holding if need be to make sure all checklists were complete. The weather was clear which helped us to maintain SA during the event. Of course this is situation dependent whether we need to get on the ground as soon as possible or have time. column121: Day 0 I was to perform a confined are landing in a field near the ZZZ airport and prior to the landing I did a site survey; walked off the the area from the tree line for rotor clearance on the left side and the front of the helicopter to ensure that I had rotor clearance on my blind side before doing the first landing. The tail section was clear of any obstacles and was not blocked. The tree line on my left side was my primary concern. I made a reference mark on the ground to place my right wheel. The video shot was to hover over the confined landing area and hold in a hover at approximately 100ft (AGL) and then descend vertically slowly to the target area mark for the right wheel. The winds were typical winds variable from the northeast at about 15kts with occasional gust to 25kts. Sky was clear and visibility was unlimited and no other aircraft was flying during this time. At approximately XA:15 I did the first landing without any problems; but from the inside the cockpit the pilots view from the right side looked closer than I was comfortable with; and decided to place my wheel chocks further to my right to provide more rotor clearance on my left blind side. The plan was still the same; lift straight up to 100ft(AGL)and hold for several minutes then descend vertically slowly to the wheel chock marker that we had moved to the right about 15 more feet. During the second second landing as I was slowly descending is when I heard heard the sound of the rotor blade tip caps hitting the tree branches; I immediately raised collective and moved farther away to my right before landing.Contributing factors:(1) Strong left Gusty Cross winds; and pilot not accounting for the leaning angle of the helicopter that changed the pilots visual reference to the landing marker; and in order for the pilot to see it he drifted to the left and had the rotor over the tree tops as he slowly descended; causing damaged to the tip caps. (2) Not having a safety ground crew person on the landing aera that would have better outside visual observations and a hand held radio to communicate with the pilot on rotor clearance; and to make corrections as needed. (3) Customer pressure pushing to get the job done in one shot. (4) Customer changed plan at the last minute from original location discussed a week prior to this new location causing the scope of work to change and making the crew become complacent in just trying to get the job done before dark.Action taken: what seemed to be a simple Photo / Video shoot became very complex with all of the last minute changes; and the should have been stopped; regroup with better weather conditions and a very clear plan for all involved with distances actually measured and verified by another person with an actual measuring device and not just walked off by the pilot. My stride was most likely shorter than usual from being distracted by the camera person and putting me closer to the tree line than expected. Preventative measures: A written plane of action and Tail board meeting will be conducted for all persons involved with more clearer directions besides the standard safety briefing; and other concerns such as the effects of weather; visibility; winds; rain; dust; obstacles will be addressed; discussed and documented with a collection of signatures. The physical distance from the tree line and gusty winds was the contributing factor on this incident.

column121: This is a general report on the overall safety and lack of basic upkeep at the WDR airport. We've for years had subpar equipment that has been tolerated and has been a contributing factor in past incidents that could have been fatal. It is a matter of time before there is an incident on field that could have been avoided.1) No wind reporting capabilities. The AWOS has been inoperative almost an entire year. Before that it reported winds unreliable" for years; but at least it was something. It's shielded by trees in a bad location. Suggest if there is ever a new one installed it is moved to another location. We often have 3 or even 4 aircraft on all runways making simultaneous approaches due to this lack of basic information that is critical to making an educated decision on which runway to use. Especially dangerous at night when the glitchy lighting (will get to that soon) doesn't illuminate the wind sock and pilots are flying on hope on windy nights.2) Runway lighting. Half the runway and taxi lights do not work. Obviously dangerous at night during surface movement. Runway lights only work at max brightness; which washes out the pilot's ability to see the pavement. No way for pilots to adjust. An extreme black hole effect is created in the round out. Results in hard landings more often than not from discussions with fellow pilots. Taxiway signs and runway signs have burned out; making runway incursions prevalent. The runway lights also pulsate. All these lighting issues have been reported to airport authorities with no resolution. The PAPIs do not work. We have obstacles that are unlit on the approach ends of 3 of the 4 runways and having no Visual Glide Slope Indicator (VGSI) combined with max brightness runway lights that affect vision is a disaster waiting to happen.3) Pavement/runway markings are not visible. Pressure washing or painting is long overdue. Every stripe or number in the touchdown zones are nearly black as opposed to white. Added to all the other issues; users of the airport are really being set up for failure and no one is listening. I'm fearful that someone will have a catastrophic accident before something is done."

column121: Just after takeoff; in light rime icing and IMC; I noticed we weren't climbing. We were at 2400 or so MSL and flaps/gear up; shortly after the after takeoff checklist was completed. It took me a minute to notice that we were right at clean maneuvering speed and not climbing because of focus elsewhere on multiple calls from ATC with climb and vector instructions. The CA disengaged the auto throttles and we manually set the appropriate climb N1. At this point; the aircraft resumed climbing and the bug jumped to 250 knots at the appropriate altitude. However; upon acceleration; the FD (Flight Director) began commanding an erroneous pitch attitude. While still hand flying; the captain followed the FD momentarily until quickly realizing following it would cause us to exceed the FMS speed of 250 knots. Because of this; we momentarily accelerated to around 270 knots (around 7-8000 MSL) until catching that the VNAV function was commanding an incorrect airspeed. The CA quickly returned to 250 knots then disregarded the FD vertical guidance until we got well above 10;000 MSL. When we got higher and above the bad weather; we tried to reengage the Auto throttle; but it started retarding the throttles again like it did earlier. Ultimately; we reset both flight directors and the auto throttle; which restored normal function to both systems. At that time; we engaged autopilot and the rest of the flight proceeded normally. ATC did not contact us about our momentary speed exceedance. During this entire event; LNAV guidance worked normally; so whatever the issue was ended up being isolated to the VNAV vertical guidance and the auto throttles.

column121: On Day 0 around XA:32 local time in Aircraft X we experienced a GPWS event where the PULL UP" command was annunciated. We were transitioning from the NTNDO1 arrival to the RNAV VISUAL 17R into HND. We were instructed to depart the arrival structure and proceed direct to HAFWA waypoint on the RNAV VISUAL approach.  NAV with FMS; VNAV; APPROACH; along with AUTO THROTTLES and AUTOPILOT were armed.  When we were issued the direct to HAFWA; VERTICAL SPEED was added so that we could increase our rate of decent to be a little closer to the 4500' at HAFWA.  I recall the captain was on com2 when the instruction to fly direct HAFWA and cleared the visual approach was issued.  Lateral navigation and vertical navigation were stable; but as we approached HAFWA the aircraft increased its descent rate significantly.  I was monitoring the instruments trying understand what the avionics were trying to do.  The captain then indicated that I need to arrest the descent as to prevent a GWPS event; as I reached up to disconnect the autopilot and correct the pitch we got the PULL UP annunciation; and responded in kind; and the annunciation quickly went away.  We were in VMC and continued the downwind and approach via raw data and reference to the approach plate.  As we turned base I noticed the command bars on the Flight director were indicating an extreme pitch down and turn to the left.  Prior to departure from KUDD; we did a full departure and arrival brief with a focus on the "all users page" for the RNAV visual to 17R  and discussed FQOA concerns.  One of the biggest factors that lead to this event was my low experience in this aircraft.  Normally; when an aircraft responds in an unexpected expected manner I immediately disconnect the autopilot and hand fly; but in this case I wanted to gain insight to what the jet was doing in this situation.  The initial sensation of the event mimicked a configuration change from flaps 2 to full flaps and then progressed to a steeper descent.  There was no configuration change taking place.  Another contributing factor was speed.  We were in excess of 200 knots approaching HAWFA waypoint requiring a steeper descent; but not the rate which triggered the GPWS response.Also; when cleared to descend from our last assigned altitude to commence the approach; I just spun the Altitude select down to an arbitrary altitude; just to start the descent.  I will never do that again. column121: Aircraft X was a ferry flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  It was the second ferry flight of the day.  CA and FO were only crew onboard.  From preflight; we had issues getting the actual fuel load on the jet updated by dispatch onto Performance Data and flight plan.  Taxiing out we exceeded our EDCT (Estimated Departure Clearance Time); because of delays in receiving a load close out.  Once we were ready; we were cleared for takeoff on runway XX and advised of arrival traffic.  Halfway through turn from taxiway to centerline of XX; tower advised traffic was short final.  As CA lined up on centerline; he called TOGA.  Aircraft then veered hard right as engines spooled up.  Between 30 and 40 knots; CA initiated a rejected TO: throttles idle; manual braking to a stop.  After full stop; we exited at 1 to the south of runway XX to evaluate.  On taxiway 2; we discussed the parameters of the reject; including no 'Thrust Set' call or RTO (Rejected Takeoff) braking; and brake temperatures.  We determined that asymmetric thrust during right turn onto runway led to asymmetric thrust during engine advancement to TO.  We decided to attempted a second static takeoff.  Second TO from runway XYL was normal and uneventful.  Flight concluded safely at ZZZ1.Cause: Minor coordination delays and then traffic calls from tower added to feeling of 'hurry up'.  While we did discuss mental status; ie 'being in the green';  this is a reminder at each break point in taxi/flight to take a deep breath and focus on the next event.Closer evaluation of throttle advancement to approximately 40 percent N1 and prioritize static takeoff; especially from maintenance base.Avoid using asymmetric thrust entering runway for takeoff.
column123: ZZZ - ZZZ1 Ferry flight to pick up a 787-8 being put back into service.  CA and FO only souls on aircraft.   During the first takeoff attempt on Rwy XX with a direct left crosswind; we were rushed to takeoff by tower because of an aircraft on short final.  Per SOP:  Rolling takeoff; lined up on runway; advanced throttles; checked EPR's; engaged TOGA.  Aircraft veered right as the left engine spooled up faster that the right.  At approximately 30 knots:  Idle; hard braking to an immediate stop.  Exited at 1 which is less than 500' into the takeoff roll.    Status at reject:  TOGA was selected; thrust set" did not occur; no RTO (Rejected Takeoff) braking.   Evaluated the aircraft: brake temperature and tire pressures remained normal.  Engines appeared normal.   I determined that it was either and engine issue or asymmetric thrust before the selection of TOGA; noting that I had been using differential power to turn on the smaller taxiways at ZZZ.  I may have had the left engine spooled up higher than the right; even though I remember checking the EPR's (Engine Pressure Ratio) before TOGA.  We decided to attempt another takeoff with a thorough run up before TOGA.  This second takeoff attempt was accomplished uneventfully and normally.  Proceeded to ZZZ1 uneventfully.Cause: Became rushed to get the takeoff completed before aircraft on final; with a clearance limit within 1 minute.  Using differential power to turn on smaller taxiways.  This technique may have carried over to my first rolling takeoff event.  Low time Captain on reserve with low experience in left seat."

column121: On Day 0; I was the First Officer for ZZZ- ZZZ1. I arrived at the airplane at about XA:20am; having taken the XA:00 am van from the hotel. After arriving at the airplane and putting my bags in the flight deck; I accomplished an origination flow; with the exception of first flight of the day items and went outside to do an exterior inspection. I completed the inspection; following the recommended inspection route; and I did not notice any damage. I returned to the flight deck; and completed first flight of the day items; having ensured that wheel chocks were in place. The Captain arrived shortly thereafter; and the flight proceeded normally without incident or any abnormal indications. On  Day 2; I received a voice mail from Person A asking me to call him back. When I did; he let me know that there was damage found on the #2 engine nacelle by the crew who was working the outbound leg after our arrival in ZZZ1. He also shared that he or someone reporting to him had looked back at the camera data in ZZZ; and found evidence that the damage was present on the ramp at ZZZ. He shared pictures of the damage with me by text.Cause: Causal factors include my failure to recognize the damage to the #2 Engine Nacelle. My recency of flight may have played a role; as this was my third day back on the line after 3 months of schoolhouse work as an IP (Flight Instructor). During the whole trip I was mindful to arrive early to each flight and give myself plenty of time to complete my duties as I knew it had been more than 3 months since I had flown the line. I went into this trip being especially mindful that I had not been around an airplane for a while; and tried especially hard to take my time and make sure that I wasn't missing anything. During the exterior inspections; I must not have looked closely enough at the aft part of the nacelle before I walked the right wing leading edge. I must have only been looking up as I inspected the leading edge and trailing edge; before walking behind the engine to inspect the right side landing gear and fuselage. I imagine that I walked right by the damage without ever seeing it on the aft portion of the nacelle while I was looking up to inspect the right wing trailing edge. My recommendation would be simply to be even more deliberate and observant during exterior inspections; and to carefully inspect the entirety of the engine nacelle and fuselage skin for damage on all sides.

column121: FO leg; at cruise; FL230; somewhere abeam ZZZ we received three simultaneous cautions:  HYD 2 LOW PRESS; ADS 1 FAIL; and AP FAIL.  My FO is now hand flying; and I'm grabbing the QRH for the hydraulic issue (top message).  By the time I'm at the hydraulic section; the HYD 2 message has disappeared; so I move to the ADS 1 fail message.  It basically says to make sure the ADS has reverted; which it did.  Next; AP (AutoPilot) FAIL... we tried unsuccessfully to re-engage the AP so no CAT II approaches.  ZZZ1  is VFR.  Now; out of curiosity; I circle back and check the HYD page to see what's going on there.  That's when I see amber dashes for the HYD SYS 2 pressure (see attached ).  After a discussion with my FO; we decide it would be best to treat this as if SYS 2 has no pressure.  First; we don't know if there is any pressure (we have a QTY indication) the flow lines are showing green.  It could be a faulty pressure sensor; but we can't rule out a faulty warning system because we initially got the warning; and then it disappeared.  We didn't want to assume everything was fine and find out on the ground that we were wrong; so we went with the HYD SYS 2 LOW PRESS procedure anyway.  Then we got a HYD 2 ELEC PUMP FAIL message (see attached).  Then we were led to the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 procedure and advising ATC.  I gave the FAs the information but I forgot to make the announcement to the passengers as we were on the arrival; and pretty busy with the QRH.  Somewhere on the approach; after we got through the Loss of Hydraulic System 2 Descent Checklist; I took the controls.  The gear extended normally; normal landing on XXR with what felt like normal braking; but as we slowed on the roll out I found that I had no steering.  I exited the high speed and came to stop on the taxiway.  I gave the passengers a brief explanation of what was going on; that we were going to be towed to the gate; and it could take some time for the tug to get out to us.  Our EICAS was now full of more messages and REMOTE CB TRIP that; I guess; had been inhibited in flight (see attached). We had multiple conversations with CFR (Crash Fire Rescue); Ground; and ops and eventually got towed to the gate.

The fire marshal inspected the aircraft and noted no visible fire or smoke. We could confirm that with the EGT decreasing. The fire marshal confirmed that at the time it was safe to taxi to the gate and that they would follow us. While I was coordinating with ATC and the fire marshal the first officer was coordinating with the purser and ZZZ operations. He also made a quick PA to the passengers. Operations confirmed what gate they wanted us at and we taxied to the gate uneventfully. It wasn't till after gate arrival that we heard we had what I'm assuming was a tailpipe fire. The fire marshal pulled some security video of flames coming out of the back of the engine. column121: -36 F initial engine startup manually due to a weak battery. Aircraft tires were chocked by pinching the tires with the hydraulically-operated snow skis. After manually starting the engine; and as the pilot entered the cabin door; the aircraft began to slowly move forward and caused the pilot to slip and fall next to the cabin door. The aircraft moving forward; the propeller contacted a snow berm. The engine continued to run after contacting the snow berm; and was shut down in the normal procedure. The problem arose from not using the aircraft parking brake. Contributing factors were the extremely cold temperature and un-willingness to use the normal parking brake and the extreme cold not allowing the pinching factor of the snow skis to deform the tires and provide braking action such as has been demonstrated in less-cold (warmer) temperatures. Additionally; the contributing factor of a weak battery due to extreme cold; and the necessity of manually starting the engine were significant.The pilot believes that manually starting an aircraft engine is not an abnormal operation; but understands that the perceptions of individuals who do not regularly perform this action will be significantly different. The ranking of contributing factors would be re-arranged by those individuals. Extreme cold; and a desire to perform a start-up; run-up; charging system check; and shutdown and engine blanket coverup in order to allow time for the engine compartment to 'heat soak' while the pilot enjoyed a warm mug of coffee are a very real human factor consideration. Thank You

column121: Whilst in the cruise at FL470 we encountered some fairly severe mountain wave activity.  This caused a loss of airspeed from M0.80 to M0.72 and with it a STALL WARNING; STICK SHAKER and Auto Pilot disconnect.The PF ( I ; as the PIC was on my crew rest); applied full power and reduced the pitch attitude of the aircraft and started a descent. The PM spoke to ZZZ ATC and requested an immediate descent. The stall warnings; almost immediately went to an over speed warning.  We eventually leveled at FL380 and away from the mountain wave activity settled down into the cruise once more.Whilst this was happening; I managed to get from crew rest and into a kneeled position between; the pilot's seats to observe what was happening. Immediately I was satisfied that we were not stalled; as it was the STALL WANRING and STICK SHAKER that had alerted me to the problem.  I could see that the pitch of the aircraft was at about 1 degree below the horizon with wings level and the power was at full.  The airspeed was showing above MMO (Maximum Mach Operating Speed)  and we were descend8ng at about 3;700ft per min.  I reassured the PF that his actions were correct and that we could now re-engage the autopilot and cruise at the lower level.  I returned to the galley and assured the Flight Attendant and when to talk to the passenger.  We landed at destination about two hours later; without incident.
column123: We were cruising at M.80 at FL450 in the vicinity of ZZZ VOR when we encountered some moderate turbulence. As this turbulence was forecasted at FL450 for the next hour; we asked the controller how the rides were at FL470. The controller asked the traffic passing by us in the opposite direction at FL470 and pilot reported the ride to be smooth. We chose to climb to FL470 hoping for a smoother ride. Once we reached FL470; it was smooth for about 5 minutes before we encountered the first mountain wave. It was relatively light with the usual gain/loss of airspeed ranging from M.76 to M.83 and very little turbulence associated with it. As we continued at FL470 at M.80 for a few more minutes in smooth air; we hit the second mountain wave which initially gave us an increase of about 100 feet in altitude; immediately followed by a sudden loss of airspeed from M.80 down to M.72 with a decreasing speed trend on the tape within a second or two. I immediately pushed the throttles full forward and grabbed the yoke. Realizing that a high altitude stall was imminent; I feel like I instinctively disconnected the autopilot and pushed forward on the yoke to initiate a stall recovery. I am not sure if my recovery or the 'stall' and shaker came first but we were immediately in a nose down attitude trying to recover from the high altitude stall.As we proceeded in the recovery procedure; the PNF reported the loss of altitude to ATC and he cleared us to a lower altitude; eventually clearing us all the way down FL300; noticing a rapid descent from our aircraft. During the recovery; I noticed that the speed tape was indicating red on both the high speed and low speed tape; indicating that we haven't recovered from the stall; even though we were most likely overspeeding the aircraft as well. Eventually; after a couple thousand feet of altitude loss; the red low speed tape cleared and we were able to gradually level the aircraft and gain positive control. By the time we fully recovered; we were at FL395. ATC informed us that FL380 would be a better altitude to continue the flight so we descended further down to FL380 and continued the last 2 hours of flight cruising at FL380 with no further incident.Due to the forecasted turbulence; about 10 minutes before the incident; we turned the seatbelt signs on and told the Flight Attendant to inform the passengers of possible turbulence and to stay seated and keep their seatbelts on; which they did. No injuries resulted from the rapid loss of altitude to either the crew or the passengers. One glass cup fell to the ground in the galley and broke but that was the only noticeable damage that resulted from the incident.Looking at PIREPs after the flight; it seems that several other aircraft encountered and reported similar or even worse Mountain Wave in the vicinity of the incident from FL400 up to FL470 with similar outcomes. Based on all the information; we believe that we used great CRM; excellent teamwork; and handled the situation the best we could with the best outcome possible.

column121: During climb to altitude on a route from ZZZ TO ZZZ1; at approximately 35000' we experienced a 'battery overheat warning' on our number two battery.  Both batteries are located at the back of the wheel wells.  The temperature rapidly increased beyond the top limit of a 160 degrees.  It quickly climbed to a peak reading of 197 degrees.  Due to the imminent risk of an uncontained thermal runaway and/or battery fire; I advised ATC; initiated an decent and requested vectors to the nearest airport (ZZZ2) for landing.  I also requested the fire services be on standby for the landing. The aircraft landed without incident.  Upon investigation it was found that the temperature sensor was faulty.  Due to the design of the aircraft there is no way to ascertain if it is a fault or potential fire; therefore the pilot has to assume the worst case and react accordingly. column121: Chain of EventsHow the Problem Arose / Contributing FactorsI am a CFII and was conducting instrument training at M54 while flying a practice RNAV (GPS) RWY 19 approach with a student. The airport was using Runway 01 for traffic pattern operations at the time. Our intention was to fly the RNAV 19 approach to LNAV minimums and perform a low approach while yielding to all traffic operating in the pattern.Throughout the approach; I made multiple CTAF position and intention reports advising traffic that we were conducting the RNAV 19 approach for a low approach only and that we would give way to all traffic in the pattern. I recall specifically making calls at approximately 9 NM; 6 NM; 4 NM; 2 NM; and again at approximately 1.5 NM final.At the time of the incident; there was only one aircraft in the traffic pattern; which was turning left base for Runway 01.While descending on a 1.5-mile final toward LNAV minimums; an aircraft identifying as Aircraft Y announced on CTAF that he intended to depart Runway 01 from the A1 intersection. Immediately after hearing that transmission; I announced that we were on a 1.5-mile final for the RNAV Runway 19 approach.The departing aircraft replied that he was 'rolling' and began the takeoff roll on Runway 01. The aircraft departed directly toward our position on opposite headings while we were established on final.From our perspective on final; the aircraft initially appeared to be a small single-engine aircraft. I did not recognize the aircraft type until after passing. After liftoff; the aircraft accelerated rapidly and continued climbing toward us.How the Problem Was DiscoveredThe conflict became apparent when the departing aircraft announced he was rolling for departure while we were already established on a 1.5-mile final for the RNAV 19 approach.Corrective ActionsAs the aircraft climbed toward our flight path; I initiated a right turn to ensure separation before resuming the runway course. The departing aircraft then began a right turn away from our position.At the closest point of approach; the aircraft appeared to pass approximately 200 feet below our altitude with an estimated 300-400 feet of horizontal separation.After passing; the departing pilot asked over CTAF why we were flying an opposite-direction RNAV approach while Runway 01 was in use. He further indicated that he believed we were flying the RNAV (GPS) 01 approach and that I was making calls for Runway 01 instead of Runway 19. I responded that multiple CTAF calls had been made advising traffic that we were flying the RNAV 19 approach as a low approach only.There were no injuries and no damage to either aircraft.Human Performance ConsiderationsPerceptions; Judgements; and DecisionsBased on the limited traffic in the pattern and the multiple CTAF advisories made during the approach; I assessed that the practice RNAV 19 approach could be conducted safely while yielding to traffic in the pattern.When the departing aircraft announced his intention to depart; I immediately transmitted our position on a 1.5-mile final. When the aircraft began climbing toward our flight path after departure; I determined that initiating a right turn would provide additional separation.Factors Affecting the Quality of Human PerformanceThis event occurred at a non-towered airport where aircraft were operating both in the traffic pattern and conducting a straight-in instrument training approach opposite the runway in use.The departing aircraft was Aircraft Y; which has high acceleration and climb performance. This reduced the time available to resolve the situation once the aircraft began its takeoff roll.Actions or InactionsMultiple CTAF calls were made throughout the approach advising traffic that we were conducting the RNAV 19 low approach. An additional call was made when the departing aircraft announced his departure.When the departing aircraft climbed toward our position; a right turn was initiated to ensure separation while continuing to monitor the aircraft's climb and trajectory.Note: After completing the final approach segment and the MAP; my student maneuvered our aircraft to the right; then back to the left. This movement was not the evasive action taken earlier during the final approach to runway 19.

column121: I was the PIC and pilot flying a Learjet LR-60 departing RWY XX at ZZZ. We obtained our IFR clearance via telephone from ZZZ Departure and were released for departure with instructions to climb and maintain 5;000 MSL. Weather at the airport was MVFR with strong gusting winds (270/G40+); snow flurries; and very cold temperatures (later determined to be approximately ISA -18). Based on the conditions; I anticipated entering IMC and encountering turbulence shortly after departure. My SIC and I conducted a thorough briefing of the takeoff and climb profile. I executed a crosswind takeoff on RWY XX without incident. After takeoff I established a climb at 250 KIAS. The SIC completed the after-takeoff checklist. Moderate turbulence was encountered shortly after departure.At approximately 2;500 MSL; just prior to entering IMC; I engaged the autopilot in heading mode (laterally) and level change (vertically) to continue the climb at 250 KIAS to the assigned altitude of 5;000 MSL. We entered solid IMC and continued climbing in moderate turbulence. Approaching the assigned altitude; I observed that the aircraft climb rate had increased to approximately 3;000-4;000 FPM and was continuing to increase. The increase in climb rate occurred without a corresponding pitch increase or thrust change; suggesting the aircraft had encountered strong vertical air movement. It became apparent that the autopilot would not capture the assigned altitude. I reduced thrust and disconnected the autopilot to manually level the aircraft. Although airspeed decreased as expected; the aircraft continued climbing at a significant rate. I reduced thrust to flight idle and lowered the pitch attitude; however; the aircraft continued to climb while the speed decreased to about 170 KIAS. The aircraft was experiencing moderate turbulence and control responses seemed atypical. I suspected a strong updraft or unstable air mass. Due to concern about imposing excessive negative-G loads on the aircraft structure; I elected not to force an abrupt level-off and instead allowed the aircraft to 'ride it out;' and stabilize. We subsequently exceeded the assigned altitude. The ZZZ Departure controller queried our status and I advised that we were 'correcting.' ATC then issued a climb to 8;000 MSL. At approximately 7;000 MSL the rate of climb began to decrease and the aircraft stabilized. I re-established a normal climb profile. As we approached 8;000 MSL I re-engaged the autopilot; however; the autopilot again failed to capture the altitude.  In retrospect I suspect this occurred because I engaged the auto pilot too close to the level off; not allowing sufficient time to capture. I again disconnected the autopilot and manually leveled the aircraft as we exited IMC into VMC on top. The aircraft leveled at approximately 8;500 MSL. ATC again queried our status and I advised that we appeared to be experiencing an autopilot issue and were working the problem. We were instructed to climb to 10;000 MSL and proceed on course and were then handed off to ARTCC. The ARTCC controller asked if we required assistance or had an emergency. We advised that we were not declaring an emergency and that the aircraft was under control. We were subsequently cleared to climb to 17;000 MSL. I hand-flew the aircraft to that altitude and leveled off.After completing the cruise checklist and confirming that all systems appeared normal; I re-engaged the autopilot. The autopilot then appeared to function normally for the remainder of the flight. Lessons Learned:  This event caused me to give serious consideration to the fact that; in conditions involving strong winds; turbulence; and cold temperatures; significant vertical air movement may be present even outside of convective activity. This highlighted the importance of more closely monitoring climb performance and autopilot modes before; during; and after altitude capture. If the aircraft energy state becomes excessive or automation behavior is unexpected; transitioning more promptly to manual control and managing the aircraft more conservatively would help prevent future altitude deviations or structural loading concerns.  The SIC and I debriefed this incident at length after the flight and discussed strategies for prevention of such occurrences in the future.

column121: On Day 0; in Aircraft X; I was the PF on an empty leg from ZZZ to MYAM. The initial plan was a visual approach to Runway 09 using the RNAV as a backup; as Runway 09 tends to be more commonly used runway at this airport. This airport does not report the weather; and we were unable to pick up any other nearby weather stations. Upon arrival in the area; traffic in the pattern was operating for Runway 27; so I asked the FO what the correct downwind is. He looked it up and found the correct pattern is left traffic for Runway 27. So we joined the correct downwind for Runway 27 to integrate with existing traffic and planned to fly a visual approach to Runway 27. We did load the RNAV approach for 27 into the FMS; but with the last minute change; we did not have time to brief it. There was a small plane in the pattern and I believe two other jets making callouts further away. On the downwind on the near side of the final approach fix; I disconnected the autopilot to fly the remainder of the approach manually; as there were people lining up and back-taxiing; and the timing required that we have a short base before the FAF.While turning onto final for Runway 27; we observed what appeared to be an aircraft positioned on the taxiway that looked as though it was holding short of the runway; as we had heard on the frequency that someone announced they were holding short. It appeared that the aircraft was waiting for traffic to land.As the approach continued; the runway and taxiway surfaces were difficult to distinguish due to very faint runway markings and the runway surface appearing slightly wet. At approximately 200 - 300 feet; we initiated a go-around due to the lack of complete certainty about the runway markings. The aircraft remained airborne during the entire maneuver and did not touch down at any point. While our go-around was in progress; and while we were on crosswind; another pilot in the sequence directly behind us transmitted on the radio asking which surface was the runway; specifically asking whether the runway was the one on the right or the left. We believed him to be joking and responded with; That's why we went around." He then responded; "No; seriously; I can't tell; is it the right or the left?" We responded that it was the left one; and he proceeded to sidestep and land on Runway 27. Shortly afterward; the third aircraft in the landing sequence (two aircraft behind us and a jet) landed on the taxiway.During our approach it became apparent that the runway markings were very faint; and with the runway surface wet the contrast between the runway and taxiway was reduced. One of the cues that helped clarify the situation was the ability to begin seeing yellow taxiway markings through the water; which helped distinguish the taxiway from the runway.After parking; we went to the airport office. We spoke with airport personnel as they initially believed the aircraft may have touched down based on the amount of fuselage visible above the surrounding tree/shrub line. We clarified to the airport manager that the aircraft did not touch the ground on go-around and that the go-around had been initiated at approximately 200 - 300 feet AGL.During the go-around and pattern activity; the aircraft immediately behind sidestepped and also went around; while the jet behind that ultimately landed on the taxiway. The only reason we were able to perform a go-around is because my FO was vigilant; and spoke up.The runway markings at MYAM appeared very faint; and with a wet surface the distinction between the runway and taxiway was reduced. Also the jet we believed was holding short when we began our approach was actually a disabled aircraft that had turned clear of Runway 09 at the end; and was positioned to look like it was holding short. Given the radio transmissions questioning runway identification and the report of an aircraft landing on the taxiway; the condition of the markings may contribute to runway and taxiway misidentification; particularly during busy traffic periods.We are lucky we went around and are safe; but this is clearly a problem if three aircraft in a row; two of which were operated by professional pilots; had mistaken a taxiway for a runway at an uncontrolled airport. This could have ended completely differently and tragically."

column121: Below is a summary of the unforeseen malfunction with the Autopilot/Trim that caused the pilot deviation while transporting 6 passengers to include infant today. This event occurred after takeoff on the initial climb out of ZZZ VFR. As I proceeded to climb to 1000ft under the Bravo shelf; I received a blinking Trim Error notification on the autopilot display panel and the plane began gradually porpoising. I followed the standard operating procedure by disconnecting the autopilot to reset the system. It worked initially; however; after 10-15 seconds and activating autopilot again; the Trim gave an error indication; once more; and the plane began an abrupt nose up pitch. After disconnecting the Autopilot again; in an attempt to recover the aircraft; the Trim wheel was still rolling aft and the plane kept increasing the rate of climb. I ran the system reset flow and recovered the aircraft after approximately 2-4min. While regaining full control of the aircraft by hand flying; I attempted to make contact with ZZZ App on XXX.X to inform them of my flight deviation; however due to the high volume of radio calls they were handling at the time because of severe weather; I never got a reply from ATC. After receiving no response; I switched frequencies and contacted ZZZ App XXY.XX to explain what had just occurred. This can be verified by the squawk code that I received to get VFR flight following. By this time; I was able to resolve the issue with the trim and eventually land the plane safely . After deplaning the passengers; I immediately contacted our lead mechanic to inform him about the event that had just occurred while in flight. I explained that this was my first time experiencing something like this and he recommended additional measures to take in the event that this ever happens again. I; in no way; had any intention of this happening and sincerely apologize for the deviation or possible inconvenience this may have caused. I pray this type of malfunction or incident does not occur again. Thank you for your time.
